module D = Datalog

type caps = < Cap.open_in; Cap.open_out; Cap.stdout; Cap.stderr; Cap.clock >

let usage = "usage: mini-datalog [-q query]... [-all] [-naive] [-j n] [-btree rel]... [-s] [-profile] file.dl...   (-h: how)"

(* -h: how, by an example *)
let help = {|usage: mini-datalog [-q query]... [-all] [-naive] [-j n] [-btree rel]... [-s] [-profile] file.dl...
Datalog: facts, and rules run until nothing new is found. A file's text is
Prolog's, without compound terms:
  edge(a, b). edge(b, c). edge(c, a). edge(c, d).     facts
  path(X, Y) :- edge(X, Y).                           rules: a path is an edge,
  path(X, Y) :- path(X, Z), edge(Z, Y).               or a path and an edge after it
  node(X) :- edge(X, _).   node(Y) :- edge(_, Y).
  apart(X, Y) :- node(X), node(Y), \+ path(X, Y).     a negation: no path from X to Y
  ?- path(a, X).                                      a query (or, on a line: path(a, X)?)
  mini-datalog graph.dl                  path(a,a). path(a,b). path(a,c). path(a,d).
  mini-datalog -q 'apart(d, X)' graph.dl apart(d,a). apart(d,b). apart(d,c). apart(d,d).
The files are read in order as one program (rules in one, facts in another),
then it is run, then each query of the files and each -q is answered: the
tuples that match, as facts, sorted. With no query, nothing is printed but by
-all: every tuple of every relation that has a rule.
A rule whose head is in its own body is no loop here, where it is one in
Prolog: path above is found whole, by any order of its rules and its atoms.
\+ p(...) (or not(p(...))) holds when no tuple matches; a relation is
computed whole before another negates it, and a negation through a recursion
is refused. = \= < > =< >= compare two values (numbers, then atoms).
-naive: every rule on every tuple each round (the definition; the default runs
a rule again only on what the last round found). -j n: n domains share a
rule's new tuples (OCaml 5's build; one elsewhere). -btree name/arity: that
relation sorted, in B-trees, as Souffle's, where the others are hashed (all:
every one). -s: the relations' sizes,
the rounds, the rules' firings. -profile: each rule's firings, new tuples,
lookups and seconds, the costliest first.
-dotnet [-o x.dll]: the files' rules compiled to a .NET assembly, Souffle's
way, and the queries; its facts are given when it runs (the program's
runtime beside it: datalog_rt.dll, mini-datalog's relations by mini-ml):
  mini-datalog -dotnet -o graph.dll -q 'path(a, X)' rules.dl
  dotnet graph.dll facts.dl              path(a,a). path(a,b). ...|}

let main (caps : < caps; .. >) (argv : string array) : int =
  let queries : string list ref = ref [] and files : string list ref = ref [] in
  let all = ref false and naive = ref false and stats = ref false and profile = ref false in
  let sorted : string list ref = ref [] in
  let dotnet = ref false and out = ref "" and runtime = ref "datalog_rt" and entry = ref "Datalog_rt" in
  let options =
    [ ("-q", Arg.String (fun (q : string) -> queries := q :: !queries), " a query: the tuples that match it");
      ("-all", Arg.Set all, " every tuple of every relation that has a rule");
      ("-naive", Arg.Set naive, " every rule on every tuple, each round");
      ("-j", Arg.Set_int Datalog_eval.jobs, " n domains share a rule's new tuples (OCaml 5's build)");
      ("-btree", Arg.String (fun (r : string) -> sorted := r :: !sorted), " name/arity: that relation sorted, in B-trees (all: every one)");
      ("-s", Arg.Set stats, " the relations' sizes, the rounds, the firings");
      ("-profile", Arg.Set profile, " each rule's firings, new tuples, lookups and seconds, the costliest first");
      ("-dotnet", Arg.Set dotnet, " the rules compiled to a .NET assembly, its facts given when it runs");
      ("-o", Arg.Set_string out, " -dotnet's assembly (the last file's name.dll)");
      ("-runtime", Arg.Set_string runtime, " -dotnet's runtime assembly (datalog_rt; mini-analyze's: analyze_rt)");
      ("-entry", Arg.Set_string entry, " -dotnet's entry, its runtime's class whose main runs it (Datalog_rt)") ] in
  match Arg.parse_argv argv options (fun (f : string) -> files := f :: !files) usage with
  | exception Arg.Help _ -> Console.print caps (help ^ "\n"); 0
  | exception Arg.Bad msg -> Console.eprint caps msg; 1
  | () -> (
      let p = D.create () in
      p.sorted <- !sorted;
      if !profile then Datalog_eval.clock := CapSys.time caps;
      try
        if !files = [] then failwith usage;
        List.iter
          (fun (f : string) ->
            let path : Fpath.t = match FS.path f with Ok path -> path | Error msg -> failwith msg in
            (* (Plan 9's error is the file's name alone) *)
            let text = try FS.read caps path with Sys_error msg -> failwith (if msg = f then f ^ ": cannot be read" else msg) in
            D.load p ~from:f text)
          (List.rev !files);
        let asked = List.map (D.query p) (List.rev !queries) in
        if !dotnet then begin
          let path (f : string) = match FS.path f with Ok p -> p | Error msg -> failwith msg in
          let out = if !out <> "" then path !out else Fpath.set_ext ".dll" (Fpath.base (path (List.hd !files))) in
          let name = Fpath.to_string (Fpath.rem_ext (Fpath.base out)) in
          let texts = List.map (fun (f : string) -> (f, FS.read caps (path f))) (List.rev !files) in
          FS.write caps out (Compile_il.assembly (!runtime, !entry) name p texts (List.rev !queries));
          FS.write caps (Fpath.set_ext ".runtimeconfig.json" out) Writer.runtime_config;
          raise Exit
        end;
        (* a relation that is read and never written: a name mistyped, most often *)
        Hashtbl.iter
          (fun (_ : string) (r : D.relation) ->
            if r.rules = 0 && r.given = 0 then
              Console.eprint caps (Printf.sprintf "warning: %s/%d has no fact and no rule\n" r.name r.arity))
          p.relations;
        let st = Datalog_eval.run ~naive:!naive p in
        let relations : D.relation list =
          List.sort
            (fun (a : D.relation) (b : D.relation) -> compare (a.name, a.arity) (b.name, b.arity))
            (Hashtbl.fold (fun (_ : string) (r : D.relation) (acc : D.relation list) -> r :: acc) p.relations []) in
        if !all then
          List.iter
            (fun (r : D.relation) ->
              if r.rules > 0 then
                List.iter
                  (fun (line : string) -> Console.print caps (line ^ "\n"))
                  (* (rev_map: List.map of millions of tuples overflowed
                   * the stack of 4.14's and of mini-ml's builds) *)
                  (List.sort String.compare (List.rev_map (D.show p r) (D.tuples r))))
            relations;
        List.iter
          (fun (q : D.query) -> List.iter (fun (line : string) -> Console.print caps (line ^ "\n")) (Datalog_eval.answers p q))
          (List.rev p.queries @ asked);
        flush (Console.stdout caps);
        if !stats then begin
          List.iter
            (fun (r : D.relation) ->
              Console.eprint caps
                (Printf.sprintf "%-32s %8d tuples, %d given, %d rules, stratum %d\n" (Printf.sprintf "%s/%d" r.name r.arity) r.count
                   r.given r.rules r.stratum))
            relations;
          Console.eprint caps
            (Printf.sprintf "%d rounds, %d firings, %d new tuples, %d lookups, %d symbols\n" st.rounds st.firings st.derived st.lookups
               p.nsymbols)
        end;
        if !profile then
          List.iter
            (fun ((rule, c) : D.rule * Datalog_eval.cost) ->
              Console.eprint caps
                (Printf.sprintf "%6.2fs %10d firings %9d new %10d lookups  %s (%s/%d)\n" c.seconds c.fired c.added c.looked rule.at
                   rule.head.rel.name rule.head.rel.arity))
            (List.sort
               (fun ((_, a) : D.rule * Datalog_eval.cost) ((_, b) : D.rule * Datalog_eval.cost) -> compare b.seconds a.seconds)
               st.profile);
        0
      with
      | Exit -> 0
      | D.Error (msg, at) -> Console.eprint caps (Printf.sprintf "%s: %s\n" at msg); 1
      | Failure msg | Sys_error msg -> Console.eprint caps (msg ^ "\n"); 1)

4329
(* mini-datalog: Datalog (docs/plans/plan_prolog.md) on a terminal:
 * files of facts and rules, run to their fixpoint, queries answered.
 * Its usage: [help] in CLI.ml, what mini-datalog -h prints.
 *
 *     edge(a, b). edge(b, c). edge(c, a). edge(c, d).     facts
 *     path(X, Y) :- edge(X, Y).                           rules
 *     path(X, Y) :- path(X, Z), edge(Z, Y).
 *     node(X) :- edge(X, _).   node(Y) :- edge(_, Y).
 *     apart(X, Y) :- node(X), node(Y), \+ path(X, Y).
 *
 *     mini-datalog -q 'path(a, X)' graph.dl
 *         path(a,a). path(a,b). path(a,c). path(a,d).
 *     mini-datalog -q 'apart(d, X)' graph.dl
 *         apart(d,a). apart(d,b). apart(d,c). apart(d,d).
 *
 * The text is a Prolog program's and mini-prolog would read it, and
 * not end: asked path(a, X), its second rule calls path again before
 * anything else, for ever; with that rule turned round it goes round
 * the cycle a b c and gives the same answers again without end.
 * Prolog goes from the question down, one way at a time. Here the
 * question comes last: the facts are put in tables, every rule adds
 * what it can to them until a whole round adds nothing (12 paths,
 * here), and a query is then a look in a table. No
 * term is ever made, only constants moved about, so the tables are
 * finite and it always ends; nothing is found twice; and the order of
 * the rules, or of a body's atoms, changes the time and no answer.
 *
 *     the files                  Prolog_read (mini-prolog's reader)
 *        | Datalog         facts, rules and queries checked (safe?)
 *     Datalog.t            relations: tables of tuples of symbols
 *        | Datalog_eval    the strata, then rounds to the fixpoint
 *     the tables full  --- answers: the tuples a query matches
 *
 * In ix it is the language program analyses are written in. A
 * compiler's front end writes a program out as facts (mini-analyze
 * -facts and -flow, C's and ML's), and an analysis is a file of rules
 * (analyzers/datalog/): Andersen's pointer analysis in 15, liveness in three,
 * the dominators, who calls whom. A dataflow analysis is a fixpoint
 * over a program's graph, which is what a compiler's own pass
 * computes with a worklist (mini-cc's Opti, mini-ml's Alloc): the
 * tests run both and ask, in Datalog, for the tuples one has and the
 * other has not.
 *
 * cs-history:
 * Datalog is Prolog seen from the databases: a fact is a row, a
 * predicate a table, a rule a view, and a rule that names itself the
 * recursive query SQL then lacked (the paths of a graph, the parts
 * of a part). It came of the meetings on logic and data bases that
 * Herve Gallaire and Jack Minker began at Toulouse in 1977. What a
 * program means was settled before: Maarten van Emden and Robert
 * Kowalski (1976) showed that the facts that follow from a set of
 * clauses are the least set closed under the rules, reached by
 * applying them from nothing. Prolog computes that set from the top
 * and may not end; Datalog computes it as it is defined.
 *
 * comeback:
 * The deductive databases of the 1980s found no market, and SQL took
 * the idea in as its recursive queries (WITH RECURSIVE, SQL:1999).
 * Datalog came back from another side in the 2000s: a points-to
 * analysis of a large Java program is a few recursive rules over
 * millions of facts, and saying it as rules, with an engine made for
 * such joins, beat writing it by hand: bddbddb (John Whaley and
 * Monica Lam, 2004), Doop (Martin Bravenboer and Yannis Smaragdakis,
 * 2009), Souffle, and the query language of CodeQL.
 *
 * References: Stefano Ceri, Georg Gottlob and Letizia Tanca, "What
 * You Always Wanted to Know About Datalog (And Never Dared to Ask)"
 * (IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering, 1989): the
 * survey to read first; M. H. van Emden and R. A. Kowalski, "The
 * Semantics of Predicate Logic as a Programming Language" (Journal of
 * the ACM, 1976); Lars Ole Andersen, "Program Analysis and
 * Specialization for the C Programming Language" (DIKU, 1994), the
 * pointer analysis; Martin Bravenboer and Yannis Smaragdakis,
 * "Strictly Declarative Specification of Sophisticated Points-to
 * Analyses" (OOPSLA, 2009). *)

type caps = < Cap.open_in; Cap.open_out; Cap.stdout; Cap.stderr; Cap.clock >

val main : < caps; .. > -> string array -> int

(* See Datalog.mli *)

module P = Prolog

type arg = Const of int | Slot of int | Any

type relation = {
  name : string;
  arity : int;
  set : Relset.t;
  mutable rows : int array;
  mutable count : int;
  mutable indexes : (int * Index.t) list;
  mutable delta_from : int;
  mutable delta_to : int;
  mutable stratum : int;
  mutable given : int;
  mutable rules : int;
}

type atom = { rel : relation; args : arg array }
type literal = Pos of atom | Neg of atom | Cmp of string * arg * arg
type rule = { head : atom; body : literal list; slots : int; at : string }
type query = { goal : atom; names : string array }

type t = {
  symbols : (string, int) Hashtbl.t;
  mutable terms : P.term array;
  mutable nsymbols : int;
  relations : (string, relation) Hashtbl.t;
  mutable rule_list : rule list;
  mutable queries : query list;
  mutable sorted : string list;
}

exception Error of string * string

let create () : t =
  { symbols = Hashtbl.create 1021; terms = Array.make 256 P.nil; nsymbols = 0; relations = Hashtbl.create 61; rule_list = []; queries = []; sorted = [] }

let ops : P.ops = P.default_ops ()
let text_of (t : P.term) : string = P.to_string ops ~quoted:true t

let symbol (p : t) (t : P.term) : int =
  let key = text_of t in
  match Hashtbl.find_opt p.symbols key with
  | Some k -> k
  | None ->
      let k = p.nsymbols in
      if k >= Array.length p.terms then begin
        let larger = Array.make (2 * k) P.nil in
        Array.blit p.terms 0 larger 0 k;
        p.terms <- larger
      end;
      p.terms.(k) <- t;
      p.nsymbols <- k + 1;
      Hashtbl.add p.symbols key k;
      k

let relation (p : t) (name : string) (arity : int) : relation =
  let key = name ^ "/" ^ string_of_int arity in
  match Hashtbl.find_opt p.relations key with
  | Some r -> r
  | None ->
      let r : relation =
        let sorted = List.mem key p.sorted || List.mem "all" p.sorted in
        { name; arity; set = Relset.create ~sorted arity; rows = Array.make (16 * arity) 0; count = 0; indexes = []; delta_from = 0; delta_to = 0; stratum = 0; given = 0; rules = 0 } in
      Hashtbl.add p.relations key r;
      r

let text (p : t) (k : int) : string = text_of p.terms.(k)

let show (p : t) (r : relation) (tuple : int array) : string =
  if r.arity = 0 then P.atom_text true r.name ^ "."
  else
    P.atom_text true r.name ^ "("
    ^ String.concat "," (List.map (fun (k : int) -> text_of p.terms.(k)) (Array.to_list tuple))
    ^ ")."

let get (r : relation) (i : int) (j : int) : int = r.rows.((i * r.arity) + j)

(* an index's key: the values of the mask's columns, in order *)
let columns (arity : int) (mask : int) : int array =
  let cols = ref [] in
  for i = arity - 1 downto 0 do
    if mask land (1 lsl i) <> 0 then cols := i :: !cols
  done;
  Array.of_list !cols

let append (r : relation) (tuple : int array) : int =
  let id = r.count and n = r.arity in
  if (id + 1) * n > Array.length r.rows then begin
    let larger = Array.make (2 * (id + 1) * n) 0 in
    for i = 0 to (id * n) - 1 do
      larger.(i) <- r.rows.(i)
    done;
    r.rows <- larger
  end;
  (* (loops, not Array.blit: into an array of the major heap, 4.14's
   * passes each value through the collector's barrier, not knowing
   * they are integers: Btree's move) *)
  for i = 0 to n - 1 do
    r.rows.((id * n) + i) <- tuple.(i)
  done;
  r.count <- id + 1;
  id

let add (r : relation) (tuple : int array) : bool =
  if not (Relset.add r.set tuple) then false
  else begin
    let id = append r tuple in
    (* (old: Index.add index (fun c -> tuple.(c)) id, a closure each) *)
    List.iter (fun ((_, index) : int * Index.t) -> Index.add_array index tuple id) r.indexes;
    true
  end

let tuples (r : relation) : int array list =
  let all = ref [] in
  for i = 0 to r.count - 1 do
    all := Array.sub r.rows (i * r.arity) r.arity :: !all
  done;
  !all

(*****************************************************************************)
(* A text read *)
(*****************************************************************************)

(* a rule's variables: each its slot; _ has none *)
type scope = { mutable slots_of : (int * int) list; mutable names_of : (int * string) list }

let rec conjuncts (t : P.term) : P.term list =
  match P.deref t with
  | P.Struct (",", [ a; b ]) -> conjuncts a @ conjuncts b
  | t -> [ t ]

let comparisons : string list = [ "="; "\\="; "=="; "\\=="; "<"; ">"; "=<"; ">=" ]

(* [named]: the variables the reader has a name for (not _) *)
let arg_of (p : t) (scope : scope) (named : (string * P.term) list) (at : string) (t : P.term) : arg =
  match P.deref t with
  | P.Var v -> (
      match List.assoc_opt v.id scope.slots_of with
      | Some k -> Slot k
      | None ->
          let name : string option =
            List.fold_left
              (fun (found : string option) ((name, t') : string * P.term) ->
                match P.deref t' with P.Var v' when v'.id = v.id -> Some name | _ -> found)
              None named in
          (match name with
           | None -> Any
           | Some name ->
               let k = List.length scope.slots_of in
               scope.slots_of <- (v.id, k) :: scope.slots_of;
               scope.names_of <- (k, name) :: scope.names_of;
               Slot k))
  | (P.Atom _ | P.Int _) as t -> Const (symbol p t)
  | t -> raise (Error ("a compound term is not Datalog's: " ^ text_of t, at))

let atom_of (p : t) (scope : scope) (named : (string * P.term) list) (at : string) (t : P.term) : atom =
  match P.deref t with
  | P.Atom name -> { rel = relation p name 0; args = [||] }
  | P.Struct (name, args) ->
      { rel = relation p name (List.length args); args = Array.of_list (List.map (arg_of p scope named at) args) }
  | t -> raise (Error ("an atom is expected, not " ^ text_of t, at))

let literal_of (p : t) (scope : scope) (named : (string * P.term) list) (at : string) (t : P.term) : literal =
  match P.deref t with
  | P.Struct (("\\+" | "not"), [ a ]) -> Neg (atom_of p scope named at a)
  | P.Struct (op, [ a; b ]) when List.mem op comparisons -> Cmp (op, arg_of p scope named at a, arg_of p scope named at b)
  | t -> Pos (atom_of p scope named at t)

let slots_in (a : atom) : int list =
  Array.fold_left (fun (acc : int list) (x : arg) -> match x with Slot k -> k :: acc | _ -> acc) [] a.args

let clause (p : t) (named : (string * P.term) list) (at : string) (t : P.term) : unit =
  let scope : scope = { slots_of = []; names_of = [] } in
  let names () : string array =
    Array.init (List.length scope.slots_of) (fun (k : int) -> List.assoc k scope.names_of) in
  match P.deref t with
  | P.Struct ((":-" | "?-"), [ goal ]) ->
      (* (a query's _ is a column not asked for: a slot with no name) *)
      let goal = atom_of p scope named at goal in
      let n = ref (List.length scope.slots_of) in
      let args = Array.map (fun (x : arg) -> match x with Any -> incr n; Slot (!n - 1) | x -> x) goal.args in
      let names = Array.append (names ()) (Array.make (!n - List.length scope.slots_of) "_") in
      p.queries <- { goal = { rel = goal.rel; args }; names } :: p.queries
  | P.Struct (":-", [ head; body ]) ->
      (* the positive atoms first: they are what gives a variable its slot *)
      let lits = List.map (fun (b : P.term) -> (b, literal_of p scope named at b)) (conjuncts body) in
      let positive : int list =
        List.concat_map (fun ((_, l) : P.term * literal) -> match l with Pos a -> slots_in a | _ -> []) lits in
      let safe (what : string) (x : arg) : unit =
        match x with
        | Slot k when not (List.mem k positive) ->
            raise (Error (Printf.sprintf "the variable %s of %s is in no positive atom of the body" (List.assoc k scope.names_of) what, at))
        | Any when what <> "a negation" -> raise (Error ("_ in " ^ what, at))
        | _ -> () in
      List.iter
        (fun ((_, l) : P.term * literal) ->
          match l with
          | Pos _ -> ()
          | Neg a -> Array.iter (safe "a negation") a.args
          | Cmp (_, x, y) -> safe "a comparison" x; safe "a comparison" y)
        lits;
      let head = atom_of p scope named at head in
      Array.iter (safe "the head") head.args;
      head.rel.rules <- head.rel.rules + 1;
      p.rule_list <- { head; body = List.map snd lits; slots = List.length scope.slots_of; at } :: p.rule_list
  | t ->
      let fact = atom_of p scope named at t in
      let tuple =
        Array.map
          (fun (x : arg) -> match x with Const k -> k | _ -> raise (Error ("a fact with a variable: " ^ text_of t, at)))
          fact.args in
      fact.rel.given <- fact.rel.given + 1;
      ignore (add fact.rel tuple)

(* the author's files' way: a line ended by ? is a query *)
let questions (text : string) : string =
  let line (l : string) : string =
    let code : string = match String.index_opt l '%' with Some i -> String.sub l 0 i | None -> l in
    let code = String.trim code in
    let n = String.length code in
    if n > 1 && code.[n - 1] = '?' && not (n > 2 && code.[0] = '?' && code.[1] = '-') then "?- " ^ String.sub code 0 (n - 1) ^ " ." else l in
  (* (rev_map: List.map's stack is a frame a line, a file of facts many) *)
  String.concat "\n" (List.rev (List.rev_map line (String.split_on_char '\n' text)))

let load (p : t) ~(from : string) (text : string) : unit =
  let place (line : int) : string = from ^ ":" ^ string_of_int line in
  let text = questions text in
  let r = Prolog_read.make ops text in
  (* a place's line, counted on from the last one asked (each clause
   * asks: from the text's start each time, a file of facts was read in
   * the square of its size) *)
  let last = ref 0 and lines = ref 1 in
  let line (pos : int) : int =
    let pos = min pos (String.length text) in
    for i = !last to pos - 1 do
      if text.[i] = '\n' then incr lines
    done;
    if pos > !last then last := pos;
    !lines in
  let stop = ref false in
  while not !stop do
    match Prolog_read.next r with
    | None -> stop := true
    | exception Prolog_read.Error (msg, pos) -> raise (Error (msg, place (line pos)))
    | Some (t, named) -> clause p named (place (line (Prolog_read.position r))) t
  done

let query (p : t) (text : string) : query =
  let before = p.queries in
  load p ~from:"-q" ("?- " ^ text ^ " .");
  match p.queries with
  | q :: _ when List.length p.queries = List.length before + 1 ->
      p.queries <- before;
      q
  | _ -> raise (Error ("a query is expected: " ^ text, "-q"))
languages/datalog/Datalog.mli
4769
(* A Datalog program (docs/plans/plan_prolog.md, "Datalog"): relations,
 * the facts in them, the rules that add to them, the queries. Its text
 * is Prolog's without compound terms, read by Prolog_read:
 *
 *   assign(p, q).                               a fact
 *   point_to(P, L) :- assign(P, Q), point_to(Q, L).     a rule
 *   live(V, P) :- succ(P, Q), live(V, Q), \+ def(V, P). a negation (or not(...))
 *   other(X, Y) :- node(X), node(Y), X \= Y.    a comparison (= \= < > =< >=)
 *   ?- point_to(p, L).                          a query; or, on a line, point_to(p, L)?
 *
 * A constant is an atom or an integer, kept as a number (a symbol); a
 * tuple is an array of them. A rule must be safe: a variable of its
 * head, of a negation or of a comparison is also in a positive atom of
 * its body (_ in a negation: any value).
 *
 * Safety is what keeps the tables finite. big(X) :- \+ small(X) asks
 * for everything that is not small: of what? A variable gets its
 * values from a table, and a negation or a comparison only refuses
 * some of them; "the variable X of a negation is in no positive atom
 * of the body" is the message.
 *
 * The same thing by the database's words (mini-chidb is ix's): a
 * relation is a table, a tuple a row, a fact an INSERT; a rule is a
 * view, its body a join of tables on the variables they share, its
 * head the SELECT's columns; and [indexes] are a database's, one for
 * each set of columns a join comes with already known:
 *
 *     path(X, Y) :- path(X, Z), edge(Z, Y).
 *
 *     for each path tuple (X, Z): edge is asked for its tuples whose
 *     first column is that Z: an index of edge by column 0 (the
 *     mask 1), from a value to the tuples that have it there
 *
 * design:
 * A constant is a small integer and a tuple an array of them: the
 * atom's text is looked up once, when the fact is read ([symbol]),
 * and after that a join compares and hashes integers. It is the
 * interning of a compiler's symbol table and of Lisp's atoms, and
 * most of what makes a million tuples affordable. *)

type arg = Const of int | Slot of int | Any

type relation = {
  name : string;
  arity : int;
  set : Relset.t;                         (* its tuples, each once, hashed or sorted *)
  (* the same, numbered in the order added: tuple i is rows.(i * arity)
   * to rows.(i * arity + arity - 1) *)
  mutable rows : int array;
  mutable count : int;
  (* by the columns that are known (a bit each): an index on them, of
   * the relation's kind *)
  mutable indexes : (int * Index.t) list;
  (* Datalog_eval's: the last round's new tuples are those numbered from
   * delta_from to delta_to - 1; this round's, from delta_to on *)
  mutable delta_from : int;
  mutable delta_to : int;
  mutable stratum : int;
  mutable given : int;                    (* its facts in the text *)
  mutable rules : int;                    (* the rules with it as head *)
}

type atom = { rel : relation; args : arg array }
type literal = Pos of atom | Neg of atom | Cmp of string * arg * arg
type rule = { head : atom; body : literal list; slots : int; at : string (* file:line *) }
type query = { goal : atom; names : string array (* a slot's variable *) }

type t = {
  symbols : (string, int) Hashtbl.t;
  mutable terms : Prolog.term array;      (* a symbol's atom or integer *)
  mutable nsymbols : int;
  relations : (string, relation) Hashtbl.t; (* by name/arity *)
  mutable rule_list : rule list;          (* in the text's order *)
  mutable queries : query list;
  (* the relations sorted (Relset.mli), by name/arity, or all; set
   * before a text names them: the others are hashed *)
  mutable sorted : string list;
}

(* a text's mistake: the message, where (file:line) *)
exception Error of string * string

val create : unit -> t

(* a text's facts, rules and queries added; its name, for a mistake's place *)
val load : t -> from:string -> string -> unit

(* one query, as -q gives it: p(X, a) *)
val query : t -> string -> query

val symbol : t -> Prolog.term -> int
val relation : t -> string -> int -> relation

(* a symbol's text, as a fact shows it (an atom quoted if it must be) *)
val text : t -> int -> string

(* a tuple as a fact: name(a,b). *)
val show : t -> relation -> int array -> string

(* a tuple added; false: it was there *)
val add : relation -> int array -> bool

(* a tuple's row added, not to the set or the indexes (the caller
 * adds them: Datalog_eval's on several domains); its number *)
val append : relation -> int array -> int

(* the numbers of the mask's columns, in order, for an arity *)
val columns : int -> int -> int array

(* the i-th tuple's j-th value *)
val get : relation -> int -> int -> int

(* every tuple, the last added first *)
val tuples : relation -> int array list

(* See Datalog_eval.mli *)

module D = Datalog

type stats = {
  mutable rounds : int;
  mutable firings : int;
  mutable derived : int;
  mutable lookups : int;
  mutable profile : (D.rule * cost) list;
}

and cost = { mutable fired : int; mutable added : int; mutable looked : int; mutable seconds : float }

(*****************************************************************************)
(* A body's plan *)
(*****************************************************************************)

(* a body as steps run in order (Souffle's RAM, smaller), chosen once a
 * rule and its atom from the new tuples: what each atom knows of its
 * columns when it is reached, which variables it binds, where each
 * negation or comparison is tested, is decided here, and a join does
 * nothing else than look up, compare and bind.
 * old: a join found out at each tuple which variables were bound (an
 * environment's -1), bound them in a list to undo, and held the tests
 * met too soon; the mask of an atom's known columns made each time *)
type step =
  | Scan of scan
  | Test of D.literal (* a negation or a comparison, its variables bound *)

and scan = {
  atom : D.atom;
  from_new : bool;          (* the last round's new tuples only *)
  mask : int;               (* the columns known, a bit each: the index *)
  keys : (int * D.arg) array;   (* (column, value): those columns' *)
  binds : (int * int) list;     (* (column, slot): a variable it binds *)
  same : (int * int) list;      (* (column, slot): the same again, p(X, X) *)
  (* the two lists again, as arrays of columns and of slots: walked by a
   * loop at each tuple, where a List.iter called a closure (Compile_il
   * reads the lists) *)
  bind_at : int array;
  bind_to : int array;
  same_at : int array;
  same_to : int array;
}

(* the order of a body's atoms: after the one from the new tuples, the
 * atom with the most columns known (a constant, a variable an atom
 * before binds), a whole tuple known first (a membership test), the
 * order written on a tie; each test as soon as its variables are bound.
 * old: the order written, the new tuples' atom first: from new
 * point_to(X, L) tuples, assign_content(P, Q), point_to(Q, X),
 * point_to(X, L) scanned every assign_content for each one (rc's
 * analysis: 20 million lookups, 1.1 million now) *)
let plan (slots : int) (first : D.atom option) (body : D.literal list) : step list =
  let bound = Array.make slots false in
  let known (x : D.arg) : bool = match x with D.Const _ -> true | D.Slot k -> bound.(k) | D.Any -> false in
  let scan (a : D.atom) (from_new : bool) : step =
    let keys = ref [] and binds = ref [] and same = ref [] in
    Array.iteri
      (fun (i : int) (x : D.arg) ->
        match x with
        | D.Any -> ()
        | D.Slot k when not (known x) ->
            if List.exists (fun ((_, k') : int * int) -> k' = k) !binds then same := (i, k) :: !same
            else binds := (i, k) :: !binds
        | _ -> keys := (i, x) :: !keys)
      a.args;
    List.iter (fun ((_, k) : int * int) -> bound.(k) <- true) !binds;
    let keys = Array.of_list (List.rev !keys) in
    let mask = Array.fold_left (fun (m : int) ((i, _) : int * D.arg) -> m lor (1 lsl i)) 0 keys in
    let cols (l : (int * int) list) : int array = Array.of_list (List.map fst l) in
    let slots (l : (int * int) list) : int array = Array.of_list (List.map snd l) in
    Scan
      { atom = a; from_new; mask; keys; binds = !binds; same = !same; bind_at = cols !binds; bind_to = slots !binds;
        same_at = cols !same; same_to = slots !same } in
  let score (a : D.atom) : int * int =
    let n = Array.fold_left (fun (n : int) (x : D.arg) -> if known x then n + 1 else n) 0 a.args in
    ((if n = Array.length a.args then 1 else 0), n) in
  let ready (l : D.literal) : bool =
    match l with
    | D.Pos _ -> false
    | D.Neg a -> Array.for_all (fun (x : D.arg) -> x = D.Any || known x) a.args
    | D.Cmp (_, x, y) -> known x && known y in
  let rec next (tests : D.literal list) (atoms : D.atom list) : step list =
    let now, later = List.partition ready tests in
    let rest =
      match atoms with
      | [] -> [] (* (a rule is safe: no test is left) *)
      | a :: others ->
          let best = List.fold_left (fun (b : D.atom) (x : D.atom) -> if compare (score x) (score b) > 0 then x else b) a others in
          let s = scan best false in
          s :: next later (List.filter (fun (x : D.atom) -> x != best) atoms) in
    List.map (fun (l : D.literal) -> Test l) now @ rest in
  let atoms = List.filter_map (fun (l : D.literal) -> match l with D.Pos a -> Some a | _ -> None) body in
  let tests = List.filter (fun (l : D.literal) -> match l with D.Pos _ -> false | _ -> true) body in
  match first with
  | None -> next tests atoms
  | Some a ->
      let s = scan a true in
      s :: next tests atoms

(*****************************************************************************)
(* A plan run *)
(*****************************************************************************)

(* (a top-level loop: List.find_opt's closure was made at each lookup,
 * 31 million on mini-scheme's Andersen) *)
let rec find_index (mask : int) (l : (int * Index.t) list) : Index.t option =
  match l with [] -> None | (m, index) :: rest -> if m = mask then Some index else find_index mask rest

(* the index of a relation by some columns, made if it is not there *)
let index (r : D.relation) (mask : int) : Index.t =
  (* (not List.assoc_opt: its compare is the polymorphic one, a call
   * into the runtime at each lookup, 2.3 million on mini-datalog's
   * facts) *)
  match find_index mask r.indexes with
  | Some index -> index
  | None ->
      let index = Index.create ~sorted:(Relset.sorted r.set) r.arity (D.columns r.arity mask) in
      for id = 0 to r.count - 1 do
        Index.add index (D.get r id) id
      done;
      r.indexes <- (mask, index) :: r.indexes;
      index

let value (env : int array) (x : D.arg) : int = match x with D.Const c -> c | D.Slot k -> env.(k) | D.Any -> -1

(* a negation's columns that are not _, a bit each *)
let known (a : D.atom) : int =
  let mask = ref 0 in
  Array.iteri (fun (i : int) (x : D.arg) -> if x <> D.Any then mask := !mask lor (1 lsl i)) a.args;
  !mask

let holds (p : D.t) (stats : stats) (env : int array) (l : D.literal) : bool =
  match l with
  | D.Pos _ -> true
  | D.Neg a ->
      (* (no tuple has those values in the columns that are not _) *)
      stats.lookups <- stats.lookups + 1;
      let mask = known a in
      if mask = 0 then a.rel.count = 0
      else if mask = (1 lsl a.rel.arity) - 1 then not (Relset.mem_by a.rel.set (fun (i : int) -> value env a.args.(i)))
      else
        let cols = D.columns a.rel.arity mask in
        not (Index.exists (index a.rel mask) (fun (i : int) -> value env a.args.(cols.(i))))
  | D.Cmp (op, x, y) -> (
      let x = value env x and y = value env y in
      match op with
      | "=" | "==" -> x = y
      | "\\=" | "\\==" -> x <> y
      | _ -> (
          let c = Prolog.compare p.terms.(x) p.terms.(y) in
          match op with "<" -> c < 0 | ">" -> c > 0 | "=<" -> c <= 0 | _ -> c >= 0))

(* a column's place in a row: its own *)
let same_place : int array = Array.init 63 (fun (c : int) -> c)

(* each way the steps hold together: [found] called with the variables
 * bound (a slot is read only after the step that binds it: nothing is
 * unbound) *)
let rec join (p : D.t) (stats : stats) (env : int array) (steps : step list) (found : unit -> unit) : unit =
  match steps with
  | [] -> found ()
  | Test l :: rest -> if holds p stats env l then join p stats env rest found
  | Scan s :: rest ->
      stats.lookups <- stats.lookups + 1;
      let r = s.atom.rel in
      if s.from_new || s.mask = 0 then begin
        let lo, hi = if s.from_new then (r.delta_from, r.delta_to) else (0, r.count) in
        for id = lo to hi - 1 do
          scanned p stats env s rest found id
        done
      end
      else begin
        (* the key's values in an array, made at each lookup (not kept in
         * the plan: the domains share it), read by a loop where the key
         * was a closure called for each column by the hash and the
         * compare (old: Relset.mem_by r.set key, and Index.iter index
         * r.rows r.arity key (fun keys base -> each ... keys base at)
         * for both kinds of index; mini-cc's Andersen 46 s, ...) *)
        let keys = s.keys in
        let n = Array.length keys in
        (* (a literal array for a key of 1 to 3 columns: made in place,
         * where Array.make is a call into the runtime, caml_make_vect,
         * 6% of mini-scheme's instructions) *)
        let k =
          match n with
          | 1 -> [| value env (snd keys.(0)) |]
          | 2 -> [| value env (snd keys.(0)); value env (snd keys.(1)) |]
          | 3 -> [| value env (snd keys.(0)); value env (snd keys.(1)); value env (snd keys.(2)) |]
          | _ -> Array.init n (fun (i : int) -> value env (snd keys.(i))) in
        if n = r.arity then (if Relset.mem_array r.set k then join p stats env rest found)
        else
          let index = index r s.mask in
          (* (a relation's indexes are of its set's kind) *)
          if not (Relset.sorted r.set) then begin
            let rows = r.rows and arity = r.arity in
            let id = ref (Index.first_array index k) in
            while !id >= 0 do
              each p stats env s rest found rows (!id * arity) same_place;
              id := Index.next index !id
            done
          end
          else
            let at = Index.at index in
            let key (i : int) : int = k.(i) in
            Index.iter index r.rows r.arity key (fun (keys : int array) (base : int) -> each p stats env s rest found keys base at)
      end

(* a tuple of a scan with no index, by its number: its known columns
 * compared (old: Array.for_all of a closure) *)
and scanned (p : D.t) (stats : stats) (env : int array) (s : scan) (rest : step list) (found : unit -> unit) (id : int) : unit =
  let r = s.atom.rel in
  let rows = r.rows and base = id * r.arity and keys = s.keys in
  let i = ref 0 and n = Array.length keys in
  while !i < n && rows.(base + fst keys.(!i)) = value env (snd keys.(!i)) do
    incr i
  done;
  if !i = n then each p stats env s rest found rows base same_place

(* a tuple that matches, column c at keys.(base + at.(c)) (a row, or an
 * index's leaf): its variables bound, the steps after (old: List.iter and
 * List.for_all of closures over s.binds and s.same) *)
and each (p : D.t) (stats : stats) (env : int array) (s : scan) (rest : step list) (found : unit -> unit) (keys : int array)
    (base : int) (at : int array) : unit =
  let bind_at = s.bind_at and bind_to = s.bind_to in
  for j = 0 to Array.length bind_at - 1 do
    env.(bind_to.(j)) <- keys.(base + at.(bind_at.(j)))
  done;
  let same_at = s.same_at and same_to = s.same_to in
  let j = ref 0 and n = Array.length same_at in
  while !j < n && keys.(base + at.(same_at.(!j))) = env.(same_to.(!j)) do
    incr j
  done;
  if !j = n then join p stats env rest found

(*****************************************************************************)
(* A rule on several domains *)
(*****************************************************************************)

let jobs = ref 1

(* the domains that wait for a job, [job d] on each, the caller's 0 *)
type pool = {
  size : int;
  lock : Parallel.lock;
  start : Parallel.cond;
  finished : Parallel.cond;
  mutable job : int -> unit;
  mutable generation : int;     (* how many jobs were given *)
  mutable left : int;           (* the workers still at this one *)
  mutable stop : bool;
  mutable failed : exn option;
}

let worker (pool : pool) (d : int) () : unit =
  let seen = ref 0 in
  Parallel.take pool.lock;
  while not pool.stop do
    if pool.generation = !seen then Parallel.wait pool.start pool.lock
    else begin
      seen := pool.generation;
      let job = pool.job in
      Parallel.give pool.lock;
      let failed : exn option = try job d; None with e -> Some e in
      Parallel.take pool.lock;
      if failed <> None then pool.failed <- failed;
      pool.left <- pool.left - 1;
      if pool.left = 0 then Parallel.signal pool.finished
    end
  done;
  Parallel.give pool.lock

let pool_make (size : int) : pool =
  let pool : pool =
    { size; lock = Parallel.lock (); start = Parallel.cond (); finished = Parallel.cond (); job = (fun (_ : int) -> ());
      generation = 0; left = 0; stop = false; failed = None } in
  for d = 1 to size - 1 do
    Parallel.spawn (worker pool d)
  done;
  pool

(* [job] on every domain, back when all are done *)
let pool_run (pool : pool) (job : int -> unit) : unit =
  Parallel.take pool.lock;
  pool.job <- job;
  pool.generation <- pool.generation + 1;
  pool.left <- pool.size - 1;
  Parallel.broadcast pool.start;
  Parallel.give pool.lock;
  let mine : exn option = try job 0; None with e -> Some e in
  Parallel.take pool.lock;
  while pool.left > 0 do
    Parallel.wait pool.finished pool.lock
  done;
  let failed = if mine <> None then mine else pool.failed in
  pool.failed <- None;
  Parallel.give pool.lock;
  match failed with Some e -> raise e | None -> ()

let pool_stop (pool : pool) : unit =
  Parallel.take pool.lock;
  pool.stop <- true;
  Parallel.broadcast pool.start;
  Parallel.give pool.lock

let pool : pool option ref = ref None

(* the new tuples a domain takes at a time, and how many make a rule
 * worth sharing out *)
let chunk = 32
let shared = 4 * chunk

(* the indexes the steps will ask for, made now: on the domains they
 * are only read *)
let prepare (steps : step list) : unit =
  List.iter
    (fun (step : step) ->
      match step with
      | Scan s when (not s.from_new) && s.mask <> 0 && Array.length s.keys < s.atom.rel.arity -> ignore (index s.atom.rel s.mask)
      | Test (D.Neg a) ->
          let mask = known a in
          if mask <> 0 && mask <> (1 lsl a.rel.arity) - 1 then ignore (index a.rel mask)
      | _ -> ())
    steps

(* the tuples found, added by the domains: each adds to the set those
 * of its own parts, then the rows are added in turn, then each adds to
 * an index the keys of its own parts (a part's hash first computed by
 * slices). Each part sees the tuples in their order, so this is D.add
 * of each in turn. *)
let add_shared (pool : pool) (r : D.relation) (found : int array array) : int =
  let m = Array.length found and size = pool.size in
  let slice (d : int) (m : int) : int * int = (d * m / size, (d + 1) * m / size) in
  let part = Array.make m 0 in
  pool_run pool (fun (d : int) ->
      let lo, hi = slice d m in
      for i = lo to hi - 1 do
        let tuple = found.(i) in
        part.(i) <- Relset.part_of r.set (fun (j : int) -> tuple.(j))
      done);
  let fresh = Array.make m false in
  pool_run pool (fun (d : int) ->
      for i = 0 to m - 1 do
        if part.(i) mod size = d then begin
          let tuple = found.(i) in
          fresh.(i) <- Relset.add r.set tuple
        end
      done);
  let first = r.count in
  Array.iteri (fun (i : int) (tuple : int array) -> if fresh.(i) then ignore (D.append r tuple)) found;
  let added = r.count - first in
  List.iter
    (fun ((_, index) : int * Index.t) ->
      Index.reserve index r.count;
      let part = Array.make added 0 in
      pool_run pool (fun (d : int) ->
          let lo, hi = slice d added in
          for k = lo to hi - 1 do
            part.(k) <- Index.part_of index (D.get r (first + k))
          done);
      pool_run pool (fun (d : int) ->
          for k = 0 to added - 1 do
            if part.(k) mod size = d then Index.add index (D.get r (first + k)) (first + k)
          done))
    r.indexes;
  added

(* what a rule found added after its join, not during it: a tree's
 * range may not change while it is walked (Souffle's rounds, likewise,
 * write their new tuples apart from those they read). On the domains
 * when there are enough. *)
let add_found (stats : stats) (r : D.relation) (found : int array array) : unit =
  match !pool with
  | Some pool when Array.length found >= shared -> stats.derived <- stats.derived + add_shared pool r found
  | _ -> Array.iter (fun (tuple : int array) -> if D.add r tuple then stats.derived <- stats.derived + 1) found

(* the new tuples of the first scan in chunks, taken by the domains in
 * turn; what each finds that is not there kept by chunk, and added in
 * the chunks' order, the same each time. The relations
 * are only read while the domains run. *)
let apply_shared (p : D.t) (stats : stats) (pool : pool) (rule : D.rule) (s : scan) (rest : step list) : unit =
  prepare rest;
  let lo = s.atom.rel.delta_from and hi = s.atom.rel.delta_to in
  let n = (hi - lo + chunk - 1) / chunk in
  let next = Atomic.make 0 in
  let results : int array list array = Array.make n [] in
  let none : stats = { rounds = 0; firings = 0; derived = 0; lookups = 0; profile = [] } in
  let counts : stats array = Array.make pool.size none in
  pool_run pool (fun (d : int) ->
      (* (its counts made here, on its own domain, and given at the
       * end: made by the caller, the domains' records are side by side,
       * several in a line of the cache, which each firing's count
       * would pass from core to core; measured, no difference here) *)
      let mine : stats = { rounds = 0; firings = 0; derived = 0; lookups = 0; profile = [] } in
      let env = Array.make rule.slots (-1) in
      let head (i : int) : int = value env rule.head.args.(i) in
      (* (what this domain found already: without it, a tuple found by
       * a thousand firings was a thousand candidates, which the caller
       * added one by one) *)
      let seen = Tuples.create (Array.length rule.head.args) and h = Relset.hint rule.head.rel.set in
      let c = ref (Atomic.fetch_and_add next 1) in
      while !c < n do
        let got : int array list ref = ref [] in
        for id = lo + (!c * chunk) to min hi (lo + ((!c + 1) * chunk)) - 1 do
          scanned p mine env s rest
            (fun () ->
              mine.firings <- mine.firings + 1;
              if not (Relset.mem_hint rule.head.rel.set h head || Tuples.mem_by seen head) then begin
                let tuple = Array.map (value env) rule.head.args in
                ignore (Tuples.add seen tuple);
                got := tuple :: !got
              end)
            id
        done;
        results.(!c) <- List.rev !got;
        c := Atomic.fetch_and_add next 1
      done;
      counts.(d) <- mine);
  stats.lookups <- stats.lookups + 1;
  Array.iter
    (fun (c : stats) ->
      stats.firings <- stats.firings + c.firings;
      stats.lookups <- stats.lookups + c.lookups)
    counts;
  let all = Array.make (Array.fold_left (fun (n : int) (l : int array list) -> n + List.length l) 0 results) [||] in
  let k = ref 0 in
  Array.iter (List.iter (fun (tuple : int array) -> all.(!k) <- tuple; incr k)) results;
  add_found stats rule.head.rel all

(* a rule applied by one of its plans: the tuples it finds that were not
 * known are added to its head, this round's new ones. Not at all if an
 * atom has no tuple (pointer.dl's assign_deref on an ML program: a lookup for each new
 * point_to, 1.7 million, found nothing) *)
let clock : (unit -> float) ref = ref (fun () -> 0.)

let apply (p : D.t) (stats : stats) (rule : D.rule) (steps : step list) : unit =
  let empty (step : step) : bool =
    match step with
    | Scan s -> if s.from_new then s.atom.rel.delta_from = s.atom.rel.delta_to else s.atom.rel.count = 0
    | Test _ -> false in
  if not (List.exists empty steps) then begin
    let env = Array.make rule.slots (-1) in
    let head (i : int) : int = value env rule.head.args.(i) in
    let fired = stats.firings and added = stats.derived and looked = stats.lookups and t0 = !clock () in
    (match (!pool, steps) with
     | Some pool, Scan s :: rest when s.from_new && s.atom.rel.delta_to - s.atom.rel.delta_from >= shared ->
         apply_shared p stats pool rule s rest
     | _ when not (Relset.sorted rule.head.rel.set) ->
         (* a hashed head: each tuple added as found (a hash's slots and
          * chains do not move under a walk) *)
         let r = rule.head.rel in
         (* the head's values into one array, tested, and added (copied)
          * if new (old: Relset.mem_hint r.set h head, the head a closure
          * called for each column, then Array.map (value env) of it) *)
         let args = rule.head.args in
         let n = Array.length args in
         let tuple = Array.make n 0 in
         join p stats env steps (fun () ->
             stats.firings <- stats.firings + 1;
             for i = 0 to n - 1 do
               tuple.(i) <- value env args.(i)
             done;
             if D.add r tuple then stats.derived <- stats.derived + 1)
     | _ ->
         let r = rule.head.rel in
         let seen = Tuples.create r.arity and got = ref [] and h = Relset.hint r.set in
         join p stats env steps (fun () ->
             stats.firings <- stats.firings + 1;
             (* (most firings find their tuple there: asked before it is made) *)
             if not (Relset.mem_hint r.set h head || Tuples.mem_by seen head) then begin
               let tuple = Array.map (value env) rule.head.args in
               ignore (Tuples.add seen tuple);
               got := tuple :: !got
             end);
         add_found stats r (Array.of_list (List.rev !got)));
    let c =
      match List.assq_opt rule stats.profile with
      | Some c -> c
      | None ->
          let c = { fired = 0; added = 0; looked = 0; seconds = 0. } in
          stats.profile <- (rule, c) :: stats.profile;
          c in
    c.fired <- c.fired + stats.firings - fired;
    c.added <- c.added + stats.derived - added;
    c.looked <- c.looked + stats.lookups - looked;
    c.seconds <- c.seconds +. !clock () -. t0
  end

(*****************************************************************************)
(* The strata, and the fixpoint *)
(*****************************************************************************)

(* each relation's stratum: at least that of what it reads, and one more
 * than that of what it negates *)
let stratify (p : D.t) : int =
  let n = Hashtbl.length p.relations in
  let changed = ref true and top = ref 0 in
  Hashtbl.iter (fun (_ : string) (r : D.relation) -> r.stratum <- 0) p.relations;
  while !changed do
    changed := false;
    List.iter
      (fun (rule : D.rule) ->
        let head = rule.head.rel in
        let raise_to (s : int) : unit =
          if s > head.stratum then begin
            if s > n then
              raise (D.Error (Printf.sprintf "%s/%d is negated through its own recursion: no order to compute it in" head.name head.arity, rule.at));
            head.stratum <- s;
            if s > !top then top := s;
            changed := true
          end in
        List.iter
          (fun (l : D.literal) ->
            match l with
            | D.Pos a -> raise_to a.rel.stratum
            | D.Neg a -> raise_to (a.rel.stratum + 1)
            | D.Cmp _ -> ())
          rule.body)
      p.rule_list
  done;
  !top

(* the body's plan with its k-th atom from the new tuples *)
let from_new (rule : D.rule) (k : int) (a : D.atom) : step list =
  plan rule.slots (Some a) (List.filteri (fun (i : int) (_ : D.literal) -> i <> k) rule.body)

let run ~(naive : bool) (p : D.t) : stats =
  let stats : stats = { rounds = 0; firings = 0; derived = 0; lookups = 0; profile = [] } in
  let top = stratify p in
  let rules = List.rev p.rule_list in
  if !jobs > 1 && Parallel.available then pool := Some (pool_make !jobs);
  for s = 0 to top do
    let mine = List.filter (fun (rule : D.rule) -> rule.head.rel.stratum = s) rules in
    (* (each once: a relation with two rules is one relation) *)
    let heads : D.relation list =
      List.fold_left
        (fun (acc : D.relation list) (rule : D.rule) -> if List.memq rule.head.rel acc then acc else rule.head.rel :: acc)
        [] mine in
    (* a round's end: the tuples added in it, numbered from delta_to on,
     * are the next one's new ones (Souffle's relations new, delta and
     * full are here three ranges of the same rows) *)
    let since (r : D.relation) (from : int) : unit =
      r.delta_from <- from;
      r.delta_to <- r.count in
    List.iter (fun (r : D.relation) -> since r r.count) heads;
    let turn () : bool =
      let any = ref false in
      List.iter
        (fun (r : D.relation) ->
          if r.count > r.delta_to then any := true;
          since r r.delta_to)
        heads;
      stats.rounds <- stats.rounds + 1;
      !any in
    (* each rule's plans: on everything; with each atom of this
     * stratum's relations from the new tuples *)
    let whole = List.map (fun (rule : D.rule) -> (rule, plan rule.slots None rule.body)) mine in
    let by_new =
      List.concat_map
        (fun (rule : D.rule) ->
          List.concat
            (List.mapi
               (fun (k : int) (l : D.literal) ->
                 match l with D.Pos a when a.rel.stratum = s && a.rel.rules > 0 -> [ (rule, from_new rule k a) ] | _ -> [])
               rule.body))
        mine in
    List.iter (fun ((rule, steps) : D.rule * step list) -> apply p stats rule steps) whole;
    while turn () do
      List.iter (fun ((rule, steps) : D.rule * step list) -> apply p stats rule steps) (if naive then whole else by_new)
    done;
    List.iter (fun (r : D.relation) -> since r r.count) heads
  done;
  (match !pool with Some pl -> pool_stop pl; pool := None | None -> ());
  stats

let answers (p : D.t) (q : D.query) : string list =
  let stats : stats = { rounds = 0; firings = 0; derived = 0; lookups = 0; profile = [] } in
  let env = Array.make (Array.length q.names) (-1) in
  let found : string list ref = ref [] in
  join p stats env (plan (Array.length q.names) None [ D.Pos q.goal ]) (fun () ->
      found := D.show p q.goal.rel (Array.map (value env) q.goal.args) :: !found);
  List.sort_uniq String.compare !found
languages/datalog/Datalog_eval.mli
11531
(* A Datalog program run: every rule applied until no tuple is new, the
 * least fixpoint. It ends on any program (no term is made, so the
 * tuples are finite), and neither the rules' order nor a body's changes
 * what is found.
 *
 * - The strata first: a relation that another negates is computed whole
 *   before it. A negation through a recursion has no such order, and is
 *   refused.
 * - In a stratum, semi-naive: after a first round of every rule, a rule
 *   is run again only with one of its body's atoms taken from the last
 *   round's new tuples (once for each atom of the stratum's relations);
 *   a rule none of whose atoms is new can find nothing new. [naive]
 *   runs every rule on everything each round: the definition, kept to
 *   check the other by.
 * - A body is joined by a plan made once for each rule (and each of
 *   its atoms that the new tuples are taken for): its atoms in an
 *   order chosen, the new tuples' atom first, then each time the atom
 *   with the most columns already known; each atom looked up by those
 *   columns, in an index made the first time they are asked for; each
 *   negation and comparison tested as soon as its variables are bound.
 *   A rule one of whose atoms has no tuple is not run.
 *
 *     edge(a, b). edge(b, c). edge(c, d). edge(d, e).
 *     path(X, Y) :- path(X, Z), edge(Z, Y).
 *     path(X, Y) :- edge(X, Y).
 *
 *     round   path's new tuples   found by                      firings
 *       1     ab bc cd de         every rule on everything         4
 *       2     ac bd ce            round 1's four, each joined      3
 *       3     ad be               round 2's three   with edge      2
 *       4     ae                  round 3's two                    1
 *       5     none: the fixpoint  round 4's one                    0
 *
 * Ten firings for ten tuples (mini-datalog -s: 5 rounds, 10 firings;
 * with the two rules in the other order the first round finds more,
 * a rule seeing at once what the one before it added: 4 rounds).
 * By -naive each round joins all of path with edge again and finds
 * again what it had: 40 firings for the same ten. The reason it is
 * right to look at the new tuples only: a rule's body is a join, and
 * a join gives something new only if one of its inputs has; so, for
 * a body p, q, what is new is (new p) with q, and p with (new q), as
 * a product's derivative is. That is the once for each atom above.
 *
 * Negation needs an order. \+ path(X, Y) is true of what is not in
 * path, which is known only when path is finished: path is in a
 * lower stratum than apart (CLI.mli's example), and is run to its
 * fixpoint first. p(X) :- node(X), \+ q(X) with q(X) :- node(X),
 * \+ p(X) has no such order, and no one least answer either (p(a),
 * or q(a)?): refused.
 *
 * reframe:
 * A compiler's worklist is this. A dataflow analysis (liveness, as
 * mini-cc's Opti and mini-ml's Alloc compute it) puts back on its
 * list the blocks whose input changed and leaves the others: the new
 * tuples are the list. The rounds here and the list there are two
 * shapes of one idea, to compute again only what depends on what
 * changed, which is also a spreadsheet's recalculation and a build
 * tool's (mini-mk).
 *
 * design:
 * The order chosen matters more than all the rest: the order written,
 * the new tuples' atom first, had Plan 9's rc analysed by pointer.dl
 * in 20 million lookups and 6.7 s, where the plan does it in 0.6
 * million and 0.2 s, the same tuples (-profile shows each rule's share).
 *
 * A relation is stored as Souffle's: its tuples numbered in the order
 * added, flat in one array of rows (Datalog's), so that the last
 * round's new tuples, this round's and all of them are three ranges of
 * numbers (Souffle's delta, new and full relations); beside them a
 * set and indexes, of one of two kinds, the relation's choice
 * (Relset.mli, -btree): hashed (Tuples, Hash_index), where an index
 * gives the tuples' numbers to read in the rows, in the order added;
 * or sorted (Btree, Tree_index), where an index is the relation
 * again with its key's columns first, giving the tuples themselves in
 * order, so that a rule's heads tested one after the other are
 * neighbours in a sorted set (its hint). A sorted relation's tuples
 * are added after the rule's join, not during it: a B-tree's leaf
 * moves under an insertion, a walk of it would lose its place; a
 * hashed one's as found, as before (a slot, a chain's head).
 *
 * A rule on several domains (-j, OCaml 5's build): its new tuples in
 * chunks, each domain taking the next chunk, testing what its firings
 * find against the relation and against what it found itself, and
 * keeping the rest. Nothing is written while the domains run (the
 * indexes they need are made before), so nothing is locked. Then they
 * add what was found: the set and the indexes are in 64 parts by
 * hash, each domain adds to its own parts, in the order found, so the
 * tuples are numbered the same whatever the domains did. mini-ml and
 * the assembler with lib_core, by OCaml 5: 101 s on one domain, 25.7 s
 * on 8, 15.4 on 32, 18.2 on 64. On 32, 9 s of it is the join, every
 * domain busy, a firing three times as long as on one core: the
 * 372 million tests of a head against 9.5 million tuples, each a miss
 * of the cache, are memory's (Neoverse N1, no huge pages).
 * old: the adding on one domain, Hashtbl's indexes: 28.8 s on 32;
 * without each domain's own set, a tuple found by a thousand firings
 * was a thousand candidates: 79.5 s on 16 domains, 11 GB.
 *
 * cs-history:
 * The fixpoint by rounds is the definition of what a program means
 * (van Emden and Kowalski, 1976). Semi-naive evaluation is from the
 * deductive databases of the 1980s (Francois Bancilhon), and
 * stratified negation from Krzysztof Apt, Howard Blair
 * and Adrian Walker (1988), who showed that a program with such an
 * order has one answer that does not depend on the order chosen.
 *
 * road-not-taken:
 * Everything is computed, though one query is asked: every path, for
 * path(a, X). The magic sets (Bancilhon, Maier, Sagiv and Ullman,
 * 1986) rewrite the rules so that, run bottom up, they find only what
 * the question needs, as Prolog would going down; tabling does it in
 * a Prolog, remembering each call's answers (XSB). Here the question
 * is every tuple (an analysis of a whole program), so they would
 * gain nothing, and are not there. They would for a question about
 * one place (what may this pointer be, asked by an editor): the
 * demand-driven pointer analyses (Heintze and Tardieu, 2001) are that.
 *
 * An analysis run again after a file changed starts here from nothing.
 * Incremental evaluation keeps the tuples and follows the change:
 * DRed (Gupta, Mumick and Subrahmanian, 1993) takes out what a deleted
 * fact may have given, then derives again what still holds; DDlog
 * (Ryzhyk and Budiu, VMware, 2019), on McSherry's differential
 * dataflow, counts each tuple's derivations by version, so that an
 * addition and a deletion both flow through the rules as differences.
 *
 * modern:
 * The engines made for analyses compile the rules: Souffle writes a
 * C++ program a file of rules, each relation with the fewest indexes
 * that cover its rules' lookups (chosen before the run, where an
 * index is made here at its first lookup), B-trees and tries for the
 * tuples, a round's outer loop on all the cores, inserted into
 * concurrent B-trees (optimistic locks) where here each domain has
 * its parts. Its join order is
 * chosen by the variables bound, as here, or given (.plan, from a
 * profile). Semmle's QL (CodeQL) orders joins by the relations'
 * estimated sizes, a database's optimizer. LogicBlox joins all the
 * atoms of a body at once (Veldhuizen's leapfrog triejoin, 2014: a
 * variable at a time, each relation a sorted trie), in a time bounded
 * by the largest answer the relations' sizes allow, where joining two
 * atoms at a time can make a larger result on the way. bddbddb
 * (Whaley and Lam, 2004) kept the relations as BDDs, where a
 * context-sensitive analysis's copies of a function for each context
 * share their nodes.
 *
 * References: Ceri, Gottlob and Tanca's survey (CLI.mli) for the
 * evaluation; K. R. Apt, H. A. Blair and A. Walker,
 * "Towards a Theory of Declarative Knowledge" (in Foundations of
 * Deductive Databases and Logic Programming, 1988); F. Bancilhon,
 * D. Maier, Y. Sagiv and J. D. Ullman, "Magic Sets and Other Strange
 * Ways to Implement Logic Programs" (Principles of Database Systems,
 * 1986); Herbert Jordan, Bernhard Scholz and Pavle Subotic,
 * "Souffle: On Synthesis of Program Analyzers" (Computer Aided
 * Verification, 2016); Pavle Subotic and others, "Automatic Index
 * Selection for Large-Scale Datalog Computation" (VLDB 2018); Todd L.
 * Veldhuizen, "Leapfrog Triejoin" (ICDT 2014); John Whaley and Monica
 * S. Lam, "Cloning-Based Context-Sensitive Pointer Alias Analysis
 * Using Binary Decision Diagrams" (PLDI 2004); Leonid Ryzhyk and Mihai
 * Budiu, "Differential Datalog" (Datalog 2.0, 2019); Ashish Gupta,
 * Inderpal Singh Mumick and V. S. Subrahmanian, "Maintaining Views
 * Incrementally" (SIGMOD 1993); Nevin Heintze and Olivier Tardieu,
 * "Demand-Driven Pointer Analysis" (PLDI 2001). *)

type stats = {
  mutable rounds : int;
  mutable firings : int;      (* a rule's body satisfied once *)
  mutable derived : int;      (* of them, a tuple that was new *)
  mutable lookups : int;
  (* each rule's share of them, and its time (-profile) *)
  mutable profile : (Datalog.rule * cost) list;
}

and cost = { mutable fired : int; mutable added : int; mutable looked : int; mutable seconds : float }

(* a body's plan, its steps in order: what each atom knows of its
 * columns (the index's mask, the keys' values), the variables it binds,
 * a variable bound again (p(X, X)), where each test is (mini-datalog
 * -dotnet compiles a plan to loops, Compile_il) *)
type step = Scan of scan | Test of Datalog.literal

  atom : Datalog.atom;
  from_new : bool;
  mask : int;
  keys : (int * Datalog.arg) array;
  binds : (int * int) list;
  same : (int * int) list;
  (* binds and same again, as their columns and their slots: the run's

  bind_at : int array;
  bind_to : int array;
  same_at : int array;
  same_to : int array;
}

(* Claude Code

(* See Index.mli *)

(* slot k of a part is cells.(k * (n + 1)) to cells.(k * (n + 1) + n):
 * the key's n values, then the last tuple's number, -1 when the slot is
 * free. The parts are Tuples's: a key's by its hash's low bits. *)
type part = { mutable cells : int array; mutable size : int; mutable keys : int }

type t = {
  n : int;
  part : part array;
  mutable chain : int array;     (* by tuple: the one before with its key *)
}

let create (n : int) : t =
  { n; part = Array.init Tuples.parts (fun (_ : int) -> { cells = Array.make (8 * (n + 1)) (-1); size = 8; keys = 0 });
    chain = Array.make 64 (-1) }

let part_of (t : t) (value : int -> int) : int = Tuples.hash t.n value land (Tuples.parts - 1)

(* in part p, the slot of the key, or the free one where it would go *)
let find (n : int) (p : part) (h : int) (value : int -> int) : int =
  let mask = p.size - 1 and w = n + 1 and cells = p.cells in
  let rec same (base : int) (i : int) : bool = i = n || (cells.(base + i) = value i && same base (i + 1)) in
  let rec walk (k : int) : int = if cells.((k * w) + n) < 0 || same (k * w) 0 then k else walk ((k + 1) land mask) in
  walk ((h lsr Tuples.part_bits) land mask)

let first (t : t) (value : int -> int) : int =
  let h = Tuples.hash t.n value in
  let p = t.part.(h land (Tuples.parts - 1)) in
  p.cells.((find t.n p h value * (t.n + 1)) + t.n)

let next (t : t) (id : int) : int = t.chain.(id)

(* first and add of a key in an array, written out: no closure called
 * for each value (Tuples.hash_array's reason) *)
(* (loops, as Tuples.find_array's; old: let rec same and walk) *)
let find_array (n : int) (p : part) (h : int) (key : int array) : int =
  let mask = p.size - 1 and w = n + 1 and cells = p.cells in
  let k = ref ((h lsr Tuples.part_bits) land mask) and found = ref false in
  while not !found do
    let base = !k * w in
    if cells.(base + n) < 0 then found := true
    else begin
      let i = ref 0 in
      while !i < n && cells.(base + !i) = key.(!i) do
        incr i
      done;
      if !i = n then found := true else k := (!k + 1) land mask
    end
  done;
  !k

let first_array (t : t) (key : int array) : int =
  let h = Tuples.hash_array t.n key in
  let p = t.part.(h land (Tuples.parts - 1)) in
  p.cells.((find_array t.n p h key * (t.n + 1)) + t.n)

(* room in the chain for the tuples numbered below [count] *)
let reserve (t : t) (count : int) : unit =
  if count > Array.length t.chain then begin
    let larger = Array.make (max count (2 * Array.length t.chain)) (-1) in
    Array.blit t.chain 0 larger 0 (Array.length t.chain);
    t.chain <- larger
  end

(* twice the part's slots, each key put again *)
let grow (n : int) (p : part) : unit =
  let old = p.cells and w = n + 1 and size = p.size in
  p.size <- 2 * size;
  p.cells <- Array.make (p.size * w) (-1);
  for k = 0 to size - 1 do
    if old.((k * w) + n) >= 0 then begin
      let value (i : int) : int = old.((k * w) + i) in
      Array.blit old (k * w) p.cells (find n p (Tuples.hash n value) value * w) w
    end
  done

let add_array (t : t) (key : int array) (id : int) : unit =
  reserve t (id + 1);
  let n = t.n and w = t.n + 1 in
  let h = Tuples.hash_array n key in
  let p = t.part.(h land (Tuples.parts - 1)) in
  let k = find_array n p h key in
  let head = p.cells.((k * w) + n) in
  t.chain.(id) <- head;
  if head < 0 then begin
    Array.blit key 0 p.cells (k * w) n;
    p.keys <- p.keys + 1
  end;
  p.cells.((k * w) + n) <- id;
  if head < 0 && 2 * p.keys > p.size then grow n p

let add (t : t) (value : int -> int) (id : int) : unit =
  reserve t (id + 1);
  let n = t.n and w = t.n + 1 in
  let h = Tuples.hash n value in
  let p = t.part.(h land (Tuples.parts - 1)) in
  let k = find n p h value in
  let head = p.cells.((k * w) + n) in
  t.chain.(id) <- head;
  if head < 0 then begin
    for i = 0 to n - 1 do
      p.cells.((k * w) + i) <- value i
    done;
    p.keys <- p.keys + 1
  end;
  p.cells.((k * w) + n) <- id;
  if head < 0 && 2 * p.keys > p.size then grow n p
languages/datalog/Hash_index.mli
2445
(* A hashed index (Index.mli, Relset.mli): the values of some of a
 * relation's columns (the key) to the tuples that have them, the
 * tuples by their number in the relation (Datalog's rows). Flat, as Tuples is: an array of slots by
 * open addressing, a slot the key's values and the number of the last
 * tuple added with that key; and an array by tuple, the number of the
 * one added with the same key before it (-1: none). A lookup walks
 * the slots to the key, then the chain (the slots in Tuples's 64
 * parts, a key's by its hash, so that domains add at once the tuples
 * whose keys are in their own parts):
 *
 *    slots                          next (by tuple)
 *    +--------+------+              0: -1
 *    | key k1 |  7 --+--> 7 -> 4 -> 0 -1      4: 0
 *    +--------+------+              7: 4
 *    | (free) |  -1  |
 *    +--------+------+
 *
 * design:
 * old: OCaml's Hashtbl, the key an array projected from the tuple
 * (made at each lookup and at each tuple added, hashed by the
 * polymorphic hash), to a list of the tuples' arrays. Here nothing is
 * made for a lookup, and an index of 9.5 million tuples is two arrays
 * of integers, not 9.5 million cells and keys for the collector.
 *
 * others:
 * Souffle's indexes are the relation itself sorted again, in the
 * key's columns first (a B-tree each order), a lookup a range; its
 * index selection finds the fewest orders that serve every lookup of
 * the rules (Subotic et al., VLDB 2018). A chained hash, as here, is
 * what databases call a hash index (System R had B-trees; hash join,
 * Gamma and Grace, the 1980s). *)

type t

(* an index on a key of n columns *)
val create : int -> t

(* the tuple numbered [id], whose key's i-th value is [key i], added.
 * The tuples are added in their numbers' order. *)
val add : t -> (int -> int) -> int -> unit

(* the last tuple added with that key, -1 if none *)
val first : t -> (int -> int) -> int

(* the tuple added with the same key before this one, -1 if none *)
val next : t -> int -> int

(* first and add of a key in an array (no closure: a compiled
 * program's, Datalog.add's) *)
val first_array : t -> int array -> int
val add_array : t -> int array -> int -> unit

(* the part of the key whose i-th value is [value i]: [add] of keys of
 * different parts may run at the same time, after [reserve] for the
 * largest number added *)
val part_of : t -> (int -> int) -> int
val reserve : t -> int -> unit

(* See Index.mli *)

(* a hashed index keeps its key's columns: its key is their values *)
type t = Hashed of int array * Hash_index.t | Sorted of Tree_index.t

(* a column's place in a row: its own *)
let same_place : int array = Array.init 63 (fun (c : int) -> c)

let create ~(sorted : bool) (arity : int) (cols : int array) : t =
  if sorted then Sorted (Tree_index.create arity cols) else Hashed (cols, Hash_index.create (Array.length cols))

let add (t : t) (value : int -> int) (id : int) : unit =
  match t with
  | Hashed (cols, h) -> Hash_index.add h (fun (i : int) -> value cols.(i)) id
  | Sorted s -> Tree_index.add s value

let iter (t : t) (rows : int array) (arity : int) (key : int -> int) (f : int array -> int -> unit) : unit =
  match t with
  | Hashed (_, h) ->
      let id = ref (Hash_index.first h key) in
      while !id >= 0 do
        f rows (!id * arity);
        id := Hash_index.next h !id
      done
  | Sorted s -> Tree_index.iter s key f

(* a hashed index's chain, walked by its caller (mini-datalog -dotnet's
 * compiled loops): the last tuple with the key, the one before *)
let first (t : t) (key : int -> int) : int =
  match t with Hashed (_, h) -> Hash_index.first h key | Sorted _ -> invalid_arg "Index.first: sorted"

let next (t : t) (id : int) : int = match t with Hashed (_, h) -> Hash_index.next h id | Sorted _ -> -1

(* the same, the key an array (no closure) *)
let first_array (t : t) (key : int array) : int =
  match t with Hashed (_, h) -> Hash_index.first_array h key | Sorted _ -> invalid_arg "Index.first_array: sorted"

let exists_array (t : t) (key : int array) : bool =
  match t with Hashed (_, h) -> Hash_index.first_array h key >= 0 | Sorted s -> Tree_index.exists s (fun (i : int) -> key.(i))

(* a tuple's number added under its key, the key its columns' values
 * (a hashed index's: no closure of the tuple's) *)
let add_array (t : t) (tuple : int array) (id : int) : unit =
  match t with
  | Hashed (cols, h) -> Hash_index.add_array h (Array.map (fun (c : int) -> tuple.(c)) cols) id
  | Sorted s -> Tree_index.add s (fun (c : int) -> tuple.(c))

let exists (t : t) (key : int -> int) : bool =
  match t with Hashed (_, h) -> Hash_index.first h key >= 0 | Sorted s -> Tree_index.exists s key

let at (t : t) : int array = match t with Hashed _ -> same_place | Sorted s -> Tree_index.at s

let part_of (t : t) (value : int -> int) : int =
  match t with Hashed (cols, h) -> Hash_index.part_of h (fun (i : int) -> value cols.(i)) | Sorted s -> Tree_index.part_of s value

let reserve (t : t) (count : int) : unit = match t with Hashed (_, h) -> Hash_index.reserve h count | Sorted _ -> ()

(* A relation's index on some of its columns (the key): the tuples that
 * have a key's values, of its relation's kind (Relset.mli):
 *
 *   Hash_index: a key to the numbers of its tuples, a chain, the
 *   tuples then read in the relation's rows, in the order added
 *   Tree_index: the relation again, sorted on the key first, the
 *   tuples read in its leaves, in the order of their other columns
 *
 * Either way a lookup gives each tuple as an array, where it starts,
 * and where each column is in it, so that the join reads both alike. *)

 * numbers, in order), sorted or hashed *)

 * tuples are added in their numbers' order. *)

 * column c is keys.(base + (at t).(c)); [rows] are the relation's
 * (Datalog's), of its arity. Not while a tuple is added. *)
val iter : t -> int array -> int -> (int -> int) -> (int array -> int -> unit) -> unit

(* a hashed index's chain, for a caller that walks it (a compiled
 * loop): the number of the last tuple with the key, -1 if none; the
 * one added before it with the same key. Not of a sorted index *)
val first : t -> (int -> int) -> int
val next : t -> int -> int

(* first and exists of a key in an array; a tuple added by its own
 * columns (no closure called for each value) *)
val first_array : t -> int array -> int
val exists_array : t -> int array -> bool
val add_array : t -> int array -> int -> unit

(* is there one? *)
val exists : t -> (int -> int) -> bool

(* each column's place in a tuple that iter gives *)
val at : t -> int array

(* the part of the tuple whose column c is [value c] (Tuples's and
 * Btree's 64): domains add at once the tuples of different parts, after
 * [reserve] for the largest number added *)
val part_of : t -> (int -> int) -> int
val reserve : t -> int -> unit

(* See Relset.mli *)

type t = Hashed of Tuples.t | Sorted of Btree.t

let create ~(sorted : bool) (n : int) : t = if sorted then Sorted (Btree.create n) else Hashed (Tuples.create n)
let sorted (t : t) : bool = match t with Sorted _ -> true | Hashed _ -> false

let mem_by (t : t) (value : int -> int) : bool =
  match t with Hashed s -> Tuples.mem_by s value | Sorted b -> Btree.mem_by b value

(* the same of a tuple in an array (a hashed set's: no closure) *)
let mem_array (t : t) (tuple : int array) : bool =
  match t with Hashed s -> Tuples.mem s tuple | Sorted b -> Btree.mem_by b (fun (i : int) -> tuple.(i))

(* (a hashed set's: none) *)
type hint = Btree.hint option

let hint (t : t) : hint = match t with Sorted b -> Some (Btree.hint b) | Hashed _ -> None

let mem_hint (t : t) (h : hint) (value : int -> int) : bool =
  match (t, h) with
  | Sorted b, Some h -> if Btree.width b = 2 then Btree.mem2_hint b h (value 0) (value 1) else Btree.mem_hint b h value
  | Hashed s, _ -> if Tuples.arity s = 2 then Tuples.mem2 s (value 0) (value 1) else Tuples.mem_by s value
  | Sorted b, None -> Btree.mem_by b value

let add (t : t) (tuple : int array) : bool =
  match t with
  | Hashed s -> Tuples.add s tuple
  | Sorted b -> if Btree.width b = 2 then Btree.add2 b tuple.(0) tuple.(1) else Btree.add_by b (fun (i : int) -> tuple.(i))

let part_of (t : t) (value : int -> int) : int =
  match t with Hashed s -> Tuples.part_of s value | Sorted b -> Btree.part_of b value

(* A relation's set of tuples, of one of two kinds, chosen for each
 * relation (mini-datalog -btree):
 *
 *   hashed (Tuples)                  sorted (Btree)
 *   ------------------------------   ---------------------------------
 *   a tuple's slot by its hash:      a tuple's leaf by its order: the
 *   one probe, a miss of the cache   tuples near it in the same leaf;
 *   whoever asked before             a test after one of a neighbour
 *                                    is in the cache (the hint)
 *   adding: a slot written           adding: the leaf's tuples after
 *                                    it moved right
 *   its indexes: Hash_index          its indexes: Tree_index
 *
 * Which wins depends on the order the rules ask in, which is why it is
 * a relation's choice: the tests of a rule's head that come out sorted
 * (Tree_index's lookups give their tuples in order) are neighbours in
 * a sorted set; a relation mostly added to, or asked at random, is
 * better hashed (languages/datalog/README.md's numbers).
 *
 * others:
 * Souffle declares a relation's representation: .decl r(x, y) btree
 * (its default), brie (a trie of the columns, for dense relations),
 * eqrel (an equivalence relation, kept as its classes, union-find).
 * Databases choose an index's kind per table and per column too: a
 * hash for equality, a B-tree for ranges and order. *)

type t

(* a set of tuples of n values, sorted or hashed *)
val create : sorted:bool -> int -> t

val sorted : t -> bool

(* is the tuple whose i-th value is [value i] there? *)
val mem_by : t -> (int -> int) -> bool
(* the same, the tuple an array (a hashed set's: no closure) *)
val mem_array : t -> int array -> bool

(* the same for a rule's heads, one after the other: a sorted set
 * tries the leaf of the one before first (Btree's hint), a pair's test
 * written out *)
type hint
val hint : t -> hint
val mem_hint : t -> hint -> (int -> int) -> bool

(* false: it was there *)
val add : t -> int array -> bool

(* the part of the tuple (Tuples's and Btree's 64): domains add at once
 * the tuples of different parts *)
val part_of : t -> (int -> int) -> int

(* order.(j): the column at place j, the key's first; at.(c): the place
 * of column c *)
type t = { key : int; order : int array; at : int array; tree : Btree.t }

let create (arity : int) (cols : int array) : t =
  let rest = List.filter (fun (c : int) -> not (Array.mem c cols)) (List.init arity (fun (c : int) -> c)) in
  let order = Array.append cols (Array.of_list rest) in
  let at = Array.make arity 0 in
  Array.iteri (fun (j : int) (c : int) -> at.(c) <- j) order;
  { key = Array.length cols; order; at; tree = Btree.create arity }

let add (t : t) (value : int -> int) : unit =
  if Array.length t.order = 2 then ignore (Btree.add2 t.tree (value t.order.(0)) (value t.order.(1)))
  else ignore (Btree.add_by t.tree (fun (j : int) -> value t.order.(j)))
let iter (t : t) (key : int -> int) (f : int array -> int -> unit) : unit = Btree.iter_prefix t.tree t.key key f
let exists (t : t) (key : int -> int) : bool = Btree.exists_prefix t.tree t.key key
let at (t : t) : int array = t.at
let part_of (t : t) (value : int -> int) : int = Btree.part_of t.tree (fun (j : int) -> value t.order.(j))
