tiny/TinyKernel.ml
3922
(* Claude Code
 * Copyright (C) 2026 Yoann Padioleau. LGPL 2.1: see license.txt. *)

(* See TinyKernel.mli *)

(* what draws, what keeps files on the disk, and what gives a process
 * its memory (TinyKernelGraphics, TinyKernelFS, TinyKernelMemory); and
 * the kernel's own parts, in their order (TinyKernel.mli): the
 * Makefile gives tiny-ml their files before this one, as one program *)
open TinyKernelGraphics
open TinyKernelFS
open TinyKernelMemory
open TinyKernelMachine
open TinyKernelFiles
open TinyKernelProcs
open TinyKernelDevices
open TinyKernelCalls
open TinyKernelScheduler

(*****************************************************************************)
(* The boot *)
(*****************************************************************************)

let () =
  k_init ();
  if cores > 1 then k_ie 27;
  counted := k_clock ();
  k_timer tick;
  load (k_end ());
  (match root with
   | Dir d ->
       d := !d @ [ "dev", Dir (ref [ "console", Tty; "draw", Screen;
                                    "mouse", Pointer; "audio", Speaker;
                                    "ps", Ps ]) ]
   | _ -> ());
  k_zero ring_at ring;
  poke speaker_dev ring_at;
  (* how the processes get memory: /lib/memory, which the Makefile's
   * MEMORY=segments puts in the image; partitions otherwise *)
  (match walk root (names [] "/lib/memory") with
   | Some node ->
       let s = contents node in
       let says w =
         String.length s >= String.length w
         && String.sub s 0 (String.length w) = w in
       segments := says "segments";
       pages := says "pages"
   | None -> ());
  puts ("tiny-kernel: TinyKernel.ml, "
        ^ string_of_int ((mem_high - mem_low) / part) ^ " MB for "
        ^ string_of_int nslots ^ " processes"
        ^ (if !segments then ", in segments\n"
           else if !pages then ", in pages\n" else "\n"));
  (* The disk, when there is one, is the root: the top becomes a union
   * of the disk's root, of /boot and /dump, and of the image's files.
   * Its snapshots are in /dump, each under the number of the boot that
   * left it. Its /bin and /usr/glenda are made at its first boot, and the
   * first shell starts in /usr/glenda. *)
  let blocks = peek disk_dev in
  if blocks > 0 then begin
    fs_io := (fun b a cmd ->
      poke disk_dev b;
      poke (disk_dev + 4) a;
      poke (disk_dev + 8) cmd;
      poke (disk_dev + 12) 0);
    fs_clock := date;
    fs_mount blocks;
    let made d name =
      match fs_lookup 0 d name with 0 -> fs_create d name 1 | j -> j in
    ignore (made 1 "bin");
    ignore (made (made 1 "usr") "glenda");
    fs_commit ();
    let dumps =
      List.map (fun (r, boot) -> string_of_int boot, Disk (r, 1))
        (fs_snapshots ()) in
    top := Union [ Disk (0, 1);
                   Dir (ref [ "boot", root; "dump", Dir (ref dumps) ]);
                   root ];
    puts ("tiny-kernel: / on a disk of " ^ string_of_int blocks ^ " KB, "
          ^ string_of_int (fs_free ()) ^ " KB free; "
          ^ string_of_int (List.length dumps) ^ " snapshots in /dump\n")
  end;
  (* the first process: /bin/sh, the console its 0, 1 and 2; and for the
   * programs it runs, which inherit them, the screen its 3 (a
   * connection) and the mouse its 4: a window system gives a window's
   * programs the same five, so a program draws in what it was given
   * and does not ask where *)
  let fds = [ 0, Console; 1, Console; 2, Console;
              3, Draw { conn = connect screen font; refs = 1 };
              4, Peek mouse ] in
  let p = {
    slot = 0; mem = mem_empty (); pid = 1; state = Ready; parent = 0;
    fds = fds; cwd = (if blocks > 0 then [ "usr"; "glenda" ] else []);
    since = -1; traced = None; core = -1; doomed = false;
    cmd = ""; memory = 0;
  } in
  incr next_pid;
  procs := [ p ];
  (try load_prog p (walk !top [ "bin"; "sh" ]) [ "sh" ]
   with Bad | No_room -> puts "no /bin/sh\n"; halt 1);
  schedule ()
tiny/TinyKernel.mli
17964
(* A tiny kernel, written in ML, for tiny-machine (TinyMachine.ml). It
 * contains the essentials of an operating system and borrows nothing
 * from an existing kernel except ideas. Its programs are in ML (most of
 * them) or in C (sh, mltests and the network's):
 *
 *     ./tiny-machine tiny-kernel   (at the top of ix; or make run in TinyKernel/)
 *     $ echo hello | wc; mkdir d; cd d; echo x > f; cd ..; cat d/f; ls
 *     $ ls /; ls /dump                          the next boot: f is still there
 *     $ mltests
 *     ./tiny-machine -window tiny-kernel      its screen in a window
 *     $ paint                                 or windows, and paint in a window
 *
 * Why it is not a twin of an existing kernel. In ix, each mini-xxx is
 * a twin of an original program, while each tiny-xxx keeps what is
 * fundamental and drops the rest according to what it costs. A kernel
 * seems to call for a twin (of xv6 or 9pi) for two reasons. First, it
 * is not a leaf: its system calls are a contract with every program
 * above it, so a new interface means a new userland. Second, a
 * reference implementation answers the hard questions (what wait
 * returns and when, what the reader of a dead pipe sees), and that has
 * been the first debugging tool of mini-9pi and mini-xv6. But xv6 is
 * tiny only for C: it has locks, a kernel stack per process, and an
 * on-disk file system. In ML other paths are shorter, so this kernel
 * keeps the concepts and chooses its own way to implement each one:
 *
 *   concept                how it is done             why it is cheap here
 *   user and kernel        a trap returns from        the machine has one way
 *   modes, system calls    k_run; a system call is a  in and one way out
 *                          match on its number
 *   preemptive scheduling  round robin on the timer   a list; the process that
 *                                                     ran is moved to the end
 *   protection             tiny-machine's relocating  no page tables to build
 *                          window, a partition per
 *                          process, of the size its
 *                          program asks
 *   processes              fork, exec, spawn, exit,   with a window, fork just
 *                          wait                       copies a partition: one
 *                                                     k_copy
 *   blocking               each waiting process has   no kernel stack per
 *                          a closure, the rest of     process, no swtch, no
 *                          its call, retried by the   sleep, no locks
 *                          scheduler
 *   files and directories  the disk's                 no log, no fsck, no map
 *                          (TinyKernelFS.ml):         of free blocks: a commit
 *                          inodes, copied on write,   is one block written; a
 *                          the root; the boot         collector finds the free
 *                          image's, a tree of ML      ones
 *                          values, in a union with
 *                          it
 *   console, pipes         other kinds of open files  pipes make a shell a
 *                                                     shell
 *   a screen, a mouse      descriptors 3 and 4 of a   TinyKernelGraphics.ml
 *                          program: it writes         draws; no memory is
 *                          drawing messages (the      shared, so nothing to map
 *                          kernel owns the pixels)
 *                          and reads the mouse
 *                          position
 *   a window system        a program                  a window's program gets
 *                          (TinyWindows.ml) using     the same kind of
 *                          pipes and a box, a pipe    interface the kernel
 *                          that keeps only the last   gives
 *                          write (for a window's
 *                          mouse)
 *   waiting for several    ready(fds, n, until): one  again a closure: a list
 *   things, or for a time  more closure, using the    is scanned, no select
 *                          clock's ticks              queues
 *
 * The files. The programs come in the boot image, after the kernel,
 * and are read from memory. With a disk (-d), the disk is the root,
 * Plan 9's way: / is a union of the disk's root, of /boot (the image's
 * files alone) and /dump (the snapshots of the boots before), and of
 * the image's files, so /bin is the disk's /bin and /boot/bin together.
 * What is written goes to the disk, and is kept; a file of the image
 * written by its /bin name is copied to the disk first. The first shell
 * starts in /usr/glenda: glenda is the user of a Plan 9 installed from
 * its CD (and the name of its bunny). With no disk, the tree is the
 * image's alone and lives in memory until the halt.
 *
 * What is dropped: paging, multiple cores, users and permissions, and signals
 * except the simplest: kill(pid) ends a process as a fault does (with
 * status -1), and ^C at the console kills every process except the
 * shell. The system calls are specific to this kernel (its programs
 * are in TinyKernel/user/), but t6's cat, echo, ls, wc, mkdir and rm
 * run unchanged, because they use only calls the two kernels have in
 * common.
 *
 * Where it fits: it is the tiny program in ix's Kernel row (see the
 * README), as mini-9pi is the mini one. It is not a new version of the
 * kernels that came before it on the same machine (v0 and t6 in
 * steps/, written in assembly and C). TinyKernel/ holds the rest:
 * entry.tm, runtime.c, the user programs, and the Makefile.
 *
 * The toolchain is entirely ix's own, and so is the bridge between ML
 * and the machine. It is small, where the bridge of mini-9pi and
 * mini-xv6 (kernels/lib_machine/: ocaml-light's C runtime, gcc, boot
 * code, C glue) cannot be:
 * - tiny-ml: the second back end of the stack machine (TinyML.ml);
 * - the runtime: TinyMLRuntime/core.c, shared with every tiny-ml
 *   program, and runtime.c, which holds the kernel's memory layout and
 *   ten functions on bytes (peek, poke, copying a string from memory
 *   and to it);
 * - entry.tm, one page of assembly: k_run (which runs the process until
 *   its next trap, so the kernel calls a process like a function, the
 *   way a hypervisor's KVM_RUN runs a guest), the trap entry, the
 *   timer, and the window; memory.tm, the loops that copy a partition
 *   at fork and zero memory.
 * The compiler needs no new primitive: the machine is reached through
 * externals, which are functions written in C or in assembly.
 *
 * How it runs. The toplevel reads the files carried by the image,
 * creates the first process (/bin/sh, with the console as its 0, 1 and 2),
 * and enters [schedule], a loop that never returns: run a process
 * until it traps, handle the trap, and choose again. A process has a
 * slot (a partition, and a frame of 17 words where entry.tm saves its
 * registers), a pid, a state, a parent, its descriptors and its
 * current directory. A system call that must wait (a read on an empty
 * pipe, or a wait) leaves its process Waiting, with the rest of the
 * call stored as a closure. The scheduler calls that closure when it
 * looks for a process to run, and the process becomes ready again once
 * the closure can finish. So there is no wakeup to forget (the
 * lost-wakeup bug of sleep and wakeup) and no channel: a process waits
 * on a condition, as with Brinch Hansen's await and Plan 9's
 * sleep(r, cond), at the price of one retry per scheduling round.
 *
 * Several cores (tiny-machine -cores n, plan_tiny_multicore.md). The
 * kernel stays core 0's, whole: one heap, one collector, written for
 * one thread. The others run processes only, in entry.tm's slave loop,
 * which runs no ML: core 0 writes a process's frame, window and slice
 * in core k's mailbox and raises k's interrupt; k runs the process
 * until its trap, writes the cause back and raises core 0's, which
 * handles the trap as one of its own ([back]). So the kernel needs no
 * lock and its structures did not change; what does not scale is the
 * system calls, one core's, which a compiler makes few of. The first
 * multiprocessor Unix kernels worked the same way, master and slaves
 * (Purdue's dual VAX, Goble and Marsh, 1982):
 *
 *     core k                                  core 0
 *     runs P (k's mailbox) ── a trap ──>      [interrupts]: P's trap,
 *     cause, value in the mailbox,            handled as its own ([back]);
 *     core 0's interrupt; waits               P or another given to k
 *                               <── k's interrupt (frame, window, slice)
 *
 * The kernel is several files, one program for tiny-ml, in this order
 * (TinyKernel/Makefile's KML). First what it stands on: TinyMemory (the
 * machine's bytes), TinyKernelGraphics, TinyKernelNetwork,
 * TinyKernelAudio, TinyKernelFS, TinyKernelMemory. Then its own parts,
 * once this file's sections: TinyKernelMachine (the externals, the
 * devices' addresses), TinyKernelFiles (the tree of files, what a
 * descriptor is), TinyKernelProcs, TinyKernelDevices (the screen, the
 * mouse, the clock, the speaker), TinyKernelIO (reads and writes),
 * TinyKernelCalls (the system calls), TinyKernelScheduler. This file is
 * the boot.
 *
 * Here is how the kernel divides the machine's 256 MB (runtime.c has
 * the numbers; a process sees only its own partition, starting at 0,
 * thanks to the machine's relocating window):
 *
 *     0x000000   the image: entry.tm, the runtime, the kernel; then the
 *                files it carries, each a name, a size, the bytes
 *                (10 MB at most: /src, the sources, are among them)
 *     0xa00000   the file system's buffers and its map of the
 *                disk's blocks (TinyKernelFS.ml)
 *     0xb00000   the value stack: the kernel's own roots (TinyML's)
 *     0xb40000   the frames, 68 bytes per slot: r1 to r15 and the pc
 *                of each process that is not running
 *     0xb41000   the cores' mailboxes, 64 bytes each
 *     0xb50000   a packet's place, sent or received
 *     0xb51000   with pages, a byte for each page of the processes'
 *                memory, its users (TinyKernelMemory.ml)
 *     0xb60000   the bounce: a buffer in several pieces, read or
 *                written through it (sys_rw; none with partitions)
 *     0xc00000   the speaker's ring
 *     0xd00000   pixels of images: the font, the hidden windows
 *     0xf00000   the screen, 1024 by 768 bytes; more images after it
 *    0x1000000   the heap, two halves of 8 MB: every file written,
 *                every pipe, descriptor table and closure
 *    0x2000000   the processes' partitions: 1 MB each, or what an
 *                a.out's header asks for (tiny-linker -a), found
 *                first-fit when a program starts
 *    0xfffffc0   the devices, reached as -64 to -4
 *
 * A process's memory is TinyKernelMemory's (TinyKernel/): a partition
 * by default, the simplest way, with its history and what came after;
 * segments with MEMORY=segments (the program's text shared by its
 * runs, read only; pages next: plan_tiny_memory.md). fork copies the
 * parent's partition whole; spawn, fork and exec in one, copies nothing
 * (tiny-build starts each recipe's rc with it: its own partition is
 * 16 MB).
 *
 * A process consists of two very different things. One is its
 * partition and its frame, plain memory that the collector never sees
 * and that is accessed with peek and poke. The other is its record, an
 * ML value, where the descriptors are a list of (number, file) pairs
 * and a file is a variant. Here is the whole mechanism for a read that
 * must wait (wc reading a pipe that nothing has been written to yet):
 *
 *     wc: sys read      the trap ends k_run; [syscall] finds the file
 *                       and the buffer and calls [block] with the
 *                       attempt, a closure that reads what is there,
 *                       puts the count in the frame's r1, and returns
 *                       true
 *     the attempt       returns false: the pipe is empty and still has
 *                       a writer; wc becomes Waiting with that
 *                       closure, and goes to the end of the round
 *     [schedule]        [runnable] goes down the list: a Ready process
 *                       is chosen; for a Waiting one, its closure is
 *                       called again
 *     echo: sys write   the pipe's buffer grows; echo keeps running
 *     [schedule]        this time wc's closure returns true: the
 *                       answer is already in its frame, wc is Ready,
 *                       and k_run runs it
 *
 * Nothing links the pipe to the processes waiting on it: no queue, no
 * channel, no wakeup. The closure holds the file, the address and the
 * count, which is exactly what a C kernel keeps the sleeping process's
 * kernel stack for.
 *
 * Exercises, each cheap in this design:
 * - a cache of the disk's blocks, and the count of the instructions it
 *   saves (each access reads its blocks again: the disk is instant);
 * - keep each waiting process's closure together with what it waits
 *   for, and retry it only when that changes (a wakeup again, but a
 *   typed one);
 * - copy-on-write fork: share the partition until one side writes,
 *   using pages (tiny-machine's Sv32), which is why pages were
 *   invented (plan_tiny_memory.md's stage 4);
 * - measure the kernel's own heap: print its live words after each
 *   collection, and at halt.
 *
 * cs-history:
 * The sixth edition Unix kernel (1975), the one that John Lions's
 * commentary turned into a textbook, blocks a process with
 * sleep(chan, pri) and wakes every process sleeping on that address
 * with wakeup(chan). Each process has a kernel stack, and swtch, which
 * switches stacks, carries the comment "You are not expected to
 * understand this". xv6 keeps all three, and adds a lock passed to
 * sleep so that a wakeup cannot slip in between the test and the
 * sleep. This file's waiting has no such window, because the test
 * itself is the waiting.
 *
 * design:
 * A kernel either keeps a stack for each process and blocks in the
 * middle of a call (Unix, Linux, xv6, Plan 9), or has a single stack
 * and must record, when a call cannot finish, what remains to be done
 * (Mach after Draves's continuations, and every event loop). Lauer and
 * Needham argued in 1978 that the two are duals: a program written in
 * one style can be mechanically turned into the other. In C the second
 * style costs a structure and a function for each place where a call
 * may stop, which is why C kernels choose stacks. In ML the compiler
 * builds that structure for us, a closure, and the second style is the
 * shorter one.
 *
 * wib:
 * Two costs are accepted. First, a waiting call is retried at every
 * round instead of being woken up, which wastes work while nothing
 * changes (the two shortcuts in [runnable] and [idle] exist because
 * this showed up). Second, fork copies the parent's whole partition
 * (16 MB for tiny-build: hence spawn), a program's memory is a guess
 * made when it is linked, and there can be only sixteen processes.
 * Both are things a real kernel spends its cleverness on, and both
 * can be measured here (the machine counts instructions).
 *
 * comeback:
 * A kernel written in a language with a garbage collector and no
 * pointer arithmetic is an old idea that keeps coming back: Burroughs's
 * MCP in an Algol dialect (1961), the Lisp machines, Xerox's Pilot in
 * Mesa (1980), SPIN in Modula-3 (1995), Microsoft's Singularity (from
 * 2003), MirageOS in OCaml (2013), and, for safety without a
 * collector, Rust in Linux (2022). Each time, the argument is that the
 * language can do some of the protection that hardware and discipline
 * do in C. Here protection is still done by the hardware (the window);
 * what the language provides is the file tree and the closures.
 *
 * others:
 * Not every system makes a process the way Unix does. VMS's $CREPRC
 * and Windows's CreateProcess start a process in a program, with no
 * fork at all; POSIX added posix_spawn (1003.1d, 1999), for machines
 * without an MMU and for speed; BSD's vfork (from memory: 3BSD's)
 * let the child borrow its parent's memory until its exec, before
 * copy-on-write; Plan 9's rfork says what the child shares. Baumann et
 * al., "A fork() in the road" (2019), argue that fork has become a
 * burden. This kernel has both: fork and exec because a shell is
 * written with them (rc's redirections are done in the child),
 * spawn because a parent of 16 MB that starts rc should not copy
 * itself first.
 *
 * References:
 *  - P. Brinch Hansen, "Structured Multiprogramming" (CACM 1972): await
 *  - R. Pike et al., "The Use of Name Spaces in Plan 9" (1993), and
 *    Plan 9's sleep and wakeup
 *  - D. M. Ritchie and K. Thompson, "The UNIX Time-Sharing System"
 *    (CACM 1974): fork, exec, pipes
 *  - R. Draves et al., "Using Continuations to Implement Thread
 *    Management and Communication in Operating Systems" (SOSP 1991)
 *  - A. Kivity et al., "kvm: the Linux Virtual Machine Monitor" (OLS
 *    2007): a guest run by a call that returns when the guest exits
 *  - G. Hunt and J. Larus, "Singularity: Rethinking the Software
 *    Stack" (2007): a kernel in a safe, garbage-collected language
 *  - A. Madhavapeddy et al., "Unikernels" (ASPLOS 2013): MirageOS, a
 *    kernel in OCaml
 *  - P. Denning, "Virtual Memory" (Computing Surveys 1970): partitions
 *    before pages
 *  - A. Baumann et al., "A fork() in the road" (HotOS 2019): spawn
 *    against fork
 *)

(* See Array.mli *)

external make : int -> 'a -> 'a array = "ml_array_make"
external length : 'a array -> int = "ml_array_length"
external get : 'a array -> int -> 'a = "ml_array_get"
external set : 'a array -> int -> 'a -> unit = "ml_array_set"

(* (no [||] in tiny-ml: an empty array is made of no element) *)
external empty : int -> unit -> 'a array = "ml_array_make"
let of_list l =
  match l with
  | [] -> empty 0 ()
  | x :: _ ->
    let a = make (List.length l) x in
    List.iteri (fun i y -> set a i y) l;
    a
let to_list a =
  let rec go i acc = if i < 0 then acc else go (i - 1) (get a i :: acc) in
  go (length a - 1) []
let init n f =
  if n = 0 then empty 0 ()
  else (let a = make n (f 0) in for i = 1 to n - 1 do set a i (f i) done; a)
let sub a off n =
  if off < 0 || n < 0 || off + n > length a then invalid_arg "Array.sub"
  else init n (fun i -> get a (off + i))
let copy a = sub a 0 (length a)
let map f a = init (length a) (fun i -> f (get a i))
let append a b =
  let n = length a in
  init (n + length b) (fun i -> if i < n then get a i else get b (i - n))
let concat l = of_list (List.concat_map to_list l)
let iter f a = for i = 0 to length a - 1 do f (get a i) done
let to_seq a = Seq.init (length a) (get a)

(* Claude Code
 * Copyright (C) 2026 Yoann Padioleau. LGPL 2.1: see license.txt. *)

(* See Buffer.mli *)

type t = { mutable buffer_bytes : bytes; mutable buffer_length : int }

(* (at most 256 bytes at first: a program's partition is 1 MB, and
 * create's size is a guess, OCaml's too) *)
let create n =
  { buffer_bytes = Bytes.make (max 16 (min n 256)) '\000'; buffer_length = 0 }

(* room for more: the bytes copied into twice as many, or more *)
let grow b more =
  let need = b.buffer_length + more in
  let cap = Bytes.length b.buffer_bytes in
  if need > cap then begin
    let n = ref (2 * cap) in
    while !n < need do n := 2 * !n done;
    let bytes = Bytes.make !n '\000' in
    Bytes.blit b.buffer_bytes 0 bytes 0 b.buffer_length;
    b.buffer_bytes <- bytes
  end

let add_string b s =
  let n = String.length s in
  grow b n;
  Bytes.blit_string s 0 b.buffer_bytes b.buffer_length n;
  b.buffer_length <- b.buffer_length + n
let add_char b c =
  grow b 1;
  Bytes.set b.buffer_bytes b.buffer_length c;
  b.buffer_length <- b.buffer_length + 1
let contents b = Bytes.sub_string b.buffer_bytes 0 b.buffer_length
let length b = b.buffer_length
let clear b = b.buffer_length <- 0

(* Claude Code

(* See Filename.mli *)

let check_suffix name suffix =
  let n = String.length name and m = String.length suffix in
  n >= m && String.sub name (n - m) m = suffix
let concat dir file =
  let n = String.length dir in
  if n = 0 || String.get dir (n - 1) = '/' then dir ^ file else dir ^ "/" ^ file

(* OCaml's: the slashes at the end, then the last name, then the
 * slashes before it, taken away; "." when no directory is left *)
let dirname name =
  let sep n = String.get name n = '/' in
  let rec trailing n =
    if n < 0 then String.sub name 0 1
    else if sep n then trailing (n - 1) else base n
  and base n = if n < 0 then "." else if sep n then between n else base (n - 1)
  and between n =
    if n < 0 then String.sub name 0 1
    else if sep n then between (n - 1) else String.sub name 0 (n + 1) in
  if name = "" then "." else trailing (String.length name - 1)

(* the last name, its slashes at the end taken away (OCaml's) *)
let basename name =
  let sep n = String.get name n = '/' in
  let rec trailing n =
    if n < 0 then String.sub name 0 1
    else if sep n then trailing (n - 1) else base n n
  and base e n =
    if n < 0 || sep n then String.sub name (n + 1) (e - n) else base e (n - 1) in
  if name = "" then "." else trailing (String.length name - 1)
let is_relative name = name = "" || String.get name 0 <> '/'
let chop_suffix name suffix =
  if check_suffix name suffix
  then String.sub name 0 (String.length name - String.length suffix)
  else invalid_arg "Filename.chop_suffix"

(* the extension: from the last dot of the last name, unless only dots
 * come before it there (OCaml's: .profile has none) *)
let remove_extension name =
  let sep i = String.get name i = '/' in
  let n = String.length name in
  let rec check dot i =
    if i < 0 || sep i then 0
    else if String.get name i = '.' then check dot (i - 1) else n - dot in
  let rec search i =
    if i < 0 || sep i then 0
    else if String.get name i = '.' then check i (i - 1) else search (i - 1) in
  String.sub name 0 (n - search (n - 1))

(* Claude Code
 * Copyright (C) 2026 Yoann Padioleau. LGPL 2.1: see license.txt. *)

(* See Hashtbl.mli *)

external hash : 'a -> int = "ml_hash"

type ('a, 'b) t = {
  mutable hashtbl_size : int;
  mutable hashtbl_data : ('a * 'b) list array;
}

let create n =
  { hashtbl_size = 0; hashtbl_data = Array.make (max 8 (min n 1024)) [] }
let length h = h.hashtbl_size
let index h k = hash k mod Array.length h.hashtbl_data

(* twice as many buckets, each binding moved to its new one *)
let resize h =
  let old = h.hashtbl_data in
  let data = Array.make (2 * Array.length old) [] in
  h.hashtbl_data <- data;
  for i = 0 to Array.length old - 1 do
    List.iter (fun (k, v) -> let j = index h k in data.(j) <- (k, v) :: data.(j))
      (List.rev old.(i))
  done

(* (the buckets copied: their lists are not changed in place) *)
let copy h =
  { hashtbl_size = h.hashtbl_size; hashtbl_data = Array.copy h.hashtbl_data }
let find_opt h k = List.assoc_opt k h.hashtbl_data.(index h k)
let find h k = List.assoc k h.hashtbl_data.(index h k)
let find_all h k =
  List.filter_map (fun (a, v) -> if a = k then Some v else None)
    h.hashtbl_data.(index h k)
let mem h k = List.exists (fun (a, _) -> a = k) h.hashtbl_data.(index h k)
let remove h k =
  let i = index h k in
  let rec drop = function
    | [] -> []
    | (a, v) :: l ->
      if a = k then (h.hashtbl_size <- h.hashtbl_size - 1; l)
      else (a, v) :: drop l in
  h.hashtbl_data.(i) <- drop h.hashtbl_data.(i)
let add h k v =
  let i = index h k in
  h.hashtbl_data.(i) <- (k, v) :: h.hashtbl_data.(i);
  h.hashtbl_size <- h.hashtbl_size + 1;
  if h.hashtbl_size > 2 * Array.length h.hashtbl_data then resize h
let replace h k v = remove h k; add h k v
let fold f h acc =
  let acc = ref acc in
  for i = 0 to Array.length h.hashtbl_data - 1 do
    List.iter (fun (k, v) -> acc := f k v !acc) h.hashtbl_data.(i)
  done;
  !acc
let iter f h = fold (fun k v () -> f k v) h ()

(* See Int64.mli *)

(* four pieces of 16 bits, the high one first and signed, the others
 * 0 to 65535: an int has 31 bits. So two equal numbers are the same
 * tuple, and compare's order on the tuples is the numbers' *)
type int64 = int * int * int * int

let sext16 p = ((p land 0xffff) lxor 0x8000) - 0x8000

let zero = (0, 0, 0, 0)
let one = (0, 0, 0, 1)
let minus_one = (-1, 0xffff, 0xffff, 0xffff)
let max_int = (0x7fff, 0xffff, 0xffff, 0xffff)
let min_int = (-0x8000, 0, 0, 0)

let of_int n =
  let s = if n < 0 then 0xffff else 0 in
  (sext16 s, s, (n asr 16) land 0xffff, n land 0xffff)
(* the low bits that fit, as OCaml's *)
let to_int (_, b, c, d) = (((b lsl 16) lor c) lsl 16) lor d

(* each piece's carry into the next *)
let add (a3, a2, a1, a0) (b3, b2, b1, b0) =
  let s0 = a0 + b0 in
  let s1 = a1 + b1 + (s0 lsr 16) in
  let s2 = a2 + b2 + (s1 lsr 16) in
  (sext16 (a3 + b3 + (s2 lsr 16)), s2 land 0xffff, s1 land 0xffff, s0 land 0xffff)
(* (the high piece is signed: lnot, land... keep it so) *)
let lognot (a, b, c, d) = (lnot a, b lxor 0xffff, c lxor 0xffff, d lxor 0xffff)
let neg x = add (lognot x) one
let sub x y = add x (neg y)
let succ x = add x one
let pred x = sub x one
let logand (a3, a2, a1, a0) (b3, b2, b1, b0) =
  (a3 land b3, a2 land b2, a1 land b1, a0 land b0)
let logor (a3, a2, a1, a0) (b3, b2, b1, b0) =
  (a3 lor b3, a2 lor b2, a1 lor b1, a0 lor b0)
let logxor (a3, a2, a1, a0) (b3, b2, b1, b0) =
  (a3 lxor b3, a2 lxor b2, a1 lxor b1, a0 lxor b0)
let equal (x : int64) y = x = y
let compare (x : int64) y = compare x y
let abs x = if compare x zero < 0 then neg x else x

(* the bytes, the low first: a product of two is 16 bits, so the
 * columns' sums fit where the pieces' products would not *)
let mul (a3, a2, a1, a0) (b3, b2, b1, b0) =
  let bytes p3 p2 p1 p0 =
    Array.of_list
      [ p0 land 0xff; p0 lsr 8; p1 land 0xff; p1 lsr 8;
        p2 land 0xff; p2 lsr 8; p3 land 0xff; (p3 land 0xffff) lsr 8 ] in
  let a = bytes a3 a2 a1 a0 and b = bytes b3 b2 b1 b0 in
  let r = Array.make 8 0 and carry = ref 0 in
  for k = 0 to 7 do
    let s = ref !carry in
    for i = 0 to k do s := !s + (a.(i) * b.(k - i)) done;
    r.(k) <- !s land 0xff; carry := !s lsr 8
  done;
  let piece k = r.(2 * k) lor (r.((2 * k) + 1) lsl 8) in
  (sext16 (piece 3), piece 2, piece 1, piece 0)

(* the pieces, the low first, unsigned; a shift is of whole pieces,
 * then of bits within them *)
let shifted (a, b, c, d) n f =
  let p = Array.of_list [ d; c; b; a land 0xffff ] in
  let at i = if i >= 0 && i < 4 then p.(i) else 0 in
  let q = Array.init 4 (fun i -> f at i (n / 16) (n mod 16) land 0xffff) in
  (sext16 q.(3), q.(2), q.(1), q.(0))
let shift_right_logical x n =
  shifted x n (fun at i k s ->
    (at (i + k) lsr s) lor (at (i + k + 1) lsl (16 - s)))
let shift_left x n =
  shifted x n (fun at i k s ->
    (at (i - k) lsl s) lor (at (i - k - 1) lsr (16 - s)))
let shift_right x n =
  if compare x zero < 0 then lognot (shift_right_logical (lognot x) n)
  else shift_right_logical x n

(* unsigned: x < y, and the quotient and remainder, a bit at a time
 * (twice a number and a bit added, its bit i), but for two numbers
 * of 30 bits, an int's division *)
let ult x y = compare (logxor x min_int) (logxor y min_int) < 0
let small (a, b, c, _) = a = 0 && b = 0 && c < 0x4000
let udivmod x y =
  let twice (a, b, c, d) bit =
    (sext16 ((a lsl 1) lor (b lsr 15)),
     ((b lsl 1) land 0xffff) lor (c lsr 15),
     ((c lsl 1) land 0xffff) lor (d lsr 15),
     ((d lsl 1) land 0xffff) lor bit) in
  let bit (a, b, c, d) i =
    let p = match i / 16 with 0 -> d | 1 -> c | 2 -> b | _ -> a land 0xffff in
    (p lsr (i mod 16)) land 1 in
  let rec go i q r =
    if i < 0 then q, r
    else
      let r = twice r (bit x i) in
      if ult r y then go (i - 1) (twice q 0) r
      else go (i - 1) (twice q 1) (sub r y) in
  if small x && small y
  then of_int (to_int x / to_int y), of_int (to_int x mod to_int y)
  else go 63 zero zero
(* truncated, as OCaml's: the remainder has the dividend's sign *)
let div x y =
  if y = zero then raise Division_by_zero;
  let q, _ = udivmod (abs x) (abs y) in
  if (compare x zero < 0) <> (compare y zero < 0) then neg q else q
let rem x y =
  if y = zero then raise Division_by_zero;
  let _, r = udivmod (abs x) (abs y) in
  if compare x zero < 0 then neg r else r

(* in decimal; read as OCaml does, in decimal or after 0x, 0o or 0b,
 * a sign before *)
let to_string x =
  (* x, unsigned, divided by 10: each piece's remainder carried into
   * the next *)
  let div10 (a, b, c, d) =
    let a = a land 0xffff in
    let v2 = ((a mod 10) * 0x10000) + b in
    let v1 = ((v2 mod 10) * 0x10000) + c in
    let v0 = ((v1 mod 10) * 0x10000) + d in
    (a / 10, v2 / 10, v1 / 10, v0 / 10), v0 mod 10 in
  let rec digits x acc =
    if x = zero then acc
    else let q, r = div10 x in digits q (string_of_int r ^ acc) in
  if x = zero then "0"
  else if compare x zero < 0 then "-" ^ digits (neg x) ""
  else digits x ""
let of_string s =
  let n = String.length s in
  let neg_ = n > 0 && s.[0] = '-' in
  let i = if n > 0 && (s.[0] = '-' || s.[0] = '+') then 1 else 0 in
  let base, i =
    if i + 1 < n && s.[i] = '0' then
      match s.[i + 1] with
      | 'x' | 'X' -> 16, i + 2
      | 'o' | 'O' -> 8, i + 2
      | 'b' | 'B' -> 2, i + 2
      | _ -> 10, i
    else 10, i in
  let digit c =
    let k = Char.code c in
    if c >= '0' && c <= '9' then k - 48
    else if c >= 'a' && c <= 'f' then k - 87
    else if c >= 'A' && c <= 'F' then k - 55
    else 99 in
  if i >= n then failwith "Int64.of_string";
  let rec go j x =
    if j = n then x
    else if s.[j] = '_' then go (j + 1) x
    else
      let d = digit s.[j] in
      if d >= base then failwith "Int64.of_string"
      else go (j + 1) (add (mul x (of_int base)) (of_int d)) in
  let x = go i zero in
  if neg_ then neg x else x

(* See List.mli *)

let length l = let rec len n = function [] -> n | _ :: l -> len (n + 1) l in len 0 l
let rev l =
  let rec rev acc = function [] -> acc | x :: l -> rev (x :: acc) l in
  rev [] l
let hd = function [] -> failwith "hd" | x :: _ -> x
let tl = function [] -> failwith "tl" | _ :: l -> l
let rec nth l n =
  match l with [] -> failwith "nth" | x :: l -> if n = 0 then x else nth l (n - 1)
let rec nth_opt l n =
  match l with
  | [] -> None
  | x :: l -> if n = 0 then Some x else nth_opt l (n - 1)
let rec map f = function [] -> [] | x :: l -> let y = f x in y :: map f l
let mapi f l =
  let rec go i = function
    | [] -> []
    | x :: l -> let y = f i x in y :: go (i + 1) l in
  go 0 l
let rec map2 f l1 l2 =
  match l1, l2 with
  | [], [] -> []
  | x :: l1, y :: l2 -> let z = f x y in z :: map2 f l1 l2
  | _ -> invalid_arg "List.map2"
let rec iter f = function [] -> () | x :: l -> f x; iter f l
let iteri f l =
  let rec go i = function [] -> () | x :: l -> f i x; go (i + 1) l in
  go 0 l
let rec fold_left f acc = function [] -> acc | x :: l -> fold_left f (f acc x) l
let rec fold_right f l acc =
  match l with [] -> acc | x :: l -> f x (fold_right f l acc)
let rec mem x = function [] -> false | y :: l -> x = y || mem x l
let rec assoc x = function
  | [] -> raise Not_found
  | (a, b) :: l -> if a = x then b else assoc x l
let rec assoc_opt x = function
  | [] -> None
  | (a, b) :: l -> if a = x then Some b else assoc_opt x l
let rec find_opt p = function
  | [] -> None
  | x :: l -> if p x then Some x else find_opt p l
let rec find p = function
  | [] -> raise Not_found
  | x :: l -> if p x then x else find p l
let rec find_map f = function
  | [] -> None
  | x :: l -> (match f x with Some y -> Some y | None -> find_map f l)
let rec rev_append l acc = match l with [] -> acc | x :: l -> rev_append l (x :: acc)
let rec combine l1 l2 =
  match l1, l2 with
  | [], [] -> []
  | x :: l1, y :: l2 -> (x, y) :: combine l1 l2
  | _ -> invalid_arg "List.combine"
let rec for_all2 p l1 l2 =
  match l1, l2 with
  | [], [] -> true
  | x :: l1, y :: l2 -> p x y && for_all2 p l1 l2
  | _ -> invalid_arg "List.for_all2"
let rec mem_assoc x = function [] -> false | (a, _) :: l -> a = x || mem_assoc x l
let rec iter2 f l1 l2 =
  match l1, l2 with
  | [], [] -> ()
  | x :: l1, y :: l2 -> f x y; iter2 f l1 l2
  | _ -> invalid_arg "List.iter2"
let rev_map f l =
  let rec go acc = function [] -> acc | x :: l -> go (f x :: acc) l in
  go [] l
let rec remove_assoc x = function
  | [] -> []
  | (a, b) :: l -> if a = x then l else (a, b) :: remove_assoc x l
let rec memq x = function [] -> false | y :: l -> x == y || memq x l
let rec exists p = function [] -> false | x :: l -> p x || exists p l
let rec for_all p = function [] -> true | x :: l -> p x && for_all p l
let rec to_seq l () = match l with [] -> Seq.Nil | x :: r -> Seq.Cons (x, to_seq r)
let of_seq s = rev (Seq.fold_left (fun acc x -> x :: acc) [] s)
let filter_map f l =
  let rec go acc = function
    | [] -> rev acc
    | x :: l ->
      (match f x with Some y -> go (y :: acc) l | None -> go acc l) in
  go [] l
let filter p l =
  let rec find acc = function
    | [] -> rev acc
    | x :: l -> if p x then find (x :: acc) l else find acc l in
  find [] l
let partition p l =
  let rec go yes no = function
    | [] -> rev yes, rev no
    | x :: l -> if p x then go (x :: yes) no l else go yes (x :: no) l in
  go [] [] l
let filteri p l =
  let rec go i = function
    | [] -> []
    | x :: l -> if p i x then x :: go (i + 1) l else go (i + 1) l in
  go 0 l
let rec concat = function [] -> [] | l :: r -> l @ concat r
let concat_map f l = concat (map f l)
let init n f =
  let rec go i = if i >= n then [] else let x = f i in x :: go (i + 1) in
  go 0

(* a merge sort, stable as OCaml's *)
let rec sort cmp l =
  let rec onto acc l = match acc with [] -> l | x :: r -> onto r (x :: l) in
  let rec take n l acc =
    if n = 0 then onto acc [], l
    else
      match l with
      | [] -> onto acc [], []
      | x :: r -> take (n - 1) r (x :: acc) in
  let rec merge a b acc =
    match a, b with
    | [], l -> onto acc l
    | l, [] -> onto acc l
    | x :: ra, y :: rb ->
      if cmp x y <= 0 then merge ra b (x :: acc) else merge a rb (y :: acc) in
  match l with
  | [] -> l
  | [ _ ] -> l
  | _ ->
      let a, b = take (length l / 2) l [] in
      merge (sort cmp a) (sort cmp b) []
(* (a function, not sort itself: a value computed at the unit's init
 * would keep sort in every program) *)
let stable_sort cmp l = sort cmp l
let sort_uniq cmp l =
  let rec uniq = function
    | x :: (y :: _ as l) -> if cmp x y = 0 then uniq l else x :: uniq l
    | l -> l in
  uniq (sort cmp l)

let hex n =
  let digit d = String.make 1 (String.get "0123456789abcdef" d) in
  let rec go n acc = if n = 0 then acc else go (n lsr 4) (digit (n land 15) ^ acc) in
  if n = 0 then "0" else go n ""

let quoted s =
  let b = Buffer.create (String.length s + 2) in
  Buffer.add_char b '"';
  String.iter (fun c ->
    match c with
    | '"' -> Buffer.add_string b "\\\""
    | '\\' -> Buffer.add_string b "\\\\"
    | '\n' -> Buffer.add_string b "\\n"
    | '\t' -> Buffer.add_string b "\\t"
    | '\r' -> Buffer.add_string b "\\r"
    | '\b' -> Buffer.add_string b "\\b"
    | c when c < ' ' || c > '~' ->
        let k = Char.code c in
        Buffer.add_char b '\\';
        Buffer.add_string b
          (string_of_int (k / 100) ^ string_of_int (k / 10 mod 10)
           ^ string_of_int (k mod 10))
    | c -> Buffer.add_char b c) s;
  Buffer.add_char b '"';
  Buffer.contents b

let pad left zero w s =
  let n = String.length s in
  if n >= w then s
  else if left then s ^ String.make (w - n) ' '
  else if not zero then String.make (w - n) ' ' ^ s
  else if n > 0 && s.[0] = '-'
  then "-" ^ String.make (w - n) '0' ^ String.sub s 1 (n - 1)
  else String.make (w - n) '0' ^ s

(* See Seq.mli *)

type 'a t = unit -> 'a node
and 'a node = Nil | Cons of 'a * 'a t

let empty () = Nil
let init n f =
  let rec go i () = if i >= n then Nil else Cons (f i, go (i + 1)) in
  go 0
let rec map f s () = match s () with Nil -> Nil | Cons (x, r) -> Cons (f x, map f r)
let rec filter p s () =
  match s () with
  | Nil -> Nil
  | Cons (x, r) -> if p x then Cons (x, filter p r) else filter p r ()
let rec filter_map f s () =
  match s () with
  | Nil -> Nil
  | Cons (x, r) ->
    (match f x with
     | Some y -> Cons (y, filter_map f r)
     | None -> filter_map f r ())

let rec append a b () =
  match a () with Nil -> b () | Cons (x, r) -> Cons (x, append r b)
let rec concat_map f s () =
  match s () with
  | Nil -> Nil
  | Cons (x, r) -> append (f x) (concat_map f r) ()

let rec iter f s = match s () with Nil -> () | Cons (x, r) -> f x; iter f r
let rec fold_left f acc s =
  match s () with Nil -> acc | Cons (x, r) -> fold_left f (f acc x) r
let rec take n s () =
  if n <= 0 then Nil
  else match s () with Nil -> Nil | Cons (x, r) -> Cons (x, take (n - 1) r)
let rec take_while p s () =
  match s () with Cons (x, r) when p x -> Cons (x, take_while p r) | _ -> Nil
let rec drop_while p s () =
  match s () with Cons (x, r) when p x -> drop_while p r () | n -> n

type t = string

(* in C, the runtime's (TinyMLRuntime/core.c), on words of 32 bits
 * (old: here, a word as its two halves of 16, an integer having 31:
 * 2.6 KB a second on tiny-kernel, where tiny-build digests every file
 * of tiny-kernel's build of itself) *)

(* the context, a string of the runtime's (ml_sha1_init) *)
type ctx = string
external init : unit -> ctx = "ml_sha1_init"
external update : ctx -> string -> unit = "ml_sha1_update"
external final : ctx -> t = "ml_sha1_final"

let reads next =
  let c = init () in
  let rec go () = match next () with "" -> final c | s -> update c s; go () in
  go ()

let to_hex t =
  let digit n = String.get "0123456789abcdef" n in
  String.init (2 * String.length t) (fun i ->
    let c = Char.code (String.get t (i / 2)) in
    digit (if i mod 2 = 0 then c lsr 4 else c land 15))

(* a number, with its sign: decimal, or hexadecimal after 0x
 * (OCaml's reads 0o, 0b and 1_000 too) *)
let int_of_string_opt s =
  let n = stdlib_length s in
  let neg = n > 1 && stdlib_get s 0 = '-' in
  let i = if neg then 1 else 0 in
  let hex = n > i + 2 && stdlib_get s i = '0' && stdlib_get s (i + 1) = 'x' in
  let base = if hex then 16 else 10 in
  let digit c =
    if c >= '0' && c <= '9' then int_of_char c - 48
    else if hex && c >= 'a' && c <= 'f' then int_of_char c - 87
    else if hex && c >= 'A' && c <= 'F' then int_of_char c - 55
    else -1 in
  let rec go i acc =
    if i >= n then Some acc
    else
      let d = digit (stdlib_get s i) in
      if d < 0 then None else go (i + 1) ((acc * base) + d) in
  if n = i then None
  else
    match go (if hex then i + 2 else i) 0 with
    | Some v -> Some (if neg then - v else v)
    | None -> None
let int_of_string s =
  match int_of_string_opt s with Some n -> n | None -> failwith "int_of_string"

(* TinyLibCore: the standard library of tiny-ml's programs (the kernel,
 * tiny-windows, the applications, the tools), in tiny-ml's ML, a
 * module a file as OCaml's: Stdlib, open in every unit, then Char,
 * Seq, List, String, Bytes, Array, Option, Int64, Filename, Buffer, Printf
 * (what tiny-ml's reading of a format calls: Printf.mli), Marshal
 * (OCaml's format, in the runtime), Hashtbl, and
 * ix's Common and Sha1 (lib_core's and lib_crypto's, which the tools
 * name). Each .mli but Printf's and Marshal's is a subset of OCaml's (lib_core's,
 * lib_crypto's):
 * the same names, the same types, the same results, so that a file
 * is built by OCaml on its own library for the host and by tiny-ml on
 * this one; TinyLibCore_test.sh has OCaml check each .mli against its
 * module, and compares a program's lines on both. What is left out is
 * what no tiny program names.
 *
 * Each module is compiled once, by tiny-ml -c -nostdlib after the ones
 * before it, to its object and its interface: on tiny-kernel in
 * /lib/ml, where tiny-ml reads the interfaces (-L another
 * directory). They are the first units of every program; what a
 * program does not call, tiny-linker leaves out (its pieces).
 * (old: the compiler carried the files' text, TinyMLPrelude.ml made of
 * them by the build, and compiled them again at each run)
 *
 *     Stdlib  Char  Seq  List  String  Bytes  Array  Option  Int64
 *        Filename  Buffer  Printf  Marshal  Hashtbl  Common  Sha1
 *     (each after those before it: String.map is List.init's)
 *
 * (old: TinyLibCore.ml, a prelude whose dotted names, List.map, were
 * single names, and TinyLibStd.ml, the rest, given to tiny-ml before a
 * tool's file; a Buffer a string grown by ^, a Hashtbl a list of pairs:
 * plan_tiny_self_hosting.md, step 5)
 *
 * This module: the operators, the machine's and the runtime's
 * (core.c's) as externals; option and the exceptions; the few
 * functions OCaml's Stdlib has that tiny programs name. max_int and
 * min_int are the target's, 31 bits. *)

(* See String.mli *)

external length : string -> int = "ml_string_length"
external get : string -> int -> char = "ml_string_get"
external make : int -> char -> string = "ml_string_make"
external unsafe_sub : string -> int -> int -> string = "ml_string_sub"
(* (a string just made, filled: bytes and a string are the same block) *)
external unsafe_set : string -> int -> char -> unit = "ml_bytes_set"
external unsafe_blit : string -> int -> string -> int -> int -> unit
  = "ml_bytes_blit_string"

(* (get s i, not s.[i], which is String.get: this module's own name
 * is get until it ends) *)
let sub s ofs len =
  if ofs < 0 || len < 0 || ofs > length s - len then invalid_arg "String.sub"
  else unsafe_sub s ofs len
let index_from_opt s i c =
  let n = length s in
  let rec go i =
    if i >= n then None else if get s i = c then Some i else go (i + 1) in
  if i < 0 || i > n then invalid_arg "String.index_from_opt" else go i
let index_opt s c = index_from_opt s 0 c
let index_from s i c =
  match index_from_opt s i c with Some j -> j | None -> raise Not_found
let index s c = index_from s 0 c
let rindex_opt s c =
  let rec go i =
    if i < 0 then None else if get s i = c then Some i else go (i - 1) in
  go (length s - 1)
let contains s c = match index_opt s c with Some _ -> true | None -> false
let exists p s =
  let n = length s in
  let rec go i = i < n && (p (get s i) || go (i + 1)) in
  go 0
let for_all p s =
  let n = length s in
  let rec go i = i >= n || (p (get s i) && go (i + 1)) in
  go 0
let iter f s = for i = 0 to length s - 1 do f (get s i) done
let iteri f s = for i = 0 to length s - 1 do f i (get s i) done

(* the result made once, by the runtime (old: in ML, the length of
 * each counted, then each copied in, three calls of the runtime a
 * piece, which Printf's many small pieces paid; older: joined by ^ two
 * by two, then their pairs..., each byte copied log n times) *)
external concat : string -> string list -> string = "ml_string_concat"
let init n f =
  let r = make n '\000' in
  for i = 0 to n - 1 do unsafe_set r i (f i) done;
  r
let map f s = init (length s) (fun i -> f (get s i))
let lowercase_ascii s =
  let upper c = c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z' in
  if exists upper s
  then map (fun c -> if upper c then Char.chr (Char.code c + 32) else c) s
  else s
let capitalize_ascii s =
  if length s > 0 && get s 0 >= 'a' && get s 0 <= 'z'
  then make 1 (Char.chr (Char.code (get s 0) - 32)) ^ sub s 1 (length s - 1)
  else s
let trim s =
  let blank c = c = ' ' || c = '\t' || c = '\n' || c = '\r' || c = '\012' in
  let n = length s in
  let rec first i = if i < n && blank (get s i) then first (i + 1) else i in
  let rec last j = if j > 0 && blank (get s (j - 1)) then last (j - 1) else j in
  let i = first 0 in
  sub s i (max 0 (last n - i))
let split_on_char c s =
  let rec go j i acc =
    if i < 0 then sub s 0 j :: acc
    else if get s i = c then go i (i - 1) (sub s (i + 1) (j - i - 1) :: acc)
    else go j (i - 1) acc
  in
  go (length s) (length s - 1) []
let starts_with prefix s =
  let n = length prefix in
  length s >= n && unsafe_sub s 0 n = prefix
let get_uint16_le s i = Char.code (get s i) lor (Char.code (get s (i + 1)) lsl 8)

(* Claude Code

(* See TinyLibDraw.mli *)

(* a number's two bytes (each byte's string made once: old, two
 * String.make a number, and a window's program spent half its time
 * making messages); the number at i of s *)
let bytes = Array.make 256 ""
let () = for c = 0 to 255 do bytes.(c) <- String.make 1 (Char.chr c) done
(* (and the two bytes of each number from 0 to 1024, a coordinate or an
 * image's number, made once: a message was two concatenations a
 * number, half of what a browser's page down cost in the program) *)
let small = Array.make 1025 ""
let () =
  for v = 0 to 1024 do
    small.(v) <- bytes.(v land 255) ^ bytes.((v asr 8) land 255)
  done
let i16 v =
  if v >= 0 && v <= 1024 then small.(v)
  else bytes.(v land 255) ^ bytes.((v asr 8) land 255)
let int16 s i =
  let v = Char.code s.[i] + (256 * Char.code s.[i + 1]) in
  if v >= 32768 then v - 65536 else v

(* tiny-machine's screen (TinyMachineDevices'), in pixels (old: 640 by
 * 480, text at 80 by 30; now 128 by 48, a pixel smaller in the window) *)
let screen_w = 1024
let screen_h = 768

(* a message: its letter, its numbers *)
let msg letter args =
  List.fold_left (fun s v -> s ^ i16 v) bytes.(Char.code letter) args

(* an image of that rectangle, filled with a colour's byte (the one
 * that had this number freed); a colour: one pixel, repeating *)
let d_image id x0 y0 x1 y1 colour = msg 'a' [ id; x0; y0; x1; y1; 0; colour ]
let d_colour id colour = msg 'a' [ id; 0; 0; 1; 1; 1; colour ]
let d_free id = msg 'f' [ id ]

(* dst's rectangle: src's pixels from (px, py) on, where mask's are
 * set (-1: no mask); a rectangle of a colour *)
let d_draw dst src mask x0 y0 x1 y1 px py =
  msg 'd' [ dst; src; mask; x0; y0; x1; y1; px; py ]
let d_fill dst src x0 y0 x1 y1 = d_draw dst src (-1) x0 y0 x1 y1 0 0

(* a line, both ends drawn; a text (a character is 8 by 16), its top
 * left corner at (x, y) *)
let d_line dst src xa ya xb yb = msg 'l' [ dst; src; xa; ya; xb; yb ]
let d_text dst src x y s = msg 's' [ dst; src; x; y; String.length s ] ^ s
let d_styled dst src x y style s =
  msg 't' [ dst; src; x; y; String.length s; style ] ^ s

(* a row of pixels, a byte each, its left end at (x, y) *)
let d_pixels dst x y s = msg 'p' [ dst; x; y; String.length s ] ^ s

(* the mouse's look: 0 the arrow, 1 a hand (over a link) *)
let d_cursor kind = msg 'c' [ kind ]

(* The message at i of s: its length, and how many of its first numbers
 * are images. The length is beyond s's end when the message is not all
 * there yet (a pipe gives what it has), and -1 when this is no message. *)
let d_shape s i =
  match s.[i] with
  | 'a' -> 15, 1
  | 'f' -> 3, 1
  | 'd' -> 19, 3
  | 'l' -> 13, 2
  | 's' ->
      if i + 11 > String.length s then 11, 2
      else if int16 s (i + 9) < 0 then -1, 0
      else 11 + int16 s (i + 9), 2
  | 't' ->
      if i + 13 > String.length s then 13, 2
      else if int16 s (i + 9) < 0 then -1, 0
      else 13 + int16 s (i + 9), 2
  | 'p' ->
      if i + 9 > String.length s then 9, 1
      else if int16 s (i + 7) < 0 then -1, 0
      else 9 + int16 s (i + 7), 1
  | 'c' -> 3, 0
  | _ -> -1, 0

(* The program side of TinyKernelGraphics.ml. This file builds the
 * drawing messages (each one a string, to be concatenated and written
 * to the file descriptor the program draws on), and it also parses
 * them (a window system reads the messages of another program,
 * renumbers their images, and passes them on: see TinyWindows.ml).
 * The Plan 9 equivalent is libdraw, the library used by programs,
 * while TinyKernelGraphics.ml plays the role of the kernel's draw
 * device and of libmemdraw. For C programs, the equivalent is
 * TinyKernel/libc/draw.h.
 *
 * The messages are described in the header of TinyKernelGraphics.mli:
 * a letter, followed by signed 16-bit numbers, low byte first.
 *
 * Here is the path of a rectangle from a program to the screen, on the
 * two machines where the same ML files run:
 *
 *     a program            TinyAppTetris on TinyLibPlayground, TinyWindows
 *        | d_fill ...      this file: makes a string of 19 bytes
 *        | written on 3    on tiny-machine: a system call (TinyKernel/
 *        |                 libml's TinyCalls.ml); on the host: TinyCalls,
 *        |                 which keeps it for the test to check
 *        | (through a pipe, renumbered by TinyWindows, when in a window)
 *        | [messages]      TinyKernelGraphics: inside TinyKernel; on the
 *        |                 host, called directly by the test
 *        | pokeb, rows     on tiny-machine: C and assembly (TinyKernel's
 *        |                 TinyMemory.ml); on the host: TinyMemory, an array
 *     the screen's bytes   at 0xf00000 on both
 *
 * So the three files between a program and its machine (this one,
 * TinyCalls and TinyMemory) are where the host takes the machine's
 * place, and everything above them is tested by dune before
 * tiny-machine ever runs it.
 *
 * Its twin in m-ix is lib_graphics's Draw and Display (libdraw's, by
 * way of xix): a Display that keeps the messages until [flush], images
 * as records, numbers of four bytes. What is ours:
 *
 * - {b A message is a string returned}: no Display, no Image record,
 *   no buffer of the library's; the program concatenates them and
 *   writes them when it wants them shown.
 * - {b Numbers of two bytes}, where libdraw's are four: a screen of
 *   1024 by 768 needs no more.
 * - {b Eight letters} (a f d l s t p c), the operations
 *   TinyKernelGraphics keeps.
 * - {b The messages are parsed too} ([d_shape]), which libdraw has no
 *   need of: on Plan 9 a window's program writes to the kernel's draw
 *   device itself, finding its window's image by the name in
 *   /dev/winname, and rio never reads its messages. Here TinyWindows
 *   forwards them, renumbered.
 *
 * plan9-is-cleaner:
 * Drawing by writing bytes to a file comes from Plan 9: its draw
 * device is a directory in /dev, and libdraw turns each call into a
 * message, a letter followed by numbers, written to one of the files
 * in that directory (there d draws, f frees an image, s draws a
 * string). Because it is a file, it can go through a pipe or over the
 * network like any other file, and a window system or a remote
 * terminal needs no protocol of its own.
 *)

(* a number's two bytes, the low one first, and the number at i of a
 * string; a message, its letter then its numbers *)
(* tiny-machine's screen, 1024 by 768 pixels *)
val screen_w : int
val screen_h : int

val i16 : int -> string
val int16 : string -> int -> int
val msg : char -> int list -> string

(* an image [d_image id x0 y0 x1 y1 colour], a colour (one pixel that
 * repeats), an image freed *)
val d_image : int -> int -> int -> int -> int -> int -> string
val d_colour : int -> int -> string
val d_free : int -> string

(* [d_draw dst src mask x0 y0 x1 y1 px py], TinyKernelGraphics's draw (-1: no
 * mask); a rectangle of a colour; a line; a text at a corner *)
val d_draw : int -> int -> int -> int -> int -> int -> int -> int -> int -> string
val d_fill : int -> int -> int -> int -> int -> int -> string
val d_line : int -> int -> int -> int -> int -> int -> string
val d_text : int -> int -> int -> int -> string -> string

(* [d_styled dst src x y style s]: a text in a style, bold 1, italic 2,
 * underlined 4, large 8 (16 by 32 a character); or 16, fat pixels, each
 * byte a colour, a square of 4 by 4 (src unused) *)
val d_styled : int -> int -> int -> int -> int -> string -> string

(* [d_pixels dst x y bytes]: a row of pixels, its left end at (x, y) *)
val d_pixels : int -> int -> int -> string -> string

(* [d_cursor kind]: the mouse's look, 0 the arrow, 1 a hand (a browser's
 * over a link). The kernel sets the machine's (by writing the mouse's
 * word), which the host shows; tiny-windows keeps each window's, and
 * shows the front window's while the mouse is in it. *)
val d_cursor : int -> string

(* the message at i of a string: its length (beyond the string's end
 * when it is not all there, -1 when it is no message) and how many of
 * its first numbers are images: what a window system renumbers *)
val d_shape : string -> int -> int * int

(* a text; a text in a box, at its right; a field typed in, and the
 * message of another text; a button and the message it sends; widgets
 * side by side, the same width each; widgets one under the other *)
type 'msg widget =
  | Label of string
  | Field of string
  | Input of string * (string -> 'msg)
  | Button of string * 'msg
  | Row of 'msg widget list
  | Col of 'msg widget list

(* a program: its first model, the model as widgets, the model after a
 * message, a key's messages *)
type ('m, 'msg) gui = {
  init : 'm;
  view : 'm -> 'msg widget;
  update : 'msg -> 'm -> 'm;
  key : int -> 'msg list;
}

(* what a box does with the mouse or the keys: a button's message; a
 * field's text, and the message of another one *)
type 'msg action = Send of 'msg | Edit of string * (string -> 'msg)

(* what is kept under the model: where the mouse's button went down
 * (px -1: it is up), where the mouse is, where its button last went
 * down (the field there has the keys) *)
type mouse = { px : int; py : int; x : int; y : int; fx : int; fy : int }

let up = { px = -1; py = -1; x = -1; y = -1; fx = -1; fy = -1 }
