(* A unit: its toplevel in <unit>.init, its names that are not static
 * (a value computed, a closure allocated) in its globals' table,
 * <unit>.globals, the collector's roots. What nothing uses is left out
 * by tiny-linker, piece by piece (a function, a static block): a
 * function of the toplevel has no free variable, so its closure is
 * static and the init names it not (old: prune, the program's
 * toplevel lets that nothing used dropped before the code was made,
 * when a program was compiled whole: a library cost a program only
 * what it called, which the link's pieces now do) *)
let compile_unit env (items : (item * int) list) =
  cur := { code = []; nslots = 1; ntries = 0 };
  arities := [];
  let table = !unit_name ^ ".globals" and nglobals = ref 0 in
  let rec arity = function TE ("->", [ _; r ]) -> 1 + arity r | _ -> 0 in
  let env, defs = List.fold_left (fun (env, defs) (it, l) ->
    try
      match it with
      | IOpen u -> opened globals u; env, defs
      | IExt (x, t, p) ->
          let b = Ext (p, arity t) in
          add_name globals x b;
          env, (x, b) :: defs
      | IExn c ->
          block (exn_id c) (header 1 0) [ DVal (static_string c) ];
          if (find_con c).arity = 0 then
            block (exn_const c) (header 1 0) [ DVal (exn_id c) ];
          env, defs
      | ILet (r, bs) ->
          (* (the names it adds, in the table: old, the env's first
           * names, counted) *)
          let added = List.map (function
            | x, Loc (Slot s, k) ->
                emit (Get s);
                emit (SetG (table, !nglobals));
                incr nglobals;
                x, Loc (Glob (table, !nglobals - 1), k)
            | b -> b) (bind env r bs) in
          List.iter (fun (x, b) -> add_name globals x b) (List.rev added);
          env, added @ defs
    with Failure m -> error (Printf.sprintf "line %d: %s" l m)) (env, []) items in
  emit (Imm (tagged 0));
  emit Ret;
  machine (!unit_name ^ ".init") 0 (!cur).nslots (List.rev (!cur).code);
  let rec drain () =
    match dequeue () with Some f -> f (); drain () | None -> () in
  drain ();
  env, defs, !nglobals

(* The program's main: ml_init, each unit's init in their order, in a
 * handler that prints an uncaught exception; the curry functions the
 * units need; the globals' tables one after the other, ml_globals, and
 * their count, ml_nglobals (what TinyMLRuntime/core.c scans) *)
let compile_main (units : (string * int) list) needed =
  unit_name := "ml";
  cur := { code = []; nslots = 1; ntries = 1 };
  let handler = label () in
  emit (TryEnter (0, handler));
  List.iter (fun (u, _) ->
      emit (Imm (tagged 0));
      emit (Call (Direct (u ^ ".init"), 0, false));
      emit Drop)
    units;
  emit (TryExit 0);
  emit (Imm (tagged 0));
  emit Ret;
  emit (Label handler);
  emit (Catch 0);
  emit (CallC ("ml_uncaught", 1));
  emit Ret;
  machine "ml_init" 0 (!cur).nslots (List.rev (!cur).code);
  List.iter (fun n -> for k = 0 to n - 1 do curry_fun n k done)
    (List.sort_uniq compare needed);
  let total = List.fold_left (fun t (_, n) -> t + n) 0 units in
  words "ml_nglobals" [ DNum (string_of_int total) ];
  Buffer.add_string data "\t.piece\nml_globals:\n";
  List.iter (fun (u, n) ->
      Buffer.add_string data
        (u ^ ".globals:\n\t.space\t" ^ string_of_int (4 * n) ^ "\n"))
    units;
  if total = 0 then Buffer.add_string data "\t.space\t4\n"

(*****************************************************************************)
(* Interfaces *)
(*****************************************************************************)

(* A unit's interface, M.tmi, what a unit compiled after it reads (as
 * OCaml's .cmi): its globals' count and the curry functions it needs;
 * the types, constructors, labels and abbreviations it added; each of
 * its names, where its value is (a static closure and its code, a
 * global, a primitive) and its type, M.mli's when there is one. A
 * record, Marshal's bytes (OCaml's on the host, the runtime's on
 * tiny-kernel: the same), a type in it as a type expression, its
 * variables 'v<number>, read as a type anew (of_texpr), as the text
 * was.
 * (old: a line each, printed and parsed again: half of a small unit's
 * compile was reading the interfaces) *)
(* (at most 7 fields, as each block in it: OCaml 5's Marshal writes a
 * block of 8 or more with two bits of its header set, 4.14's and
 * TinyLibCore's do not, and the host's interface was not tiny-kernel's
 * (bugs/ix.md). old: iname, iglobals, icurry, three fields of eight) *)
type interface = {
  iunit : string * int * int list;  (* its name, globals, curry functions *)
  icons : (string * kind * int * int * int * texpr) list;
  ilabels : (string * string * int * bool * string list * texpr) list;
  iabbrevs : (string * (string list * texpr)) list;
  iforgotten : string list;
  ivals : (string * binding * texpr) list;
}

(* a type as its expression: what is linked followed, a variable by its
 * number *)
let rec texpr_of_ty t =
  match repr t with
  | TVar { contents = Unbound (n, _) } -> TEVar ("v" ^ string_of_int n)
  | TCon (c, ts) -> TE (c, List.map texpr_of_ty ts)
  | TVar _ -> TE ("?", [])

(* what the program's tables held before a unit: its interface has only
 * what the unit added, as OCaml's .cmi (old: the whole program's so far,
 * each unit's .tmi repeating every one before it, all read again by
 * each unit after: 310 KB of interfaces for tiny-kernel's programs) *)
let snapshot () =
  let c = Hashtbl.copy cons and l = Hashtbl.copy record_labels
  and a = !abbreviations and f = !forgotten in
  (fun k ci ->
    match Hashtbl.find_opt c k with Some ci' -> ci' == ci | None -> false),
  (fun k li -> List.memq li (Hashtbl.find_all l k)),
  (fun ab -> List.memq ab a),
  (fun t -> List.mem t f)

let write_interface (old_con, old_label, old_abbrev, old_forgotten)
    (exports : (string * binding) list) types nglobals =
  (* the tables by their names, a label's records the latest first, as
   * the table has them (old: Hashtbl.iter's order, which is OCaml's
   * or TinyLibCore's: an interface was not the same from the two
   * builds of tiny-ml) *)
  let names tbl =
    List.sort_uniq compare (Hashtbl.fold (fun k _ acc -> k :: acc) tbl []) in
  let icons = List.filter_map (fun c ->
    let ci = Hashtbl.find cons c in
    if old_con c ci then None
    else
      Some (c, ci.kind, ci.arity, ci.nconst, ci.nblock, texpr_of_ty ci.scheme))
    (names cons) in
  let ilabels = List.concat_map (fun l -> List.filter_map (fun li ->
    if old_label l li then None
    else
      Some (l, li.lrec, li.idx, li.mut, li.lnames, texpr_of_ty li.lscheme))
    (Hashtbl.find_all record_labels l)) (names record_labels) in
  (* a name defined twice: the later, first in exports, as OCaml's
   * shadowing (old: both, the earlier read last, so the one the units
   * after saw, with the later's type: www's trap, bugs/ix.md) *)
  let seen = Hashtbl.create 64 in
  let ivals = List.filter_map (fun (x, bd) ->
    if Hashtbl.mem seen x then None
    else begin
      Hashtbl.add seen x ();
      match List.assoc_opt x types, bd with
      | Some t, (Loc ((Static _ | Glob _), _) | Ext _) ->
          Some (qualify !unit_name x, bd, texpr_of_ty t)
      | _ -> None
    end) exports in
  Marshal.to_string
    { iunit = !unit_name, nglobals, !arities; icons = icons; ilabels = ilabels;
      iabbrevs =
        List.filter (fun a -> not (old_abbrev a)) (List.rev !abbreviations);
      iforgotten = List.filter (fun t -> not (old_forgotten t)) !forgotten;
      ivals = ivals }
    (* (No_sharing: which of two equal names is the same string depends
     * on a table's order, OCaml's or TinyLibCore's; shared, the host's
     * and tiny-kernel's interfaces differed in 3 of the system's 40) *)
    [ Marshal.No_sharing ]

(* an interface read: its types the program's, its names in the tables
 * (globals, tglobals); its unit's name, globals and curry functions *)
let read_interface text env tenv =
  if String.length text < 4 || String.sub text 0 4 <> "\132\149\166\190" then
    error "not an interface of tiny-ml's";
  let (i : interface) = Marshal.from_string text 0 in
  let iname, iglobals, icurry = i.iunit in
  let ty te = of_texpr (ref []) te in
  known_units := iname :: !known_units;
  List.iter (fun (c, kind, arity, nconst, nblock, te) ->
      Hashtbl.replace cons c
        { kind = kind; arity = arity; nconst = nconst; nblock = nblock;
          scheme = ty te })
    i.icons;
  List.iter (fun (l, r, idx, mut, lnames, te) ->
    let others =
      List.filter (fun li -> li.lrec <> r) (Hashtbl.find_all record_labels l) in
    while Hashtbl.mem record_labels l do Hashtbl.remove record_labels l done;
    List.iter (Hashtbl.add record_labels l) (List.rev others);
    Hashtbl.add record_labels l
      { lrec = r; idx = idx; mut = mut; lnames = lnames; lscheme = ty te })
    i.ilabels;
  List.iter (fun (t, (ps, te)) ->
    abbreviations :=
      (t, (ps, te))
      :: List.filter
           (fun (t', (ps', _)) -> t' <> t || List.length ps' <> List.length ps)
           !abbreviations)
    i.iabbrevs;
  List.iter (fun t ->
      if not (List.mem t !forgotten) then forgotten := t :: !forgotten)
    i.iforgotten;
  (* (a val's name is M.x already; Stdlib's x too) *)
  let n = String.length iname in
  List.iter (fun (x, b, te) ->
    let t = ty te in
    List.iter (fun x -> Hashtbl.replace globals x b; Hashtbl.replace tglobals x t)
      (if implicit iname then
         [ x; String.sub x (n + 1) (String.length x - n - 1) ]
       else [ x ]))
    i.ivals;
  env, tenv, (iname, iglobals), icurry

(* M.mli's vals, their types in place of what M.ml's inferred: its
 * types and exceptions are M.ml's too, and skipped *)
let mli_types text =
  toks := lex text; pos := 0;
  let starts () =
    match peek () with
    | LID "val" | KW ("type" | "exception" | "external") | EOF -> true
    | _ -> false
  in
  let rec go acc =
    match peek () with
    | EOF -> acc
    | LID "val" ->
        advance ();
        let x =
          match peek () with
          | LID x -> advance (); x
          | KW "(" ->
              advance ();
              let o = (match peek () with KW o -> advance (); o | _ -> fail ()) in
              expect (KW ")");
              o
          | _ -> fail ()
        in
        expect (KW ":");
        let t = ty () in
        go ((x, of_texpr (ref []) t) :: acc)
    | _ -> advance (); while not (starts ()) do advance () done; go acc in
  go []

(* ml_start called by C (the value stack's base at 0(sp)), ml_init's
 * closure slot 1, a unit (not what r13 held, which the collector would
 * scan); ml_raise: to the latest handler, the exception in r13 *)
let start =
  String.concat "\n\t"
    [ "ml_start:"; "ldw\tr12, 0(sp)"; "li\tr13, 1"; "la\tr11, ml_init";
      "jalr\tzero, 0(r11)";
      "ml_raise:\n\tla\tr1, ml_handler"; "ldw\tr1, 0(r1)"; "ldw\tsp, 0(r1)";
      "ldw\tr12, 4(r1)"; "ldw\tr2, 12(r1)"; "la\tr3, ml_handler";
      "stw\tr2, 0(r3)"; "ldw\tr2, 8(r1)"; "jalr\tzero, 0(r2)" ]
  ^ "\n"

let parse s = toks := lex s; pos := 0; items ()

(* a file's unit: its name without the directory and the extension,
 * capitalized, as OCaml's module *)
let unit_of f =
  String.capitalize_ascii (Filename.remove_extension (Filename.basename f))

(* the standard library, TinyLibCore/'s modules in their order, the
 * first units of every program: each compiled once, by tiny-ml -c
 * -nostdlib after the ones before it, and read as interfaces from a
 * directory, /lib/ml on tiny-kernel (-L another), its objects
 * linked as any unit's.
 * (old: their text the compiler's, TinyMLPrelude.ml made of them by the
 * build, compiled again at each run: a unit of one line took 47 s on
 * tiny-kernel, and every program's main the library's code, 420 KB of
 * assembly;
 * older: the prelude, TinyLibCore.ml, one unit, its List.map a name
 * with a dot) *)
let library =
  [ "Stdlib"; "Char"; "Seq"; "List"; "String"; "Bytes"; "Array"; "Option";
    "Int64"; "Filename"; "Buffer"; "Printf"; "Marshal"; "Hashtbl"; "Common";
    "Sha1" ]

(* a file that cannot be read or made, said apart from an error in one *)
exception File_error of string

let main
    (caps : < Cap.argv; Cap.open_in; Cap.open_out; Cap.stdout; Cap.stderr; .. >)
    =
  let output = ref "" and file = ref "" and files = ref []
  and separate = ref false and lib = ref (Some "/lib/ml") in
  let rec args l = match l with
    | "-o" :: o :: r -> output := o; args r
    | "-c" :: r -> separate := true; args r
    | "-L" :: d :: r -> lib := Some d; args r
    | "-nostdlib" :: r -> lib := None; args r
    | f :: r -> files := f :: !files; args r
    | [] -> ()
  in
  let argl = List.tl (TinyLibSystem.argv caps) in
  args argl;
  let files = List.rev !files in
  let read f =
    file := f;
    try TinyLibSystem.read_file caps f with Failure m -> raise (File_error m) in
  let tmis = List.filter (fun f -> Filename.check_suffix f ".tmi") files
  and mls = List.filter (fun f -> Filename.check_suffix f ".ml") files in
  if List.mem "-h" argl || List.mem "--help" argl then
    (TinyLibSystem.print caps help; 0)
  else if List.length mls + List.length tmis <> List.length files || files = []
          || (!separate && List.length mls <> 1) then
    (TinyLibSystem.eprint caps (usage ^ "   (-h: how)\n"); 2)
  else
  let write f text =
    let fd =
      try TinyLibSystem.open_out caps f with Failure m -> raise (File_error m)
    in
    TinyLibSystem.write fd text; TinyLibSystem.close fd in
  try
    (* the interfaces read, in their order: the library's, then the
     * units before this one *)
    let lib =
      match !lib with
      | Some d -> List.map (fun m -> d ^ "/" ^ m ^ ".tmi") library
      | None -> []
    in
    let env, tenv, units, needed =
      List.fold_left (fun (env, tenv, units, needed) f ->
          let env, tenv, u, n = read_interface (read f) env tenv in
          env, tenv, units @ [ u ], needed @ n)
        ([], [], [], []) (lib @ tmis) in
    if !separate then begin
      (* one unit: its object and its interface *)
      let f = List.hd mls in
      Buffer.clear text; Buffer.clear data;
      unit_name := unit_of f;
      known_units := !unit_name :: !known_units;
      (* (before the parse: a type's constructors are the parser's) *)
      let old = snapshot () in
      let items = parse (read f) in
      let _, tdefs = type_unit tenv items in
      let _, exports, n = compile_unit env items in
      let mli = Filename.remove_extension f ^ ".mli" in
      (* (old: Sys.file_exists mli, then read) *)
      let mli_text =
        try Some (TinyLibSystem.read_file caps mli) with Failure _ -> None in
      let types =
        (match mli_text with Some t -> file := mli; mli_types t | None -> [])
        @ tdefs in
      let out =
        if !output = "" then
          Filename.remove_extension (Filename.basename f) ^ ".tm"
        else !output in
      (* (.data: tiny-linker -n's, the statics after the text) *)
      write out (Buffer.contents text ^ "\t.data\n" ^ Buffer.contents data);
      write (Filename.remove_extension out ^ ".tmi")
        (write_interface old exports types n)
    end else begin
      (* the files one after the other, a unit each, then the main *)
      let _, _, units, needed =
        List.fold_left (fun (env, tenv, units, needed) f ->
          unit_name := unit_of f;
          known_units := !unit_name :: !known_units;
          let items = parse (read f) in
          let _, tdefs = type_unit tenv items in
          let _, defs, n = compile_unit env items in
          unit_done ();
          export globals !unit_name defs env,
          export tglobals !unit_name tdefs tenv,
          units @ [ (!unit_name, n) ],
          needed @ !arities)
          (env, tenv, units, needed) mls in
      compile_main units needed;
      let asm =
        start ^ Buffer.contents text ^ "\t.data\n" ^ Buffer.contents data in
      if !output = "" then TinyLibSystem.print caps asm else write !output asm
    end;
    0
  with
  | Failure m -> TinyLibSystem.eprint caps (!file ^ ": " ^ m ^ "\n"); 1
  | File_error m -> TinyLibSystem.eprint caps (Printf.sprintf "tiny-ml: %s\n" m); 1

let () = TinyLibSystem.main "tiny-ml" main
tiny/TinyML.mli
16596
(* A tiny ML compiler for tiny-machine, in one file. Its full-size twin
 * is mini-ml (languages/ml/, planned in docs/plans/plan_ml.md), which
 * behaves like ocaml-light's native compiler: same dialect, modules,
 * and the kernel as a target. This file is what is left of an ML
 * compiler when the language is small and the code only needs to be
 * correct. Its usage, by examples, is in [help] below, which is what
 * tiny-ml -h prints.
 *
 * It reads ML files, a unit each (with -c, one, after the interfaces
 * of the units it uses), and writes
 * its assembly for tiny-machine (the CPU of TinyMachineCPU.ml): words
 * of 4 bytes, integers of 31 bits. The runtime (the allocator, Cheney's
 * collector, the primitives, and the printing of an uncaught
 * exception) is in C, TinyMLRuntime/core.c, compiled by tiny-c; the
 * program's own main gives it memory. TinyKernel.ml is the
 * program it was made for: a kernel in ML, which reaches the machine
 * through externals (functions in C or assembly), so the compiler
 * needs no special primitive for it.
 *
 * How a file is compiled:
 *
 *     file.ml ...         a unit each (and M.tmi, the units' before it)
 *        | lexer, parser     tokens to a tree, by recursive descent
 *        | type checker      checks types; records each label's index
 *        |                   and which comparisons are on integers
 *        | tree to stack     finds each function's free variables,
 *        | machine           turns patterns into tests, marks tail
 *        |                   calls: one [ir] list per function
 *        | machine           turns the list into assembly, and
 *        |                   static blocks into .word
 *     file.tm, for tiny-assembler (with M.tmi when alone, -c)
 *
 * The passes are TinyML/'s modules: TinyMLLexer, then TinyMLParser,
 * which makes the tree of TinyMLTree (and reads Printf's formats as the
 * concatenations they make, TinyMLPrintf), TinyMLTypes, the type
 * checker, then TinyMLCompile, the tree to the stack machine, whose
 * [ir] and assembly are TinyMLMachine's. This file is the program
 * around them: a unit compiled, the program's main, the interfaces
 * (M.tmi) a unit leaves for the next ones.
 *
 * What a value looks like at run time (TinyMLRuntime/core.c has the
 * same picture, from the other side):
 *
 *     a word:   2n+1        the integer n: 10 is 21, false is 1, true
 *                           is 3, a constant constructor is its number
 *          or   an even address, of a block's first field
 *                    |
 *                    v
 *      | header | field 0 | field 1 | ...     a tuple, a record, a ref,
 *        size << 10, with the tag in          a constructor's arguments,
 *        the low byte                         an array: one word a field
 *
 *      | header, tag 247 | unary code | n-ary code | free variables...
 *                           a function value (a closure)
 *      | header, tag 252 | the bytes...       a string: holds no values
 *
 * And where values live, which is what the collector needs to know:
 *
 *     the value stack, top in r12       the machine stack, top in sp
 *       a function's frame:               return addresses
 *         its closure                     C frames (the runtime's)
 *         its parameters                  a try's record: both stack
 *         its variables                   tops, the handler's address,
 *         one slot per register, filled   the previous record
 *         at a call or an allocation
 *       every word is a value: these    never holds a value: the
 *       are the roots, along with the   collector never looks at it
 *       program's globals
 *
 * Between two calls a value may sit in r1..r11. At a call or an
 * allocation, the only two moments when a collection can happen, all
 * of them are stored in their slots and read back afterwards, because
 * the collector moves blocks.
 *
 * The language: integers (31 bits), characters, strings, booleans,
 * unit, tuples, lists, variants (type declarations, polymorphic and
 * recursive), records (mutable fields; e.l, e.l <- v, { l = e; ... },
 * and { l; ... } for { l = l; ... }; in patterns too, where _ stands
 * for the fields not named, as in { view; update = u; _ }; and
 * { e with l = e'; ... }, a copy of the same type),
 * arrays (Array.make, length, get and set, a.(i), a.(i) <- v),
 * references, and exceptions (declared, raised, caught). The constructs
 * are let, let rec, and, fun, function, match with guards, as and
 * or-patterns (without variables), if, sequences, while, for, and type
 * annotations (p : t). There is external, used by the standard
 * library (TinyLibCore/, written in ML; see below). Types are
 * Hindley-Milner with the value restriction. Strings
 * can span several lines. ix's capabilities are parsed and then ignored:
 * an object type in an annotation, or declared under a name, means any
 * type, and a coercion to one, (e :> t), is just e; OCaml checks them
 * when it builds the same file. A type can have a second name, as in
 * type word = piece list, or with parameters, type 'a t = unit -> 'a
 * node (Seq's). A module is a file, a unit (M.x, open M); its types,
 * constructors and labels are the program's, one name space, so M.C
 * is C. {|quoted strings|}, OCaml's, are read (a help's text). Left
 * out: modules inside a file and functors, floats, labels, objects,
 * or-patterns with names in their
 * alternatives, character ranges and inline records: the tools and the
 * toolchain were written again without them.
 *
 * What keeps it small while still being an ML compiler:
 *
 * - {b Types are checked, then forgotten.} The checker (Hindley-Milner,
 *   with Rémy's levels for generalization) is a pass whose result the
 *   code generator uses in only two places: a comparison whose operands
 *   are integers is inlined, while the others call the runtime's
 *   polymorphic compare; and a record label becomes its field's index.
 *   Everything else has one representation: a word, which is either an
 *   integer 2n+1 or a pointer to a block (a header, then fields).
 * - {b A record is a tuple, and a label has a scheme like a
 *   constructor's}: %l(record, field), instantiated at each use. When
 *   the type of e is already known (from an annotation such as
 *   (p : proc)), a label is looked up in that record type, so two
 *   records can share a label name. This is OCaml's type-directed
 *   disambiguation, done cheaply (ocaml-light just takes the last
 *   declared label).
 * - {b A stack machine in between}, the same as TinyC's (IR, below):
 *   each expression pushes its value, the stack is kept in r1..r11, and
 *   a pattern becomes a sequence of tests, each jumping to the next
 *   clause on failure.
 * - {b A value stack for the roots} (plan_ml.md, decision 5;
 *   Henderson's shadow stack): each function's variables, and the
 *   registers spilled at a call or an allocation, are words on a stack
 *   of values whose top is r12 (after a call of C, which keeps no
 *   register, it comes back from ml_vsp).
 *   The machine stack holds return addresses, C frames and exception
 *   handlers, but never a value. So the collector finds every root
 *   without a frame table, and can move them: it is Cheney's copying
 *   collector, in C.
 * - {b Closures, and direct calls of known functions.} A function is a
 *   block [unary code; n-ary code; free variables...]. Applying an
 *   unknown function passes one argument at a time through the first
 *   field; for an arity above 1, that field holds a curry function
 *   (ml_currynk), which gathers the arguments in blocks and then calls
 *   the n-ary code, like ocaml-light's caml_curryN. Calling a let-bound
 *   function with all its arguments calls its n-ary code directly, and
 *   a function without free variables is a static block. Calls in tail
 *   position are jumps, so a let rec loop runs in constant space.
 * - {b Units, and what nothing uses left out by the link.} A file is a
 *   unit: its symbols prefixed with its name (TinyLibGUI.f12_layout),
 *   its toplevel in TinyLibGUI.init, the values it computes in its
 *   globals' table. Compiled alone (-c), it writes its interface,
 *   M.tmi (OCaml's .cmi: the types and constructors it added, each of
 *   its names with where its value is, a static closure or a global,
 *   and its type, M.mli's when there is one; a record, marshalled),
 *   which the units after it read; a program's main (ml_start, each
 *   unit's init in their order, the curry functions, the tables) is
 *   made of the interfaces. A unit
 *   is a module: its names are M.x in the units after it, or x after
 *   open M; Stdlib is open in all, and with it TinyLibCore/'s modules,
 *   the standard library, are the first units of every program, each
 *   compiled once (-nostdlib), their interfaces read from a directory
 *   (/lib/ml, or -L's). The types, the constructors and the labels
 *   are the program's, one name space: a record's label is the latest
 *   record's unless the type says which. Each function and static block
 *   is a piece (.piece), which tiny-linker leaves out when nothing
 *   reaches it: a function of the toplevel has no free variable, so
 *   its closure is static and the init does not name it, and a library
 *   costs a program only what it calls: tiny-kernel's calc is 153 KB,
 *   206 KB with all of its libraries.
 *   (old: prune, the program's toplevel lets that nothing used dropped
 *   before the code was made, all of a program's files compiled as one)
 * - {b Exceptions with no assembly in the runtime.} try pushes a record
 *   on the machine stack (the stack pointer, r12, the handler's
 *   address, and the previous record); raise restores both stack
 *   pointers from the latest record and jumps. The handler's address is
 *   what a call jumping over the handler leaves in lr, as with setjmp.
 * - {b Its own frames.} The compiler writes each function's prologue
 *   and epilogue itself, so a tail call can pop the frame and jump.
 * - {b The standard library is in ML.} raise, the operators, ref, ! and
 *   := are externals whose names give the instruction ("%add");
 *   print_string and ^ name C functions of the runtime; List.map and
 *   the others are ML, TinyLibCore/'s units, and only what the program
 *   uses is linked (above).
 *
 * Its behavior follows ocaml-light's arm64 ocamlopt, which was the
 * contract, quirks included (plan_tiny_self_hosting.md takes the quirks
 * out, OCaml being the reference now): arguments, tuples and record fields are
 * evaluated right to left, except a.(i) <- v, which evaluates i, then
 * a, then v; stdout is buffered by 4096 bytes and the buffer is lost on
 * an uncaught exception; that exception is printed the way
 * ocaml-light's printexc.c prints it, with exit status 2; division by
 * zero gives what the machine's div does instead of raising an
 * exception; an
 * out-of-bounds index into a string or an array is a fatal error; and
 * the empty array is a static block (OCaml's atom).
 *
 * Exercises, each cheap thanks to the stack machine or the value stack:
 * - arm32: a second back end for the stack machine (tiny-machine's
 *   took 150 lines);
 * - inline allocation: keep the heap pointer and limit in two
 *   registers, and call the collector only when a block does not fit;
 * - fewer spills: at a call, spill only the registers below the
 *   arguments (the arguments are passed in registers and could stay
 *   there);
 * - a switch on constructor tags instead of one test per clause;
 * - exhaustiveness warnings (Maranget, "Warnings for pattern
 *   matching", 2007).
 *
 * Where it stands: every program in ML of tiny-kernel is its, the
 * kernel first and tiny-ml itself, and OCaml compiles the same files
 * on the host. Its runtime is C compiled by TinyC, and its
 * assembly is TinyMachineCPU's. The stack machine, with
 * its stack kept in registers, comes from TinyC, so the two compilers
 * read as one design used twice: what differs is everything C does not
 * have (type inference, closures, patterns, a collector). The ML
 * compiler that compiles ix itself is the other one, mini-ml (with
 * Typing, Resolve, and one back end per machine).
 *
 * What it shares with its twin, and where it parts: mini-ml's simple
 * back end (Gen) is the same design, a stack machine kept in
 * registers, the values on a stack of their own, Cheney's collector in
 * C (plan_ml.md's decision 5 is both's), and mini-ml has no functor
 * either. Its parser is ocamlyacc's, tiny-ml's recursive descent; it
 * writes Plan 9's assembly for arm and arm64, and has -O and an SSA
 * back end with a register allocator, where tiny-ml has one machine
 * and no optimization. One road goes the other way: mini-ml has no
 * compiled interface (a unit's .mli is read again by each unit that
 * names it), tiny-ml writes M.tmi, OCaml's .cmi, with where each value
 * is, which an .mli does not say.
 *
 * cs-history:
 * ML is the Meta Language of Edinburgh's LCF, a proof assistant (Robin
 * Milner and others, 1973 to 1978): it was the language in which users
 * wrote proof strategies. Its types were there to make cheating
 * impossible, since a theorem was a value of an abstract type that only
 * the inference rules could build; its exceptions were how a strategy
 * failed; and type inference was there so that mathematicians did not
 * have to write types. The language outlived the prover's needs:
 * Standard ML (1980s), Caml at INRIA (1985), Xavier Leroy's and Damien
 * Doligez's Caml Light (1990), small enough for a PC, and OCaml
 * (1996). ocaml-light, whose outputs this compiler first matched, is
 * OCaml 1.07 without objects and functors (plan_ml.md).
 *
 * design:
 * Using one representation for every value, a word, is what makes
 * polymorphism free: List.map is compiled once and works on a list of
 * anything, since it only moves words around. The price is paid
 * elsewhere: an integer loses a bit to say it is not a pointer, a float
 * would need a block of its own, and comparing two values of unknown
 * type means walking them at run time. The other road compiles a
 * function again for each type it is used at (MLton, C++ templates,
 * Rust): no tags, no boxes, but more code, and the whole program is
 * needed at once.
 *
 * modern:
 * OCaml and Go keep values in the machine's registers and stack, and
 * the compiler writes, for each call site, a table saying which slots
 * hold pointers; the collector uses it to walk the stack. That costs
 * nothing while the program runs, but a lot in the compiler and the
 * runtime (the stack must be parsed, in assembly or with great care).
 * The second stack used here costs a store and a load for each live
 * value around every call, but almost no code. LLVM offers the same
 * trade-off under the name shadow stack.
 *
 * others:
 * MinCaml (Eijiro Sumii, 2005) is the ML compiler people usually read
 * first: about two thousand lines of OCaml compiling to SPARC, one pass
 * per file (typing, K-normal form, closure conversion, register
 * allocation), with no polymorphism, no data types, and no collector.
 * Andrew Appel's Compiling with Continuations (1992) is the book about
 * the other road, through CPS, the one taken by Standard ML of New
 * Jersey.
 *
 * References (plan_ml.md's related work lists them too):
 *  - Robin Milner, "A Theory of Type Polymorphism in Programming"
 *    (1978)
 *  - Didier Rémy's levels, as explained in Oleg Kiselyov's "How OCaml
 *    type checker works" (2013)
 *  - Andrew Wright, "Simple imperative polymorphism" (1995): the value
 *    restriction
 *  - C. J. Cheney, "A nonrecursive list compacting algorithm" (CACM,
 *    1970)
 *  - Fergus Henderson, "Accurate garbage collection in an uncooperative
 *    environment" (ISMM 2002)
 *  - Simon Marlow and Simon Peyton Jones, "Making a fast curry"
 *    (ICFP 2004)
 *  - Xavier Leroy, "The ZINC experiment" (1990): the representation of
 *    values
 *)

(* a unit's phrases (each with its line), with the names of the units
 * before it, to assembly added to the output: every function's code,
 * and <unit>.init, its toplevel; the names then, those it defined, and
 * its globals' count *)
val compile_unit :
  (string * TinyMLCompile.binding) list -> (TinyMLTree.item * int) list ->
  (string * TinyMLCompile.binding) list * (string * TinyMLCompile.binding) list
  * int

(* the program: files of ML to a file of assembly (-h: how) *)
val main : < Cap.argv; Cap.open_in; Cap.open_out; Cap.stdout; Cap.stderr; .. > -> int
tiny/TinyMLRuntime/core.c
26354
/* Claude Code
 * Copyright (C) 2026 Yoann Padioleau. LGPL 2.1: see license.txt.
 *
 * TinyML's runtime, its part common to every program (the host's,
 * runtime.c; TinyKernel.ml's, TinyKernel/runtime.c): the allocator
 * and Cheney's copying collector, the primitives the prelude names,
 * stdout's buffer, the uncaught exception. Its includer gives the
 * memory (ml_run) and write and exit. A word is intptr's: 8 bytes on
 * arm64, 4 on tiny-machine (tiny-ml).
 *
 * A value is a word: an integer n as 2n+1, or the address of a block's
 * first field, the block's header the word before it (its size in
 * words << 10, its tag in the low byte: 247 a closure, 252 a string,
 * whose fields hold no value). The roots are the value stack, from its
 * base to ml_vsp (which the ML code stores before calling C), and the
 * program's globals (ml_globals, ml_nglobals, written by tiny-ml). A C
 * function that allocates pushes its values on the value stack first,
 * and reads them back: the collector moves them.
 */

typedef intptr value;
typedef unsigned char uchar;

#define W sizeof(value)

extern long write(int, void*, long);
extern void exit(int);

extern void ml_start(value*);
extern value ml_globals[];
extern value ml_nglobals;

value *ml_vsp;
void *ml_handler;
/* the value stack's end, when the includer says it (mlsys.c): past it,
 * a recursion too deep is said at the next allocation (old: none, the
 * stack ran into the heap's first blocks: tiny-c's List.map over a
 * file's tokens, wrong values, then a loop or an exception) */
value *ml_vlimit;

/*****************************************************************************/
/* The heap, the collector */
/*****************************************************************************/

/* the memory, the includer's (ml_init_heap): the value stack's base,
 * the heap's two halves and their size in words */
static value *vbase;
static value maxheap;
static value *from;           /* the heap: from..limit, allocated up to hp */
static value *other;          /* the other half */
static value *hp;
static value *limit;
static value size;
static value *lo;             /* the collector's: the space collected, */
static value *hi;
static value *next;           /* and where the next copy goes */

static void
fatal(char *msg)
{
	long n;

	for(n = 0; msg[n] != 0; n++)
		;
	write(2, msg, n);
	exit(2);
}

/* a value's copy in to-space: an integer or a pointer outside the space
 * collected (a static block) as is; a copied block's header is 0, its
 * first field the copy's address */
static value
copy(value v)
{
	value *p;
	value *q;
	value h;
	value n;
	value i;

	p = (value*)v;
	if((v & 1) != 0 || p < lo || p >= hi)
		return v;
	h = p[-1];
	if(h == 0)
		return p[0];
	n = h >> 10;
	q = next + 1;
	q[-1] = h;
	for(i = 0; i < n; i++)
		q[i] = p[i];
	next = q + n;
	p[-1] = 0;
	p[0] = (value)q;
	return (value)q;
}

/* Cheney: the roots copied, then the copies scanned, breadth first,
 * scan chasing next; the halves swapped */
static void
collect(void)
{
	value *to;
	value *scan;
	value *v;
	value n;
	value i;
	value h;

	to = other;
	lo = from;
	hi = limit;
	next = to;
	for(v = vbase; v < ml_vsp; v++)
		*v = copy(*v);
	for(i = 0; i < ml_nglobals; i++)
		ml_globals[i] = copy(ml_globals[i]);
	for(scan = to; scan < next; scan = scan + n + 1){
		h = *scan;
		n = h >> 10;
		if((h & 255) < 251)
			for(i = 1; i <= n; i++)
				scan[i] = copy(scan[i]);
	}
	other = from;
	from = to;
	hp = next;
}

/* if less than half is free after, the heap grows: its halves are
 * the includer's, as big as they can be (maxheap words), and size the
 * part in use */
static void
gc(value need)
{
	collect();
	while((hp - from + need) * 2 > size && size < maxheap)
		size = size * 2;
	if(size > maxheap)
		size = maxheap;
	limit = from + size;
	if(hp + need > limit)
		fatal("Fatal error: out of memory\n");
}

value
ml_alloc(value n, value tag)
{
	value *p;

	if(hp + n + 1 > limit)
		gc(n + 1);
	if(ml_vlimit && ml_vsp > ml_vlimit)
		fatal("Fatal error: stack overflow\n");
	p = hp + 1;
	p[-1] = (n << 10) | tag;
	hp = p + n;
	return (value)p;
}

static void
push(value v)
{
	*ml_vsp = v;
	ml_vsp++;
}

static value
pop(void)
{
	ml_vsp--;
	return *ml_vsp;
}

static value
wosize(value v)
{
	return ((value*)v)[-1] >> 10;
}

/*****************************************************************************/
/* Strings, bytes */
/*****************************************************************************/

/* strings: the last byte the number of padding bytes before it */
static value
string_alloc(value len)
{
	value w;
	value s;

	/* (W as a value: sizeof's type has no sign, and tiny-cpu divides
	 * signed only, so len / W was a call of __udivmod, some thousand
	 * instructions for each string made) */
	w = len / (value)W + 1;
	s = ml_alloc(w, 252);
	((value*)s)[w - 1] = 0;
	((uchar*)s)[w * W - 1] = w * W - 1 - len;
	return s;
}

static value
length(value s)
{
	value w;

	w = wosize(s);
	return w * W - 1 - ((uchar*)s)[w * W - 1];
}

value
ml_string_length(value s)
{
	return length(s) * 2 + 1;
}

value
ml_string_get(value s, value i)
{
	i = i >> 1;
	if(i < 0 || i >= length(s))
		fatal("Fatal error: out-of-bound access in array or string\n");
	return ((uchar*)s)[i] * 2 + 1;
}

value
ml_string_make(value n, value c)
{
	value s;
	value i;

	n = n >> 1;
	s = string_alloc(n);
	for(i = 0; i < n; i++)
		((uchar*)s)[i] = c >> 1;
	return s;
}

value
ml_string_sub(value s, value ofs, value len)
{
	value r;
	value i;

	push(s);
	r = string_alloc(len >> 1);
	s = pop();
	for(i = 0; i < len >> 1; i++)
		((uchar*)r)[i] = ((uchar*)s)[(ofs >> 1) + i];
	return r;
}

// bytes are strings that are changed: Bytes.set, the copy of
// Bytes.to_string, Bytes.blit_string's
value
ml_bytes_set(value s, value i, value c)
{
	i = i >> 1;
	if(i < 0 || i >= length(s))
		fatal("Fatal error: out-of-bound access in array or string\n");
	((uchar*)s)[i] = c >> 1;
	return 1;
}

value
ml_bytes_to_string(value s)
{
	return ml_string_sub(s, 1, ml_string_length(s));
}

value
ml_bytes_blit_string(value src, value so, value dst, value d, value n)
{
	value i;

	so = so >> 1;
	d = d >> 1;
	n = n >> 1;
	if(n < 0 || so < 0 || so + n > length(src) || d < 0 || d + n > length(dst))
		fatal("Fatal error: out-of-bound access in array or string\n");
	for(i = 0; i < n; i++)
		((uchar*)dst)[d + i] = ((uchar*)src)[so + i];
	return 1;
}

value
ml_concat(value a, value b)
{
	value la;
	value lb;
	value s;
	value i;

	la = length(a);
	lb = length(b);
	push(a);
	push(b);
	s = string_alloc(la + lb);
	b = pop();
	a = pop();
	for(i = 0; i < la; i++)
		((uchar*)s)[i] = ((uchar*)a)[i];
	for(i = 0; i < lb; i++)
		((uchar*)s)[la + i] = ((uchar*)b)[i];
	return s;
}

/* String.concat: the strings of a list (a cell a block of two fields,
 * [] an integer, as ML makes them) joined by sep, the result made once
 * (old: in ML, TinyLibCore's String.concat, three calls of the runtime
 * a piece: Printf's strings, many pieces of a few bytes, cost more than
 * the ^ they replaced) */
value
ml_string_concat(value sep, value l)
{
	value n;
	value ls;
	value c;
	value s;
	value r;
	value pos;
	value i;
	value k;

	ls = length(sep);
	n = 0;
	for(c = l; (c & 1) == 0; c = ((value*)c)[1])
		n += length(((value*)c)[0]) + ls;
	if((l & 1) == 0)
		n -= ls;
	push(sep);
	push(l);
	r = string_alloc(n);
	l = pop();
	sep = pop();
	pos = 0;
	for(c = l; (c & 1) == 0; c = ((value*)c)[1]){
		s = ((value*)c)[0];
		k = length(s);
		for(i = 0; i < k; i++)
			((uchar*)r)[pos + i] = ((uchar*)s)[i];
		pos += k;
		if((((value*)c)[1] & 1) == 0){
			for(i = 0; i < ls; i++)
				((uchar*)r)[pos + i] = ((uchar*)sep)[i];
			pos += ls;
		}
	}
	return r;
}

/* n's digits at the end of buf; where they start */
static value
digits(value n, char *buf)
{
	value i;
	value d;
	value neg;

	neg = n < 0;
	i = 24;
	do {
		i--;
		d = n % 10;
		if(d < 0)
			d = -d;
		buf[i] = '0' + d;
		n = n / 10;
	} while(n != 0);
	if(neg){
		i--;
		buf[i] = '-';
	}
	return i;
}

value
ml_string_of_int(value v)
{
	char buf[24];
	value i;
	value k;
	value s;

	i = digits(v >> 1, buf);
	s = string_alloc(24 - i);
	for(k = 0; k < 24 - i; k++)
		((uchar*)s)[k] = buf[i + k];
	return s;
}

/*****************************************************************************/
/* Compare */
/*****************************************************************************/

/* OCaml's compare: integers before blocks, then the tags, strings by
 * their bytes, the other blocks by their sizes then their fields */
static value
compare(value a, value b)
{
	value ta;
	value tb;
	value n;
	value m;
	value i;
	value c;
	uchar *p;
	uchar *q;

	if(a == b)
		return 0;
	if(a & 1){
		if(b & 1)
			return a < b ? -1 : 1;
		return -1;
	}
	if(b & 1)
		return 1;
	ta = ((value*)a)[-1] & 255;
	tb = ((value*)b)[-1] & 255;
	if(ta != tb)
		return ta < tb ? -1 : 1;
	if(ta == 252){
		n = length(a);
		m = length(b);
		p = (uchar*)a;
		q = (uchar*)b;
		for(i = 0; i < n && i < m; i++)
			if(p[i] != q[i])
				return p[i] < q[i] ? -1 : 1;
		return n < m ? -1 : n > m ? 1 : 0;
	}
	n = wosize(a);
	m = wosize(b);
	if(n != m)
		return n < m ? -1 : 1;
	for(i = 0; i < n; i++){
		c = compare(((value*)a)[i], ((value*)b)[i]);
		if(c != 0)
			return c;
	}
	return 0;
}

// two integers compared here, before compare's frame of eight locals
// (old: 100 instructions for min 3 4, the prelude's min being
// polymorphic; a sound's sample clamped by min and max was 175 of them)
value
ml_compare(value a, value b)
{
	if(a & b & 1)
		return a < b ? -1 : a == b ? 1 : 3;
	return compare(a, b) * 2 + 1;
}

value
ml_equal(value a, value b)
{
	if(a & b & 1)
		return a == b ? 3 : 1;
	return compare(a, b) == 0 ? 3 : 1;
}

/*****************************************************************************/
/* Arrays */
/*****************************************************************************/

/* arrays: a block of tag 0, as a tuple; the empty one (and a
 * negative size's, which OCaml refuses) static, as
 * OCaml's atom: a block of no field has no room for the collector's
 * forwarding address */
static value empty_array[2];

value
ml_array_make(value n, value v)
{
	value a;
	value i;

	n = n >> 1;
	if(n <= 0)
		return (value)&empty_array[1];
	push(v);
	a = ml_alloc(n, 0);
	v = pop();
	for(i = 0; i < n; i++)
		((value*)a)[i] = v;
	return a;
}

value
ml_array_length(value a)
{
	return wosize(a) * 2 + 1;
}

static value*
index(value a, value i)
{
	i = i >> 1;
	if(i < 0 || i >= wosize(a))
		fatal("Fatal error: out-of-bound access in array or string\n");
	return (value*)a + i;
}

value
ml_array_get(value a, value i)
{
	return *index(a, i);
}

value
ml_array_set(value a, value i, value v)
{
	*index(a, i) = v;
	return 1;
}

/*****************************************************************************/
/* Hashtbl */
/*****************************************************************************/

// a value's hash, for TinyLibCore/Hashtbl.ml: its integers, its
// strings' bytes, its blocks' tags and fields, as OCaml's Hashtbl.hash
// walks one, ten values at most; never an address, which the collector
// changes (a closure is its tag alone)
static unsigned
hash(value v, value *budget)
{
	unsigned h;
	value n;
	value i;
	value t;
	uchar *p;

	if(*budget <= 0)
		return 0;
	*budget = *budget - 1;
	if(v & 1)
		return (unsigned)(v >> 1) * 0x9e3779b1;
	t = ((value*)v)[-1] & 255;
	h = t;
	if(t == 252){
		n = length(v);
		p = (uchar*)v;
		for(i = 0; i < n; i++)
			h = (h ^ p[i]) * 16777619;
		return h;
	}
	if(t == 247)
		return h;
	n = wosize(v);
	for(i = 0; i < n && *budget > 0; i++)
		h = h * 31 + hash(((value*)v)[i], budget);
	return h;
}

value
ml_hash(value v)
{
	value budget;

	budget = 10;
	return ((hash(v, &budget) & 0x3fffffff) << 1) | 1;
}

/*****************************************************************************/
/* Stdout */
/*****************************************************************************/

/* stdout: ocaml-light's channel, a buffer written when full, flushed
 * by print_newline and at exit, lost on an uncaught exception */
static uchar obuf[4096];
static long olen;

/* all of the buffer, in as many writes as it takes: a pipe of
 * tiny-kernel's takes 512 bytes at a time, and a write says how many
 * it took (old: one write, and in a pipe what was over 512 lost) */
static void
writeall(void)
{
	long done, k;

	for(done = 0; done < olen; done += k)
		if((k = write(1, obuf + done, olen - done)) <= 0)
			break;
	olen = 0;
}

static void
outc(value c)
{
	if(olen == 4096)
		writeall();
	obuf[olen] = c;
	olen++;
}

static void
flush(void)
{
	writeall();
}

value
ml_print_string(value s)
{
	value n;
	value i;

	n = length(s);
	for(i = 0; i < n; i++)
		outc(((uchar*)s)[i]);
	return 1;
}

value
ml_print_char(value c)
{
	outc(c >> 1);
	return 1;
}

value
ml_print_newline(value u)
{
	outc('\n');
	flush();
	return u;
}

value
ml_exit(value n)
{
	flush();
	exit(n >> 1);
	return 1;
}

/*****************************************************************************/
/* Exceptions */
/*****************************************************************************/

/* an uncaught exception, as ocaml-light's printexc.c prints it: its
 * name, then its integer and string arguments (a single tuple's
 * fields, as Match_failure's) */
static char ebuf[256];
static long elen;

static void
eadd(char *s, value n)
{
	value i;

	for(i = 0; i < n && elen < 255; i++){
		ebuf[elen] = s[i];
		elen++;
	}
}

value
ml_uncaught(value exn)
{
	char buf[24];
	value b;
	value v;
	value i;
	value start;
	value name;

	name = ((value*)((value*)exn)[0])[0];
	eadd((char*)name, length(name));
	if(wosize(exn) >= 2){
		b = exn;
		start = 1;
		v = ((value*)exn)[1];
		if(wosize(exn) == 2 && (v & 1) == 0 && (((value*)v)[-1] & 255) == 0){
			b = v;
			start = 0;
		}
		eadd("(", 1);
		for(i = start; i < wosize(b); i++){
			if(i > start)
				eadd(", ", 2);
			v = ((value*)b)[i];
			if(v & 1)
				eadd(buf + digits(v >> 1, buf),
					24 - digits(v >> 1, buf));
			else if((((value*)v)[-1] & 255) == 252){
				eadd("\"", 1);
				eadd((char*)v, length(v));
				eadd("\"", 1);
			}else
				eadd("_", 1);
		}
		eadd(")", 1);
	}
	write(2, "Fatal error: uncaught exception ", 32);
	write(2, ebuf, elen);
	write(2, "\n", 1);
	exit(2);
	return 1;
}

/*****************************************************************************/
/* The start */
/*****************************************************************************/

/* the heap and the value stack: the includer's memory; then the
 * program's toplevel */
void
ml_run(value *stack, value *space0, value *space1, value words, value initial)
{
	vbase = stack;
	maxheap = words;
	size = initial;
	if(size < 16)
		size = 16;
	if(size > maxheap)
		size = maxheap;
	from = space0;
	other = space1;
	hp = from;
	limit = from + size;
	ml_vsp = vbase;
	ml_start(vbase);
}

/*****************************************************************************/
/* Marshal */
/*****************************************************************************/

/* Marshal: a value as bytes and back, in OCaml's format (its small
 * header: the magic number, the data's length, the blocks, their words
 * on 32 and on 64 bits; then the value depth first, a code each: an
 * integer, a string, a block and its fields, or a block met before, so
 * what is shared stays shared), the format lib_core's Marshal.ml writes
 * for mini-ml: a value written by the host's tiny-ml (OCaml's Marshal)
 * and by tiny-kernel's ml is the same bytes, when its blocks are. No
 * float, no custom block, no closure.
 *
 * Writing goes twice over the value, once to count the bytes, then
 * into the string made of that size: nothing is allocated meanwhile,
 * so nothing moves. A block met has its header marked (bit 8, its
 * number above it), the header kept in the trail, which is the
 * collector's other half, free between two collections; the headers
 * are put back at the end. Reading makes every block in one allocation
 * of the words the header says (as OCaml's intern), so no collection
 * happens while the blocks are filled; its table of the blocks read is
 * in the other half too. */
static value *trail;
static value ntrail;
static uchar *mout;     /* the bytes written, or 0: only counted */
static value mlen;
static value mwords32;
static value mwords64;
static value msharing;  /* 0: No_sharing asked (OCaml's: each copy
			 * written anew, no block counted) */

static void
mbyte(value b)
{
	if(mout)
		mout[mlen] = b;
	mlen++;
}

/* n's low bytes, the high one first */
static void
mput(value n, value bytes)
{
	value i;

	for(i = bytes - 1; i >= 0; i--)
		mbyte((n >> (8 * i)) & 255);
}

static void
mint(value n)
{
	if(n >= 0 && n < 64)
		mbyte(0x40 + n);
	else if(n >= -128 && n < 128){
		mbyte(0x00);
		mput(n, 1);
	}
	else if(n >= -32768 && n < 32768){
		mbyte(0x01);
		mput(n, 2);
	}
	else {
		mbyte(0x02);
		mput(n, 4);
	}
}

static void
extern_value(value v)
{
	value *p;
	value h;
	value n;
	value tag;
	value i;
	value len;
	value ago;

	for(;;){
		if(v & 1){
			mint(v >> 1);
			return;
		}
		p = (value*)v;
		h = p[-1];
		if(msharing && (h & 0x100)){
			ago = ntrail - (h >> 10);
			if(ago < 256){
				mbyte(0x04);
				mput(ago, 1);
			} else if(ago < 65536){
				mbyte(0x05);
				mput(ago, 2);
			} else {
				mbyte(0x06);
				mput(ago, 4);
			}
			return;
		}
		n = h >> 10;
		tag = h & 255;
		if(n == 0){
			mbyte(0x80 + tag);
			return;
		}
		if(msharing){
			if((ntrail + 1) * 2 > maxheap)
				fatal("Fatal error: Marshal.to_string: too many blocks\n");
			trail[2 * ntrail] = v;
			trail[2 * ntrail + 1] = h;
			p[-1] = (ntrail << 10) | 0x100 | tag;
			ntrail++;
		}
		if(tag == 252){
			len = n * W - 1 - ((uchar*)p)[n * W - 1];
			if(len < 32)
				mbyte(0x20 + len);
			else if(len < 256){
				mbyte(0x09);
				mput(len, 1);
			} else {
				mbyte(0x0A);
				mput(len, 4);
			}
			for(i = 0; i < len; i++)
				mbyte(((uchar*)p)[i]);
			mwords32 = mwords32 + 2 + len / 4;
			mwords64 = mwords64 + 2 + len / 8;
			return;
		}
		if(tag >= 247)
			fatal("Fatal error: Marshal.to_string: a closure, a float or a custom block\n");
		if(tag < 16 && n < 8)
			mbyte(0x80 + tag + n * 16);
		else {
			mbyte(0x08);
			mput(n * 1024 + tag, 4);
		}
		mwords32 = mwords32 + 1 + n;
		mwords64 = mwords64 + 1 + n;
		for(i = 0; i < n - 1; i++)
			extern_value(p[i]);
		/* (the last field in this loop: a long list is no deep stack) */
		v = p[n - 1];
	}
}

/* the value counted (out 0) or written into out; the headers put back */
static void
extern_pass(value v, uchar *out)
{
	value i;

	trail = other;
	ntrail = 0;
	mout = out;
	mlen = 20;
	mwords32 = 0;
	mwords64 = 0;
	extern_value(v);
	for(i = 0; i < ntrail; i++)
		((value*)trail[2 * i])[-1] = trail[2 * i + 1];
}

value
ml_marshal_to_string(value v, value flags)
{
	value s;
	value l;

	/* No_sharing, the flags' first constructor: 0, an integer */
	msharing = 1;
	for(l = flags; (l & 1) == 0; l = ((value*)l)[1])
		if(((value*)l)[0] == 1)
			msharing = 0;
	extern_pass(v, 0);
	push(v);
	s = string_alloc(mlen);
	v = pop();
	extern_pass(v, (uchar*)s);
	/* the header, now that its numbers are known */
	mlen = 0;
	mput(0x8495A6BE, 4);
	mput(length(s) - 20, 4);
	mput(ntrail, 4);
	mput(mwords32, 4);
	mput(mwords64, 4);
	return s;
}

/* Reading */
static uchar *min;
static value mpos;
static value *mobj;
static value nobj;
static value *mnext;   /* where the next block's header goes */
static value unfinished;

static value
mget(value bytes)
{
	value n;
	value i;

	n = 0;
	for(i = 0; i < bytes; i++){
		n = (n << 8) | min[mpos];
		mpos++;
	}
	return n;
}

static value
msigned(value bytes)
{
	value n;

	n = mget(bytes);
	if(bytes < 4 && (n >> (8 * bytes - 1)) != 0)
		n = n - (1 << (8 * bytes));
	return n;
}

static value
mstring(value len)
{
	value *b;
	value w;
	value i;

	w = len / W + 1;
	b = mnext + 1;
	b[-1] = (w << 10) | 252;
	b[w - 1] = 0;
	for(i = 0; i < len; i++)
		((uchar*)b)[i] = min[mpos + i];
	((uchar*)b)[w * W - 1] = w * W - 1 - len;
	mpos = mpos + len;
	mnext = b + w;
	mobj[nobj] = (value)b;
	nobj++;
	return (value)b;
}

static value intern_value(void);

/* a block of n fields: all but its last read, unfinished set */
static value
mblock(value tag, value n)
{
	value *b;
	value i;

	if(n == 0)
		return (value)&empty_array[1];
	b = mnext + 1;
	b[-1] = (n << 10) | tag;
	mnext = b + n;
	for(i = 0; i < n; i++)
		b[i] = 1;
	mobj[nobj] = (value)b;
	nobj++;
	for(i = 0; i < n - 1; i++)
		b[i] = intern_value();
	unfinished = 1;
	return (value)b;
}

/* the next item: a value, or a block whose last field is still to read */
static value
intern_item(void)
{
	value code;

	unfinished = 0;
	code = min[mpos];
	mpos++;
	if(code >= 0x80)
		return mblock(code & 15, (code >> 4) & 7);
	if(code >= 0x40)
		return (code & 63) * 2 + 1;
	if(code >= 0x20)
		return mstring(code & 31);
	if(code == 0x00)
		return msigned(1) * 2 + 1;
	if(code == 0x01)
		return msigned(2) * 2 + 1;
	if(code == 0x02)
		return msigned(4) * 2 + 1;
	if(code == 0x04)
		return mobj[nobj - mget(1)];
	if(code == 0x05)
		return mobj[nobj - mget(2)];
	if(code == 0x06)
		return mobj[nobj - mget(4)];
	if(code == 0x08){
		code = mget(4);
		return mblock(code & 255, code >> 10);
	}
	if(code == 0x09)
		return mstring(mget(1));
	if(code == 0x0A)
		return mstring(mget(4));
	fatal("Fatal error: Marshal.from_string: what this runtime does not read\n");
	return 1;
}

static value
intern_value(void)
{
	value v;
	value last;
	value b;

	v = intern_item();
	b = v;
	while(unfinished){
		last = intern_item();
		((value*)b)[wosize(b) - 1] = last;
		b = last;
	}
	return v;
}

value
ml_marshal_from_string(value s, value ofs)
{
	value words;
	value *chunk;

	ofs = ofs >> 1;
	min = (uchar*)s + ofs;
	mpos = 0;
	if(mget(4) != 0x8495A6BE)
		fatal("Fatal error: Marshal.from_string: bad object\n");
	mpos = 12;
	words = mget(4);
	if(words * 2 > maxheap)
		fatal("Fatal error: Marshal.from_string: too many blocks\n");
	if(words > 0){
		push(s);
		chunk = (value*)ml_alloc(words - 1, 0);
		s = pop();
		mnext = chunk - 1;
	}
	min = (uchar*)s + ofs;
	mpos = 20;
	mobj = other;
	nobj = 0;
	return intern_value();
}

/*****************************************************************************/
/* SHA-1 */
/*****************************************************************************/

/* SHA-1: the digest of a string, 20 bytes, in C on the machine's words
 * of 32 bits (old: TinyLibCore's Sha1 in ML, a word as two halves of
 * 16, as tiny-ml's integers have 31: 2.6 KB a second on tiny-kernel,
 * hours of tiny-build's digests in tiny-kernel's build of itself) */
static value sha_h[5];
static value sha_w[80];
static uchar sha_last[128];

/* a block of 64 bytes; a rotation left by n written out, x << n | x >>
 * (32 - n), the high bits that >> (arithmetic) brings masked off (tiny-c
 * has no macro with parameters, and a call each was a third of the
 * time) */
static void
sha_block(uchar *p)
{
	value x;
	value a;
	value b;
	value c;
	value d;
	value e;
	value f;
	value k;
	value t;
	value temp;

	for(t = 0; t < 16; t++)
		sha_w[t] = (p[4 * t] << 24) | (p[4 * t + 1] << 16) |
			(p[4 * t + 2] << 8) | p[4 * t + 3];
	for(t = 16; t < 80; t++){
		x = sha_w[t - 3] ^ sha_w[t - 8] ^ sha_w[t - 14] ^ sha_w[t - 16];
		sha_w[t] = (x << 1) | ((x >> 31) & 1);
	}
	a = sha_h[0];
	b = sha_h[1];
	c = sha_h[2];
	d = sha_h[3];
	e = sha_h[4];
	for(t = 0; t < 80; t++){
		if(t < 20){
			f = (b & c) | (~b & d);
			k = 0x5A827999;
		} else if(t < 40){
			f = b ^ c ^ d;
			k = 0x6ED9EBA1;
		} else if(t < 60){
			f = (b & c) | (b & d) | (c & d);
			k = 0x8F1BBCDC;
		} else {
			f = b ^ c ^ d;
			k = 0xCA62C1D6;
		}
		temp = ((a << 5) | ((a >> 27) & 31)) + f + e + k + sha_w[t];
		e = d;
		d = c;
		c = (b << 30) | ((b >> 2) & 0x3FFFFFFF);
		b = a;
		a = temp;
	}
	sha_h[0] = sha_h[0] + a;
	sha_h[1] = sha_h[1] + b;
	sha_h[2] = sha_h[2] + c;
	sha_h[3] = sha_h[3] + d;
	sha_h[4] = sha_h[4] + e;
}

/* the end: the rest of n bytes (fewer than 64), a 1 bit, zeros, the
 * length in bits: one block or two; the digest's 20 bytes */
static value
sha_end(uchar *p, value rest, value n)
{
	value i;
	value total;
	value bits;
	value r;

	for(total = 0; total < 128; total++)
		sha_last[total] = 0;
	for(total = 0; total < rest; total++)
		sha_last[total] = p[total];
	sha_last[rest] = 128;
	total = rest + 9 <= 64 ? 64 : 128;
	bits = n * 8;
	sha_last[total - 4] = (bits >> 24) & 255;
	sha_last[total - 3] = (bits >> 16) & 255;
	sha_last[total - 2] = (bits >> 8) & 255;
	sha_last[total - 1] = bits & 255;
	sha_block(sha_last);
	if(total == 128)
		sha_block(sha_last + 64);
	r = string_alloc(20);
	for(i = 0; i < 5; i++){
		((uchar*)r)[4 * i] = (sha_h[i] >> 24) & 255;
		((uchar*)r)[4 * i + 1] = (sha_h[i] >> 16) & 255;
		((uchar*)r)[4 * i + 2] = (sha_h[i] >> 8) & 255;
		((uchar*)r)[4 * i + 3] = sha_h[i] & 255;
	}
	return r;
}

static void
sha_start(void)
{
	sha_h[0] = 0x67452301;
	sha_h[1] = 0xEFCDAB89;
	sha_h[2] = 0x98BADCFE;
	sha_h[3] = 0x10325476;
	sha_h[4] = 0xC3D2E1F0;
}

value
ml_sha1_string(value s)
{
	value n;
	value i;
	uchar *p;

	sha_start();
	n = length(s);
	p = (uchar*)s;
	for(i = 0; i + 64 <= n; i = i + 64)
		sha_block(p + i);
	return sha_end(p + i, n - i, n);
}

/* a digest made piece by piece (Sha1.reads: a file is not read whole
 * to be digested, tiny-build's boot.img of 8 MB in its 16): its context
 * a string of 96 bytes, the five words, the length so far, then the
 * bytes of the block begun */
value
ml_sha1_init(value u)
{
	value c;
	value i;

	c = string_alloc(96);
	sha_start();
	for(i = 0; i < 5; i++)
		((value*)c)[i] = sha_h[i];
	((value*)c)[5] = 0;
	return c;
}

value
ml_sha1_update(value c, value s)
{
	value *w;
	uchar *buf;
	uchar *p;
	value n;
	value i;
	value have;

	w = (value*)c;
	buf = (uchar*)c + 32;
	for(i = 0; i < 5; i++)
		sha_h[i] = w[i];
	n = length(s);
	p = (uchar*)s;
	have = w[5] & 63;
	w[5] = w[5] + n;
	i = 0;
	while(have > 0 && have < 64 && i < n){
		buf[have] = p[i];
		have = have + 1;
		i = i + 1;
	}
	if(have == 64){
		sha_block(buf);
		have = 0;
	}
	if(have == 0){
		while(i + 64 <= n){
			sha_block(p + i);
			i = i + 64;
		}
		while(i < n){
			buf[have] = p[i];
			have = have + 1;
			i = i + 1;
		}
	}
	for(i = 0; i < 5; i++)
		w[i] = sha_h[i];
	return 1;
}

value
ml_sha1_final(value c)
{
	value i;

	for(i = 0; i < 5; i++)
		sha_h[i] = ((value*)c)[i];
	return sha_end((uchar*)c + 32, ((value*)c)[5] & 63, ((value*)c)[5]);
}
tiny/TinyMachine/TinyMachineCPU.ml
8765
(* Claude Code
 * Copyright (C) 2026 Yoann Padioleau. LGPL 2.1: see license.txt. *)

(* See TinyMachineCPU.mli. Its laws are checked by tests/TinyCPU_test.sh:
 * the first on the programs of tests/TinyCPU_tests/, the second on
 * random programs of every instruction. *)

(* The instructions, their words: TinyMachineISA's, in what tiny-ml
 * compiles too, for tiny-assembler and tiny-linker on tiny-kernel *)
open TinyMachineISA
let error fmt = Printf.ksprintf (fun s -> raise (Error s)) fmt

let m32 v = v land 0xffffffff
let signed v = ((v land 0xffffffff) lxor 0x80000000) - 0x80000000
(* a < b, both unsigned words. A word is 0 to 2^32-1 where an int has
 * 63 bits; where it has 32 (js_of_ocaml: TinyMachineWeb.ml) the same
 * bits are a signed int, m32 and signed change nothing, and a plain <
 * would be the signed one: the top bit turned first is right for both *)
let ult a b = a lxor min_int < b lxor min_int

(*****************************************************************************)
(* The machine: the interpreter *)
(*****************************************************************************)

(* 2^20 bytes, TinyCPU's; a machine around the CPU may have more
 * (TinyMachine's 16 MB), set before its boot *)
let memsize = ref (1 lsl 20)

type machine = { r : int array; mutable pc : int; mem : Bytes.t }

(* what the program that runs the CPU decides *)
type env = {
  fetch : machine -> int -> int;           (* the instruction's word at pc *)
  load : machine -> size -> int -> int;
  store : machine -> size -> int -> int -> unit;
  sys : machine -> int -> unit;  (* the call's number, pc past the sys *)
  illegal : machine -> int -> unit;        (* the word, pc still on it *)
}

let addr a = a land (!memsize - 1)
let word a = addr a land lnot 3
(* old: let load m = function W -> fun a -> ... | B -> fun a -> ...
 * A function given m and the size returned a function of the address:
 * a closure made at every load, and at every fetch, which is a load
 * (js_of_ocaml: 11% of the time in it, and the collector after it;
 * 4.5 million instructions a second became 5.2, natively 11.5 became
 * 13.5: tests/TinyMachine_bench.sh). *)
let load m s a = match s with
  | W -> Int32.to_int (Bytes.get_int32_le m.mem (word a)) land 0xffffffff
  | B -> Char.code (Bytes.get m.mem (addr a))
let store m s a v = match s with
  | W -> Bytes.set_int32_le m.mem (word a) (Int32.of_int (m32 v))
  | B -> Bytes.set m.mem (addr a) (Char.chr (v land 0xff))

let alu op a b =
  let sa = signed a and sb = signed b in
  m32 (match op with
    | Add -> a + b | Sub -> a - b | Mul -> a * b
    | Div ->   (* truncated *)
        if b = 0 then -1 else if sa = -0x80000000 && sb = -1 then sa
        else Int.div sa sb
    | Rem ->
        if b = 0 then a else if sa = -0x80000000 && sb = -1 then 0
        else Int.rem sa sb
    | And -> a land b | Or -> a lor b | Xor -> a lxor b
    | Shl -> a lsl (b land 31) | Shr -> a lsr (b land 31)
    | Sar -> sa asr (b land 31)
    | Slt -> if sa < sb then 1 else 0 | Sltu -> if ult a b then 1 else 0)

let compare c a b =
  match c with
  | Eq -> a = b | Ne -> a <> b
  | Lt -> signed a < signed b | Ge -> signed a >= signed b
  | Ltu -> ult a b | Geu -> not (ult a b)

(* memory alone, and an unknown word an error *)
let plain ~sys = {
  fetch = (fun m pc -> load m W pc);
  load; store; sys;
  illegal = (fun m w -> error "illegal instruction %08x at 0x%x" w m.pc);
}

(*****************************************************************************)
(* Faster: the words already decoded *)
(*****************************************************************************)

(* The simple step decodes its word each time: decode makes a value (an
 * Alu, a Load...) that is used once and left to the collector, eight
 * million times a second. But decode is a function of the word alone,
 * so its answer can be kept by the word: no store in memory can make
 * it wrong, and nothing has to be forgotten when a program writes
 * over its code or another is loaded. A table of [kept] places, a
 * word's place by its bits folded; a place holds the last word that
 * fell there and its instruction. With [keep_decoded] false the step
 * is the simple one. (tests/TinyMachine_bench.sh, tiny-kernel's
 * paint.events: by js_of_ocaml under node, 6.8 million instructions a
 * second without it, 8.1 with it; natively 21.3 and 22.0, OCaml's own
 * allocation being a few instructions.) *)
let keep_decoded = ref true
let kept = 16384
(* 0 is no instruction *)
let decoded : (int * instr option) array = Array.make kept (0, None)

let decode_kept w =
  let k = (w lxor (w lsr 11) lxor (w lsr 22)) land (kept - 1) in
  let (w', i) = decoded.(k) in
  if w' = w then i else begin
    let i = decode w in
    decoded.(k) <- (w, i);
    i
  end

(*****************************************************************************)
(* The step *)
(*****************************************************************************)

(* old: a function inside step, let set d v = if d <> 0 then r.(d) <-
 * m32 v, which closes over r: js_of_ocaml makes that closure at every
 * step (OCaml's native compiler inlines it). *)
let set (r : int array) d v = if d <> 0 then r.(d) <- m32 v

(* one step: the word at pc fetched (from memory, or through the
 * machine's pages), decoded and run *)
let step env m =
  let pc = m.pc in
  let w = env.fetch m pc in
  match if !keep_decoded then decode_kept w else decode w with
  | None -> env.illegal m w
  | Some i ->
      let r = m.r in
      m.pc <- addr (pc + 4);
      (match i with
       | Alu (op, d, a, b) -> set r d (alu op r.(a) r.(b))
       | Alui (op, d, a, imm) -> set r d (alu op r.(a) (m32 imm))
       | Lui (d, imm) -> set r d (imm lsl 16)
       | Load (s, d, a, off) -> set r d (env.load m s (r.(a) + off))
       | Store (s, d, a, off) -> env.store m s (r.(a) + off) r.(d)
       | Branch (c, d, a, off) ->
           if compare c r.(d) r.(a) then m.pc <- addr (pc + 4 + (4 * off))
       | Jal (d, off) -> set r d (pc + 4); m.pc <- addr (pc + 4 + (4 * off))
       | Jalr (d, a, off) ->
           let t = word (r.(a) + off) in set r d (pc + 4); m.pc <- t
       | Sys n -> env.sys m n)

(* the machine at its start: the image at 0, sp at the top of memory *)
let boot image =
  let m = { r = Array.make 16 0; pc = 0; mem = Bytes.make !memsize '\000' } in
  Bytes.blit_string image 0 m.mem 0 (String.length image);
  m.r.(sp) <- !memsize;
  m

(*****************************************************************************)
(* An image *)
(*****************************************************************************)

(* the memory's first bytes, no header: the CPU starts at 0 (tiny-linker
 * made it) *)
let image name text =
  if String.length text > !memsize then
    error "%s: larger than the memory" name;
  text

(* the listing: address, word, instruction, as assembly again *)
let listing ~show ~origin image =
  List.init (String.length image / 4) (fun k ->
    let w = Int32.to_int (String.get_int32_le image (4 * k)) land 0xffffffff in
    Printf.sprintf "%x:\t%08x\t%s\n" (origin + (4 * k)) w
      (match decode w, show w with
       | Some i, _ -> print (origin + (4 * k)) i
       | None, Some s -> s
       | None, None -> Printf.sprintf ".word\t0x%x" w))
  |> String.concat ""

(*****************************************************************************)
(* A profile *)
(*****************************************************************************)

(* Each instruction run, counted by where it was: the program's or the
 * kernel's (a mode), the base of the user's window (which program),
 * its address. Every instruction, not a sample: the machine is slow
 * enough for that to cost little more than running it, and two runs
 * give the same profile. *)
type profile = (int, int ref) Hashtbl.t

let profile () : profile = Hashtbl.create 4096

(* an env that counts each instruction it fetches; [where m] is its mode
 * (1 the kernel's, 0 a program's) and the window's base *)
let profiled (env : env) (p : profile) (where : machine -> int * int) =
  { env with fetch = (fun m pc ->
      let mode, base = where m in
      let k = (((base lsl 1) lor mode) lsl 32) lor (pc land 0xffffffff) in
      (match Hashtbl.find_opt p k with
       | Some n -> incr n
       | None -> Hashtbl.add p k (ref 1));
      env.fetch m pc) }

(* the profile as lines "k|u base pc count", the addresses in hexadecimal,
 * the most counted first *)
let profile_lines (p : profile) =
  let l = Hashtbl.fold (fun k n acc -> (k, !n) :: acc) p [] in
  let l = List.sort (fun (_, a) (_, b) -> b - a) l in
  String.concat "" (List.map (fun (k, n) ->
    Printf.sprintf "%c %x %x %d\n" (if (k lsr 32) land 1 = 1 then 'k' else 'u')
      (k lsr 33) (k land 0xffffffff) n) l)

tiny/TinyMachine/TinyMachineCPU.mli
11567
(* A tiny CPU of our own: its instruction set, its encoding, and an
 * interpreter; a CPU and its memory, no devices. The library of two
 * programs: TinyCPU.ml, the CPU run alone, its system calls answered
 * by the host; and TinyMachine.ml, the CPU with what a kernel needs
 * around it, its system calls traps. Knuth's road with MIX and MMIX:
 * when the machine is for teaching, design it; mini-5i (machine/)
 * emulates the machine history left us, this one the machine fifty
 * years of hindsight would draw.
 *
 * The machine is new, so nothing else writes its words: it comes with
 * its assembler, tiny-assembler (TinyAssembler.ml), and its linker,
 * tiny-linker (TinyLinker.ml), as MIX came with MIXAL, the notation
 * the book's programs are written in; mini-5i borrows a real
 * toolchain's, mini-asm's and mini-ld's. Both are kept small by the
 * machine's design: one format, every instruction 4 bytes, every
 * immediate its low 16 bits.
 *
 * The machine: 16 registers of 32 bits, r0 always 0 (a zero at hand
 * and a place to throw a result away, RISC-V's and MIPS's choice); a
 * byte-addressed memory of 2^20 bytes, the addresses taken modulo its
 * size (nothing faults), a word's two low address bits ignored (MMIX:
 * no alignment trap, and no alignment check either); no flags: a
 * branch compares two registers, slt makes a comparison a value (ARM's
 * flags are what an instruction set can do without). One format: an
 * 8-bit opcode, two 4-bit registers d and a, and a 16-bit immediate
 * whose low 4 bits name the third register of the three-register
 * instructions:
 *
 *     31      24 23  20 19  16 15                0
 *     |  opcode  |  d   |  a   |   immediate / b |
 *
 * add sub mul div rem and or xor shl shr sar slt sltu   d = a op b
 * addi andi ori xori shli shri sari slti sltiu        d = a op imm
 * lui                                                  d = imm << 16
 * ldw ldb stw stb                                      d, imm(a)
 * beq bne blt bge bltu bgeu                            d, a, label
 * jal jalr                                             d = pc + 4
 * sys                                                  imm: the call's number
 *
 * The immediate is signed but for andi, ori, xori (and lui); a shift
 * takes its amount modulo 32; a division by 0 gives -1 and leaves the
 * dividend as the remainder, and the one overflow (-2^31 / -1) gives
 * -2^31 and 0 (RISC-V's answers: an instruction set defines every
 * case). A system call takes its arguments in r1-r3 and answers in
 * r1 (what it does is the program's that runs the CPU). By
 * convention sp is r14 (the top of memory at the start), lr r15; the
 * assembler's pseudo-instructions: li, la (a value, an address: lui
 * and ori, or addi), mov, call, ret, j, nop.
 *
 * A program, and its listing (tiny-cpu -l: the address, the word, the
 * word decoded again):
 *
 *             li    r1, 3            0:   11100003   addi r1, r0, 3
 *     loop:   addi  r1, r1, -1       4:   1111ffff   addi r1, r1, -1
 *             bne   r1, r0, loop     8:   3110fffe   bne  r1, r0, 0x4
 *             li    r2, 0x12345678   c:   20201234   lui  r2, 0x1234
 *                                    10:  17225678   ori  r2, r2, 22136
 *             sys   0                14:  3f000000   sys  0
 *
 * A word reads off in hexadecimal, the format being cut at its
 * digits: 11 1 0 0003 is opcode 0x11 (addi), d 1, a 0, the immediate
 * 3. li is no instruction: a small value is an addi from r0, a large
 * one lui for the high half and ori for the low. A branch's immediate
 * is counted in words from the next instruction: from 0xc back to 4
 * is -2, fffe. Zero is no opcode, so memory never written stops a
 * program that runs into it.
 *
 * Who is around it:
 *
 *     .tm files: by hand (v0), by tiny-c, by tiny-ml
 *                  |  tiny-assembler, tiny-linker: an image
 *     this file:   the CPU ([step], given an [env]), the encoding
 *                  they use, the listing
 *                 /                          \
 *     TinyCPU: the env is memory and       TinyMachineDevices: the env is
 *     three calls of the host's            pages, devices and a trap;
 *                                          TinyMachine's and
 *                                          TinyMachineWeb's
 *
 * What makes it small:
 *
 * - {b The interpreter is the definition.} [step] is the machine's
 *   semantics, a match on the decoded word; memory holds the program,
 *   so a program may compute its code.
 * - {b A machine changes five things}, the fields of [env]: the fetch,
 *   a load, a store, a system call, and a word [decode] does not know.
 *   TinyCPU gives memory, the host's calls, and an error; a machine
 *   gives its pages, its devices behind addresses, a trap, and its own
 *   instructions (which the listing learns by a [show]). What
 *   happens between two instructions (an interrupt) is the loop's
 *   that calls [step], not [step]'s.
 * - {b The laws}: each program of TinyCPU_tests/ prints what is
 *   known otherwise (Python's answers); and a program's listing is
 *   assembly again, which reassembled gives the same words (print,
 *   parse, encode and decode agree; not for data, whose words may
 *   decode as instructions with bits the encoding ignores).
 *
 * Exercises, each cheap because the interpreter is the definition and
 * a machine changes the CPU only through env:
 * - a translator back (to arm32, as QEMU's): written once, 185 lines,
 *   then removed as a second topic (git history has it); the law, the
 *   same output interpreted and translated;
 * - a decode cache (threaded code): each word decoded once, into a
 *   closure kept by its address, and dropped when a store hits it;
 *   measure the speed against step;
 * - compressed instructions: 16-bit forms of the commonest (RISC-V's
 *   RVC), the density measured on tiny-kernel's programs, the listing's
 *   law checking them;
 * - a debugger by env: breakpoints as a word decode does not know,
 *   caught by illegal, the program's registers and memory then shown.
 *
 * The twin, mini-5i, keeps its decoded words too, by address (Cpu): a
 * program that wrote over its code would run the old one, and
 * mini-qemu's loop empties the cache when a mapping changes. Here they
 * are kept by the word itself ([keep_decoded], in the .ml), which no
 * store can make wrong. mini-5i also has a second execute for what a
 * kernel runs most, which allocates nothing (Arm32_fast), Arm32's
 * staying the definition; here [step] is both.
 *
 * cs-history:
 * Knuth designed MIX in the 1960s for The Art of Computer Programming
 * so that the book's programs would be real ones with costs one can
 * count, and tied to no manufacturer. It is a machine of its time: a
 * byte of 64 to 100 values so that it is neither binary nor decimal,
 * a sign apart from the magnitude, and a subroutine that returns by
 * storing its return address into its own last instruction. By the
 * 1990s no reader had seen such a machine, and he replaced it with
 * MMIX (1999), a RISC of 64 bits designed with advice from the
 * architects of MIPS and Alpha. The lesson kept here is
 * the first one: the machine a book is written for can be drawn to
 * fit the book.
 *
 * design:
 * Leaving out the flags removes a register that every instruction
 * writes and no instruction names. With them (ARM, x86) a comparison
 * and the branch that uses it are two instructions joined by hidden
 * state, which an interrupt must save and which a processor that
 * runs instructions out of order must rename like any register;
 * mini-5i's arm64 computes four of them at each s-instruction.
 * Without them (MIPS, Alpha, RISC-V, here) a branch reads two
 * registers, and a comparison kept for later is a value in a
 * register (slt). The price is on arithmetic wider than a register:
 * a carry is then computed, by an sltu, not found.
 *
 * design:
 * A register that is always zero costs one of sixteen and pays for
 * itself in opcodes not needed: mov is an addi of 0, li an addi from
 * r0, nop an addi into r0, a negation a sub from r0, a jump a jal
 * that throws its link into r0, and an absolute address (a device's,
 * a kernel's variable) an offset from r0, with no register to load
 * first.
 *
 * others:
 * The other machines drawn for a course: Hennessy and Patterson's
 * DLX (1990), MIPS with its accidents removed, the one this is
 * nearest to; Patt and Patel's LC-3, 16 bits and eight registers,
 * with flags; Nisan and Schocken's Hack, two kinds of instruction
 * and no call. RISC-V (Berkeley, 2010) began as a summer's project
 * for a laboratory's own research and courses, and is the case of an
 * academic machine that became an industry's.
 *
 * References: D. E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, vol. 1
 * (MIX, 1968; MMIX, fascicle 1, 2005): a machine designed to teach;
 * D. A. Patterson and J. L. Hennessy, the MIPS and RISC-V books: the
 * load-store machine; J. R. Bell, "Threaded Code" (CACM,
 * 1973); F. Bellard, "QEMU, a Fast and Portable Dynamic Translator"
 * (USENIX, 2005); A. Waterman, "Design of the RISC-V
 * Instruction Set Architecture" (PhD thesis, 2016), the
 * compressed instructions. *)

(* a word's 32 bits of an int that may have more; a < b, both unsigned
 * words *)
val m32 : int -> int
val ult : int -> int -> bool

(* The instructions and their words are TinyMachineISA's (a load's
 * size, sp and lr, the exception Error); its error, by a format *)
val error : ('a, unit, string, 'b) format4 -> 'a

(* the memory's size, a power of two (a host sets it before [boot]);
 * an address in the memory, and its word's *)
val memsize : int ref
val addr : int -> int
val word : int -> int

(* the CPU: sixteen registers, a pc, the memory's bytes *)
type machine = { r : int array; mutable pc : int; mem : Bytes.t }

(* what is around it, the host's or a machine's: how a word is
 * fetched, loaded and stored (plain memory, or pages and devices),
 * what a sys does, and a word the CPU does not know *)
type env = {
  fetch : machine -> int -> int;
  load : machine -> TinyMachineISA.size -> int -> int;
  store : machine -> TinyMachineISA.size -> int -> int -> unit;
  sys : machine -> int -> unit;
  illegal : machine -> int -> unit;
}

(* plain memory's load and store, and the env of a program alone *)
val load : machine -> TinyMachineISA.size -> int -> int
val store : machine -> TinyMachineISA.size -> int -> int -> unit
val plain : sys:(machine -> int -> unit) -> env

(* The interpreter: one instruction; and a machine with an image at 0 *)
val step : env -> machine -> unit
val boot : string -> machine

(* An image: a file's bytes, checked to fit in the memory (its name,
 * for the error); its listing, the words a machine adds by [show]
 * (TinyMachineDevices.show) *)
val image : string -> string -> string
val listing : show:(int -> string option) -> origin:int -> string -> string

(* A profile: every instruction run, counted by where it was (the
 * kernel's or a program's, the base of the user's window, the address).
 * [profiled env p where] is env counting into p, [where m] the mode (1
 * the kernel's, 0 a program's) and the window's base; [profile_lines p]
 * the counts as lines "k|u base pc count" (hexadecimal addresses), the
 * most counted first, which tiny-prof reads (TinyProfiler.mli).
 * tiny-cpu's -prof and tiny-machine's write them. *)
type profile
val profile : unit -> profile
val profiled : env -> profile -> (machine -> int * int) -> env
val profile_lines : profile -> string
